GIVING THANKS. Oir hay is all saved, and our wheat is all reaped, Our corn is all garnered, our barns are all heaped; Thanksgiving! thanksgiving! For the sun and the dew and the bountiful rain, For the honey aud fruit, for the nourishing grain, For the rose and the song, let us render again Thanksgiving! thanksgiving! For the quick tide of trade that gives life to our land, For the skill and the wealth of the working man's hand, Thanksgiving ! thanksgiving! For the brains that have toiled with some wonderful thought, For the dreams that the artist ana poet have caught, For the old fight with evil so patteatfr fought, Thanksgiving! thanksgiving! For the homes that with trLiest affect" • are b Where love neS lest, ties - • ...du like a bird in its nest, • Thanksgiving! thanksgiving! Por the worth and the will that have made us so free, For our beautiful land from sea unto sea, 0 God of our fathers, we give unto Thee Thanksgiving! thanksgiving —Leeds Weekly Mercury.

" reloimation—of character. Faith, says Augustine, is to believe what we do not see, and the reward of this faith is to see what we believe. There is nothing that weighs more heavily upon a right- minded man than the slow progress he makes in overcoming

his faults. One of the illusions is that the present hour is not the critical, decisive hour. Write it on your heart that every day is the best day in the year.—Drterson. Very concise verdict that of a coroner's jury in Idaho, and racy of the soil—" We find that the deceased came to ifis death by calling Tom Watlings a liar." The number of different languages and dialects spoken in , the known world is 2,623, of which 51 belong to Europe, 196 to Asia, 376 to Africa, and 1,264 to America. Nobody likes to be nobody, but everybody is certainly pleased to think himself somebody; and everybody is some- body. But, when anybody thinks himself to be somebody, he generally thinks everybody else to be nobody. We have often had to wait for the slaking, but it has never failed to come, and the lesson of this waiting is one that it becomes u 3 to study and apply to many things besides the return of spring. It is harder to wait than to work. The widow of i French chemist, famous for his researches in toxicology, was on trialefor poisoning her husband. It was proved that arsenic was the medium employed. "Why did you use that poison?" asked the presiding -magistrate. " BiCause," sobbed the fair culprit, "it was the one he

liked best." At the Egyptian War Exhibition, London, the most -^enler object of intereet ie a Bible which intercepted a shot and saved te", :Z. 31 a soldier. It is a remarkable fact that there has hardly been an English war for a whole con- wry in which a Bible or a Testament has not played the same useful part. NINE YEARS wergoter A BCIRTAL.—An ancient record was found, some years ago, at Alton, in the Vale of Pewsey, Wilts, of which the following ie a copy :—" In nine yeares together, front the years Of Our Lord 1592, unto the years 1601, there was (God be thanked) neyther man, woman, or child buried in this parysh," " Wife, bring me some cold beef," stid a shiftless husband, when, for the first time in his life he discovered that he was more hungry than thirsty. "There is no beef in the house," was the mild reply." Fetch me some pork, then." "No pork, either." "Well, then, let me have some potatoes." "Not a potatoe left." "Thunder and lightning! get some bread, then." "The bread is all gone, too." "Well, then, give me a knife and fork, and let me go through the motions." AN ARTIST'S ADVICE TO HIS PUPIL.—" Look at the best drawings for corroboration and encouragement. Avoid bad works as you would fly from evil. Come back again to nature, again and again, and you will have the greatest comfort. Work, work, work is the word, both with head and hand. We cannot get anything good and true and beautiful without going through suffering for it; and work . is the price we must pay for all enjoyment we may have from the divine art of painting."—Good Words .for October. A CHINESE EXECUrtos.—The following terrible mode of punishment is peculiar to the criminal code of China. In 18.50 a Chinese merchant at Amoy, convicted of the murder of his wife, was condemned to die by the total deprivation of sleep. The condemned was placed in prison, under the surveillance of three guardians, who relieved each other every alternate hour, and who prevented the criminal from taking any sleep night or day. At the commencement of the eighth day his sufferings were so great that he begged to be killed by strangulation, and the terrible request was carried into execution. RESTITUTION.—It is said to be susceptible of proof that a gentleman, who had taken up his summer quarters with his family in a pretty village remote from London, recently purchased seven pounds of sugar from his family grocer, and found it sadly adulterated with sand. Next day he in- serted the following in the village paper:—" Notice.—l bought of a grocer in this village seven pounds of sugar, from which I have extracted one pound of sand. If the rascal who cheated me will send to this office seven pounds of sugar (the Scriptural measure of restitution) I will be satisfied. If not, I will expose him." The next day nine seven-pound packages of sugar were left at the newspaper eke, there being nine grocers in the village. FIXING THE TITLE.—A. good story is told of Dr. Newman Hall, of London, which we do not remember to have seen in print. It has had quite an extensive private circulation, having gone from mouth to mouth in a quiet way, and it has excited merriment whenever told. Dr. Hall is, as is well known in religions circles, the author of a tract entitled "Come to Jesus," the circulation of which by the Tract Society has been simply enormous, the copies printe.l run- ning up beyond the hundreds of thousands into the six ciphers. Some very severe criticisms had been passed upon him on account of his words or conduct, and he became greatly excited over them, and replied, or rather wrote a reply replete with sarcasm and bitterness, and carried it to Dr. Binney, of London, since dead, for suggestion and. ap- proval. Dr. Hall read it, bringing out the bitter things with peculiar emphasis, and when he had finished he said, "Well, Dr. Binney, how do you like it ?" "Oh," was the careful reply, "I think it is remarkably well written, and ;here are many slurp and biting things in it. By the way, Hll,hioe you fixed npon a title for it as yet ?" "No, I hive not," replied Dr. gall. ‘` Peelia2e you can assist me in that matter." Then Dr. Binnev said slowly and. Miber, at,dy—" While you. were reading some of thoee hard hits it oceerred to me that this would be a good title,' Go to the Devil,' by the author of Come to Jesus.' " It is needless to say that the hot-tempered manuscript was never printed —indeed, theztery goes that it was torn up in Dr. Binney's study. THE BEST BRANDS —An invalid, gradually recovering from an attack of sickness which had left him very weak, was recommended by his physician to rub himself all over every night on going to bed with brandy, as a means of re- gaining his strength. Accordingly he sent to his family grocer, with whom he had dealt for years, and ordered a quantity of the very best " old cognac," after applying which for several successive nights he felt much better. So he continued the process until one morning, to his horror, he found his entire cuticle of a deep crimson colour—darker by a good many shades than boiled lobster. Springing up in alarm, he roused the family, and the doctor was sent for in haste. The doctor could hardly forbear smiling when he saw the ludicrous appearance of his patient, Viet, finding the sick man and his family deeply alarmed, he sobered his reaibles and asked," Has he rubbed himself every night, as I ordered ?"—" Yes, faithfully."—" The best of brandy ? " —" Yes, Doctor, the very best; we never use any other."— "Let me see it."—So the bottle was brought, the doctor tasted it, shook his head, and, thinking a moment, said: "I'll take it home and analyse it—there are so many tricks among liquor dealers."—" oh, no fear of that with our gro- cer. He sells none but the very beat; imports them all directly himself."—" Well, I'll look into it."—And, calming the family fears, the good doctor departed, taking the pure old cognac in his pocket. In a short time a note from him was handed in: "Dear L—,—Make yourself perfectly easy; the cognac is only whisky, and won't hurt you. It was the logwood in it that gave you the brilliant coloar."— garper's Monthly. SAVED BY A PORTMANTEAU.—At Georgivo, a straggling Danubian town in Ronmania, I had hired a three-b", 5 drosky to take me from that place along the bank; of the Danube as far as Zimnitza. We started of enthusiasm for the front. The weather was cle,e,,e, but intensely cold, so much so that our furs, thick as they were, seemed quite unequal to the oecaelon, and we were obliged to swing our arms and legs about in the wildest contortions to keep Jack Frost at a distance. If it be the custom of Grand Dukes to thus assert themselves, or if Russian generals are given to such antics, I know not: but true it is that we attracted direct attention from the Turkish outworks near Rustchuck, two shells being sent unpleasantly near us. The horses be- came unmanageable, and got eo helplessly mixed and en. tangled that some moments elapsed before we were again on the way. Our stoppage had given the gunners a steadier aim. Another all-too-familiar boom, a prolonged screech, and then the crash of a shell, which seemed to lift us from oar seats, and throw us and our already scared steeds into, if possible, greater confusion than before. This last shot had the effect of 90 startling the horses that, haying at first plunged to a considerable extent, they started off in head- long flight, soon taking us round a corner, and so out of sight of the enemy. Arriving at Zimnitza we decided on re- maining there for the night, and crossing by the now his- toric bridge of boats into Bulgaria in the morning. This being the case, I went in quest of some necessaries which I wanted from my portmanteau, that had served as a back to my seat on the drosky during our journey. Imagine my astonishment to find it smashed, and its contents mulched into a confused mass within ! That shell had struck home rather closer than I at the time had any notion of—my life having been saved by that well-packed valise. All that re- mains is now much treasured by my wife, who has astonished more than one servant at the care she takes of "that there old portmanter, as she wouldn't be seen a-carryin' on no account."—" Good Words" for October. A teacher having asked his pupils one day, " What is the worst side of naval warfare ?" one little fellow shouted, the broad-side, sir !" RELIGIOUS BODIES.—There are said to be no fewer than 180 denominations or sects in England. Thirteen new bodies were registered last year at Somerset House. and these include "Army of the King's Own," "Christian Pioneers," "Holiness Army," "Hosanna Army," "Royal Gospel Army," and "Salvation Navy." A darkey on Pecano Plantation not long since was much tried by the obstinacy of a mule. After much urging and kindness toward the brute, he broke out with, "Look hyer, now! mebby you think 'cause I jined the church last Sun- day that I can't use big words; but I'll hab you know I'm gwine make a special 'ception in your case." An Irishman not long since was summoned before a bench of county magistrates for being drank and disorderly. "Do you know what brought you here ?" was the question put to him. "Faix, yer honour, two policemen," replied the Prisoner. "Had not drink something to do with bringing you here ?" said the magistrate, frowning. "Sortinly," answered Paddv, unabashed; "they were both drunk." "Au," said the worthy old Mrs. Stubbs, as she stood stare ing at a placard on which was inscribed "Youth Wanted" ‘ Yes I de-"a3'• Most on us who have got a bit oldish, as y say, might carry a ticket about with Youth wanted' mnteda'yprTted on it. But what with old Father Time, and what with troubles and trials, most of us will have to go on saying'Youth wanted' I expect, for a long time to come." A minister and his wife having called at a hospitable farmhouse and stayed to dinner, a fine hen turkey was killed and served up at table. All the company partook of it ex- cept the youngest boy, who persistently refused to eat any. After dinner most of the party, including the parson, were shown round the yard, and were soon engaged in admiring the cattle, horses, &c. Just as they were passing the fowl run, the whole brood of little turkeys came running out and began to follow the party. At last they made such a noise, that the small boy turned round and called out indignantly, and loud enough for all to hear, " Ye need na' come yam- smering at me! I did na' eat yer mother !"

Compactness of territory and great diversity of soil, coupled with the enterprise of the settlers, have there- fore made the colony, which is perhaps best known to the outside world as the gold colony, also a thriving farming community. Everything points to grazing and agriculture of various sorts becoming more and more the mainstay of this land. The figures which I have given at the com- mencement of this letter attest that there is an extensive tract still untouched, and with this available and the most that can be got made of that which at present is in the hands of the private holder, there would seem to be scarcely any limit to the success of Victoria's producing industry. Many of those selectors who have hitherto applied themselves mainly to growing cereals are now combining grazing with cultivation so that the yield of wool and hides and the supply of beef and mutton are calculated to increase. There is naturally a great amount of interest taken by the pastor- alists in the trade of frozen meat now being established be- tween Australia and England. First small girl: I know what I'm going to be when I grow up !" Second ditto: "What are you going to be when you grow up ?" First small girl: "A widder." Teacher: "Define the word excavate." Scholar: "It means to hollow out." Teacher: "Construct a sentence in which the word is properly used." Scholar: "The baby excavates when it gets hurt." A teacher, defining a transitive verb as one that expresses an action which is "passed over" from the doer, gave, for illustration, "The dog wags his tail," whereupon a younster rose with the criticism, "Please, ma'am, the action don't pass over; it stays in the dog." A child, while walking through an art gallery with her mother, was attracted by a statue of Minerva. "Who is that ?" said she. "My child, that is Minerva, the goddess of wisdom." "Why didn't they make her husband, too?" 1" Because she had none, my child." "That was because ' she was wise, wasn't it, mamma ?" was the artless reply. "I am an agnostic !" remarked a young man, in swelling accents. "And an agnostic is what?" inquired an elderly gentleman. "An agnostic," replied the fresh youth, in a manner expressive of his pity for his interlocutor's ignor- ance, "an agnostic is a fellow, you know, who isn't sure of anything." I see," replied the old gentleman; "but how does it happen that you are sure you are an agnostic ?" A little bright-eyed boy, upon hearing his father read the story of Joan of Arc, was greatly moved by her sad trials; but when the part was reached where she was about to be burned to death at the stake, the poor little fellow could not contain himself any longer, but sobbingly clutched his father's arm, and with big tears running down his plump ittll cheeks, cried," But, pa-papa, wh-e-re were the police?"

COTTAGE GARDENING.

Cauliflowers, if sown as advised, will now be sufficiently advanced to require pricking out 3in. or 4in. each way, and in beds 4ft. wide, elevating the centre of the bed as advised for lettuce. Thousands of plants survive the winter in this way in some parts, by simply elevating a shutter over them, or an old light to throw oil the wet. If a small frame is at the disposal of the cottager, he cannot do better than use it to protect lettuce and cauliflowers, and in that case the formation of the bed must be changed from the convex to a declivity from the back to the front. The best soil in the garden should be put in the frame, till it is within 6in, of the glass. It will be obvious that the bed will be several inches above the level of the ground, and this assists to keep them in a drier medium than they would otherwise be. The light is best left on the plants day and night till it be found that they will not flag. POTA'TOF.S,—Look over those stored for seed or for eon.l - • ; . --e sumptdon, as a ca.• communicate the disease to all that it may come in contatt with The late ones are now as well out of the ground, and should be dug forthwith. The gale of Sunday night and that of Weduesday wrought mischief amongst fruit trees. Several val:„es that would have remained on the trees for some days longer are strewn on the ground in all directions, and utterly worthless for storing. Wind is most disastrous for fruit. From the oscillation of the branches the fruit is first knocked against each other. When it falls it comes in con- tact with the branches, and finally with the hard ground, so that it is almost a jelly. Where the fence of the vegetable garden is a hedge, this is an appropriate time to see to it and cut it. All the trim- mings and other rubbish should be burnt, and the ashes spread over the garden. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The beauty of the tender subjects in this department is passed. There are a few hardy plants that still look bright. Anemone japonica seems to defy the wind and the pelting rain, so does chrysanthemum leucan- themum. They and the following should be in every gar- den—phloxes, lupines, pensternons, harpalium rigidum, which looks like a miniature sunflower, and pyrethrums, all of which will continue to flower for some time. Geraniums should now be taken up, and have all their leaves stripped off except two or three of the smaller ones at the points of the shoots. They may then be potted or packed together in boxes with sufficient soil, which should be half sand, to cover the roots. They will not require any water for some week, not till the material becomes dust dry. The best place for them for a time will be underneath an open shed, where the air can play round them and dry the superfluous sap out of them. All that is required to preserve these over the winter is to keep them dry and from the reach of frost. I Those who grow pansies for exhibition should look out for some good light loam, such as the topmost 2in. or 3in. from an old pasture; add a fourth of two-year-old manure and mix them well, allowing it to remain in a heap for two or three months, when it might again be turned when it is frozen. Six or eight inches of this dug into the bed before planting will make an excellent pansy bed. Arum lilies or calla that May have been planted out should be taken up and potted ino as small foot; es thfv can be got into, and when potting is completed give a good soaking f.. 4 water, always keeping them in a tolerably moist condition. They I may still remain outside till there are signs of frost. tHa WINOOW.—HYA.CINTIIS.—That easily grown plant, the Hyacinth, may now be potted, in a compost made up of light loam and a quarter decayed manure and a sixth of silver or river sand. Five-inch pots are sufficiently large for them, and they should be thoroughly cleaned, especially inside, Place a crock or an oyster shell over the the bottom of the pot, and on that small p`:,./ales of crocks to the depth of one. inch, and s9lO of the rougher portion lOf the soil over the Crocks. Partially decayed leavea answers the same purpose, which is to prevent the small I particles of soil from mixing up with the crocks and ob- structing the free passage of water. The pots are now I ready to be filled with the soil, which should be slightly pressed, adding more if required, and the bulb may then be placed on the top, and pressed with the forefinger and thumb of each hand, pressing the soil also moderately firm round the bulb, so that one-fonrth of it will be above the soil. Water will not be required if the soil is moderately moist. The pots may be placed on a hard surface outside, so that there is no possibility of worms entering them; or they may be placed in a cellar; or a dark cupboard not too warm. In this case we should procure a box and place the pots in covering them over Sin, deep with sand or ashes. These and COCOA nut fibre are the best materials for cover- ing indoors or out, and those outside should have a thicker covering, also a few b oarde or a sheet of zinc or iron to throw off the wet. In seven or eight weeks' time, it will be as well to uncover them to see if they have grown suf- ficiently to be taken out. Should they only be starting to push, they had better be left covered for two or three weeks longer, as it is ruinous to bring them ta the light before there are any roots, which there cannot be, if there is no top. BATON (BRADS:TAW-GATE). —An exciting Contest was played at Wargrave Mom, Earlestown on Saturday afternoon last, between the first teams of these two clubs. Though the weather was showery there was a comparatively large attendance of spectators, who manifested the greatest in- terest throughout the match. The toss was won by the visitors. who chose ti play against the wind the first half. Dageall kieked off for Earlestown, and a Visit was at once paid to the Bolton quarters. A determined atlack was made upon the goal. and after about 15 minutes play Ogden be4aied the lath,te through the uprights. The yi'dWrA (pliekly retaliated, and ! after pressing their opponents for a short time R. Wood suc- cee led in equalising the score. Toe Earlestonians again pressed the B,ltonlans, the home forwards playing remarkably well. Several exciting scrimmages occnrred near the Bolton goal, but the defenders prevented any additi n to the Earlestown score. Ends were clisnged at half time with the score at one goal each No sooner had the leather been re-started than the home for- wards again secured possession of the ball and Dagnall added a second goal after a clever run up the field amid the hearty cheers of the spectators. 'Not to be denied. however, the visitors .put forth every effort to equalise matters, and amid increasing excitement Gorse succeeded in scor- ing a second goal for Bolton. For a long time afterwards the game was of a very fast and even character, but towards the flaida Earlestown pr -ailed their opponents severely, and had many attempte to scare. The leather was several times kicked against the cross-bar and uprights. but only two more goals were scored, Rich and Mather each sending the bail through the posts. The home team played remarkably well throughout the match, and the victory for Earlestown by four goals to two was hard-won and well deserved. The teams were :—Earlestown : J. Appleton, goal: R. div.head: COMPLAII:P.
div.p: A COMPLAII:P.

Mr. Nash, Heatley, wrote the Board drawing their atten- tion to the fact that loads of hay were left on the green in front of his house, sometimes during the night and occa- sionally during the day. Having without success reade efforts to stop the nuisance, he was now obliged to appeal to the Board.—Mr. Mort (nuisance inspector) was instructed to see that no obstruction was caused to the highway at the point referred to.

div.head: LOCKING UP A GAS METER.
div.p: LOCKING UP A GAS METER.

The CLERK said that the gas manager had taken the record of the meters, as usual, with the exception of One belonging to Mr. Callender (a member of the Board), which lockPti up The gas manager hal been no less than five times to taktJ the record of the meter but had been unable to get the key. The Act of Parliament said that any person preventing at any reasonable time free access to the meter was liable to £5. The meter being locked up stopped the book being balanced a it ought to Was resoiVed that Mr. Callender's attention be -drawn to the requirements of the Act:

COMPELLED TO PAY TWO RATES. Mr. THOMASON complained that the members of his place of worship had been compelled to pay two rates. They had paid the rate for the house in New-road which their minister, who had just removed from the circuit, had occupied, but in addition to that they also had had to pay the rate for another house which their new minister had taken. He did not see that they should pay the rate for another house in the same village. He also complained that the house was assessed at more than Its value.—lt was pointed out that the Board could not lawfully take any action in the matter of the two rates.—Mr. THOMASON said that whatever the law was, it was obviously unfair that they should have to pay two rates.—With regard to the assessment of the house it was ultimately agreed to make the necessary reduction.

div.head: PROGRESS OF THE SEWERAGE WORKS.
div.p: THE PROGRESS OF THE SEWERAGE WORKS.

Messrs. WILSON and MuLLINEa (the Board's engineers) I reported that the bridge at Statham Pools was now practi- cally complete, and the approaches thereto had progressed so far as to allow the traffic to be carried over. The canal alteration was nearly complete, and the shafts only required to be finished. The piers for carrying the iron pipes be- tween the canal and the flour mill were also complete, and ready for the iron founders to fix them. They had had appointments with the assistant engineer to the London and North-Western Railway Company; and the railway culvert over Sow Bridge was now in progress. Mr. Worthington, the company's engineer, had certain conditional stipulations in the order to proceed with the construction of the culvert which would rather increase the amount given in to this work by the contractor. Whitbury-lane, Statham-lane, and Thelwall-road had now been put in order, and the paving relaid or nearly so. They had investigated the pools at the rising of the flood ; at Statham Pools it had risen to the level of the sewer pipes, and as there was at the junction of Statham-lane sewer a few yards unconnected the water was flowing through the pipes to the outfall. The flood water was then only beginning to cover the meadows adjoining Lastly Brook. On their inspection on Monday they found that the flood pools had been 1 foot 8 inches above the planks of the bridge or 8 feet above the ordinary level. There were places where the fenders had been damaged and partially lowered by cattle. THE LOAN OF £7,000.
It was resolved to apply to the Public Works Loan Com- missioners for 1:1,580, the remaining balance of the loan of £7,000 granted for the sewerage works.
ANOTHER CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.

The Rey. George Dickinson made a claim on the Board for £25, compensation for a sewer passing through his field. The sewer far same distance was raised two feet, and the reason why ha claimed this sum was that he had proposed to build himself a house on that land.—The matter was left over. There was no other business of interest.
NOTES ON A.GRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &e.

A LEVERET IN A WHEAT Suzer.—During the working of one of the new Howard sheaf-binding reaping machines in a crop of wheat on Mr. C. Harrison's farm at Fulford, near York, a leveret was caught by the gathering reel, lifted on to the platform of the machine, taken up the elevator, bound tightly in the wheat sheaf, and, singularly enough, when released, appeared little the worse for the exraordi- nary occurrence. BLINKERS.—Mr. PhiUpson, of the Northumberland Carri- age and Harness Manufactory, Newcastle, writes :—" The North-Eastern Railway Company and the Midland Railway Company are working all their horses (about 8,000) without wilikers, bearing reins, or cropper docks, and they cannot at- tach a single accident to the want of winkers—indeed, they think it has been a great safeguard, and the horses do their work so much more pleasantly." In London the proportion of the horses used without blinkers is very rapidly in- creasing, both in cabs, omnibuses, and railway vans, and all these horses appear to do their work quite as well and quite as safely as those do which wear blinkers. LORD KENSINGTON, M.P., AND THE IMPORTATION OF , CATTLE.—Replying to a resolution of the Welsh miners' protesting against the existing tariffs on foreign cattle and sheep imports, Lord Kensington, M.P., writes—" I under- stand you to refer to orders and regulations respecting the slaughter of cattle at ports of landing. All such regula- tions are either directly or,indirectly under the Privy Coun- cil, or the local authorities acting under the power given them by Acts of Parliament. I am in favour of as little restriction as possible on any trade that would supply food for the people, but, at the same time, precaution must be taken against the introduction of disease amongst the flocks and herds of the country." AN INDIAN AGRICULTURAL Strow.—The Iroquois Indi- ans on the Caughnawaga reserve will shortly hold their first great exhibition in agriculture and their own native indus- tries. Among the novelties introduced in the prize list will be competitions for the best papoose, for the best display of bead and fancy work, for the best collection of Indian an- tiquities, and for the best basket work. Among the prizes in the agricultural department will be some for the best set of agricultural implements, the best team of horses, thebest eggs and butter, &o. Following the example of the attrac- tions at the past exhibitions in Montreal, the Indians are arranging for a number of outside attractions during the time of their exhibition, among which will be canoe races, war danees, and a lacrosse tournament, in which the Caugh- nowagas will cross sticks with teams from all the other Indian reserves in Canada. RABBITS ATTACKING A STOAT.-.-011 August 25th, writes a correspondent, while standing near a house, in the grounds of which is an immense rabbit warren, I was attracted by the scream of a rabbit about a hundred yards off, and, know- ing that stoats were numerons, I ran as hard as I could towards the place from whence the sounds of distress pro- ceeded. As I expected, I saw a full grown rabbit in the clutches of a stoat, which had nearly killed him. While thinking how I could best circumvent the stoat, to my sur- prise a second rabbit appeared, which immediately rushed at the stoat, and knocked him literally head over heels off the first rabbit's back, persuing him until he disappeared into an adjoining hush, when he returned to his now dead companion and sniffed him all over, evidently comprehend- ing the catastrophe. In about a minute the stoat again appeared, creeping cautiously forward, but was a second time obliged to take to his heels, pursued by the rabbit open mouthed. On coming back again to his defunct friend the latter saw me and made off, the stoat doing ditto, hotly pursued this time by me; he, however, saved himself by diving into a hole. A FARMER ON DECIMATS.—Mr. Buckmaster told a good story in the course of a lecture which he delivered at Cro- mar the other day. He said :—Farmers sometimes spend as much as represents two-thirds of their rent in artificial manures and feeding-stuffs. A Wiltshire farmer told me he was a good deal interested in this, as he spent £6OO a year in artificials. I said "That's a large sum; I hope you have a guarantee." " Oh," he replied, "leave me alone for that; I'll guarantee 'em. Fast, I look at it; and then I smell it" I said, "Is that all ?" "Well," he said, "if I have any doubt about it I asks for a table that tells you what it is all made up of." The farmer produced a table—the analysis —which was this: "Moisture, 18." That I told him was water. Then there was "inorganic matter, containing nitrogen, equal to 2:41 of ammonia." I asked him what that meant, and he replied, "I know. I took a little of that manure in the shovel, and it was all moving about like rot- ten cheese." I said "Oh!" "Yes," he answered, adding, "Don't you think them was the decimals ?" I see one Nor- folk gentleman, writing to a Norfolk paper, complains that this was not in good taste before an audience of farmers. But surely farmers are not so thin-skinned as not to be able to bear a good joke at the expense of one of their class.

A little fellow more accustomed to contemplate the "cruet" than the changes of the seasons, being asked one day to name the four seasons of the year, answered, "Pep- per, salt, vinegar, and mustard." They are now telling a story about a Chicago girl who insisted upon throwing her shoe after a newly married couple. The carriage is a total wreck; a doctor has the bride and the horse under treatment, and large numbers of men are searching the ruins for the coachman. MANCHESTER ELECTION: RESULT OF POLL.—The lin at Manchester, on Thursday, resulted in the defeat of Dr. Pankhurst, the Independent Radical candidate, by a majority of 11,972 votes. The numbers were—For Mr. Holdsworth, the Conservative candidate, 18,188; Dr. Pank- burst, 6,216. "Grant me, 0 Lord," said a humble soul, " that I may pass unnoticed through the world," This should be the wish, or rather the aim, of all true devotion. Small virtues require the praise of Man to sustain them, just as little children require encouragement to walk or stand alone. But true virtue goes quietly through the world, scattering good around, and, performing noble deeds, without even the knowledge that what it does is heroic. MISCELLANN /Lid; The number of visitors to the Fisheries Exhibiann from . the Opening has reached the total of 2,000,000. strike against fleeting in winter began On Monday among the members of the Hull Trawl Fishernien's e Ten persons were injured, though none seriously, by an -ar•Cident at the Waverley station, Edinburgh, on Saturday 'morning. Another incendiary fire occurred on Saturday at Mr. Stone's farm, near Rochester. A stack valued at £lOO was destroyed. A domestic servant named Mary Louisa Jones, late in ser- vice in Chelsea, who was bitten by a cat in May last, has died from hydrophobia Burgan, the absconding manager of the Union Bank, Bir- mingham, has been apprehended at Havre on board a Steamer bound for South America. A great strike of steel and ironworkers of Glamorganshire against a reduction of 10 per cent. took niece on Monday. It Is Said that from 10,000 to 15,000 men are out. Snow fell heavily en Saturday and again on Sunday on the Grampian and other ranges of Scotland, and on Monday the higher mountains were white as in winter. Canon Scott, vicar of St. Mary's, Hull, has been appointed vicar of St. John's, Leeds. The applicants for the living, Which is worth .£ooo_per annum, numbered over 200. Mr. William Strickland, one of the borough auditors of Leeds, was remanded at the police court in that town-on Tuesday, charged with misappropriation of trust funds. A destructive fire took place at the Belle-vue Gardens, Manchester, on Tuesday morning, by which a large por- tion of the scenic reprssentation of the battle of Tel-el- ICebir was burnt. Speaking at Eastbourne on Saturday night, Mr. Booth, of the blue ribbon band, said that Mr. Gladstone had "pro- mised to iutroduce and support local option in a bill to be introduced next session." John Shields, aged 17, teacher at Fleetham-street Board School Middhsburough, committed suicide on Monday by hanging himself in a hayloft. Two bottles labelled laud- anum were by his side. It is stated that on Saturday defalcations were discovered amounting to nearly £3,000 on the part of a "confidential elerk " employed by Messrs. James and Lister Lea, auc- tioneers, of Birmingham. At Brentford, on Saturday, Hannah Longdon, 20, was charged with murdering her illegitimate child at Boston House, Brentford, while in the service of Colonel Stracey Clitherow. She was committed for trial. Through the breaking of a chain, by which six men were being lowered into a coal pit, at Tyldesley, on Tuesday raonaing, the ceze fell to the bottom, a distance of nearly 200 yards. All the occupants were killed. TEE DEFAULTING BARRISTER'S CLERK, DANES, was brought before the Birmingham magistrates on Saturday, and remanded for a week. The prisoner is charged with forgery and embezzlement. It is stated that his defalcations amount to i.',2,C00. Captain Drayer essayed to cross the Channel from Dover to Calais on Tuesday evening in the miniature paddle-boat exhibited by him at the Fisheries Exhibition, South Ken- afrigton. The attempt was, however, unsuccessful, the boat °slog beaten back by the surf and damaged. THE ALLEGED FORGERY AT BIRMINGHAM.—At Birming- ham, on Monday, Albert Westbury, saddler, Easy-row, was brought up on remand charged with forging the accep- tances to two bills of exchange on the Birmingham and Midland Bank: He was committed to the assizes. A BURGLAR IN A POLICEMAN'S lIOUSE.—At Leicester, °n Monday, John Cummitegs, who said he came from Man- Chester, was committed for trial charged with burglary. It aPPeared that seven houses in the town had been entered during Saturday nieht, the last being that of a policeman, Who Pursued and caught Cummings. e A NEW RAILWAY FOR THE ISLE OF MAN.—Arrangements nave been made for the prompt carrying out of the works of the Douglas, Laxey, and Ramsey Railway in the Isle of ;,..14,413. This line will complete the railway circuit of the 'laud, connecting Douglas, the•chief town, with the rich mines of Laxey, the beautiful Dhnon glen, and other charm- s_ulg scenery of the east coast, and the rising and important meval of Ramsey. ▪ STRANGE PROCEEDINGS OF A VISITOR—Edward Collins, hairdresser, was on Monday remanded at the Marylebone Police Court, charged with cutting the throat of the butler If.t A house in Harley-street. Collins visited the butler on Saturday night, and early on Sunday morning the la tkr was found in his room bleeding from a wound in the thrat and trotn what he said Collins was arrested. The injured man 18 lYing in hospital. ATTEMPTED MURDER.—Joseph Simber, wheelwright, was e'ommitted, at Wednetbury, on Tuesday, for trial at the assizes, charged with attempting to murder Charles Burner, foreman at a factory, He was instructed to do some work Thich exaeperated him, and he dec:ared that he would mur- QS( Burner, at whose head he aimed a blow with a mallet. desperate struggle followed, and two men who went to tuner's assistance were badly injured. e. The prisoner took an infant child of Alfred Culleen from its bed, wrapped Merely in a shawl, and walked with it from Oldham to !.10.0chdale, where she "gave it away" to a man named lt, in whose possession the babe was found next day. It bad suffered greatly from cold and exposure. Gibbons was committed for trial at the sessions. lb:Mennen DRATH.—A singular accident occurred at Wrexham on Saturday night A collier named William wiiiie ;ntoxicated quarrelled with his wife, and turned4ther and the children out of the house. e hen appears to have gone upstairs for Some purpose, ntying a lighted paraffin lamp in his hand. In returning, '8 auPposed, he slipped and fell. The lamp was broken, aod the oil pouring aver him he was soon in a blaze, and lras burnt to death. It was elso found that his skull was "sreatured. c Tun POACHING AFFRAY NEAR WARWICK. Essex and Vann, who nu been previously convicted, were sentenced to six months' t'ard labour each, and Bastock and E lnev to three months. At the evening meeting Mr. Parnell did not reside, as had been expected, and Mr. T. P. O'Connor again _°ie the chair. Mr. Sexton, M.P., was the principal neaker. Resolutions were passed expressing unabated con- °le nee in Mr. Parnell, and pledaing the meeting to adopt a 13°Iic7 calculated to advance Irish interests. AN ABSCONDING ORDERLY AND THE PARCEL Posy.— Zrard Farmer, commanding officer's orderly at the Bir- a...angbam barracks, has absconded with a cheque which had irtl drawn for the payment of the wages to one of the ;3°l's of the 11th Hassars. Farmer disappeared on Satur- day, but at first it was not suspected that he had absented eina,seif with a fraudulent intent, his character hitherto ia teytng been an exemplary one. div.p: The prisoner O'Donnell received £3OO from America on Tuesday for his defence. • _ _ _ _

IA mill, in Woodbine-street, RoclacWe, occapied by Mr. William Pilling, was destroyed by fir? pn Thursday. The IlotS i 8 Uttimatea at a...11J £lO,OOO. Alderman Avery, to whom the dispute between hi: South Staffordshire irenworkers and their employers was referred, has given his decision in favour of the sliding scale. A reward of £lOO is offered for the apprehension of Mr. George Warden, secretary of the London and River Plate Bank, who has absconded. His defalcations are reported to amount to .£llO,OOO. The strike of weavers at Ashton-under-Lyne was partially renewed on Thursday, when about 1,500 hands turned out from two mills, on the ground that the employers have not complied with the terms on which work was resumed. ' FOUR CHILDREN AT A BIRTIL—At Blackburn, early on Thursday morning, a woman named Mary Brown gave birth to four children, two boys and two girls. They a were all born alive and quite perfect, bet they subsequently died. T-,,0 Irishmen were, on Tuesday, night apprehended in Glasgow on a charge of being concerned in the dynamite outrage at Tradeston gasworks. They were taken before the magistrates on Weclneday and committed for trial. . Martin Nicholson, an Irish labourer, was remanded at Leeds, on Wednesday, on the charge of causing the death of James Strangeways, a shoemaker. On Tuesday night the deceased and prisoner had an altercation at the Lloyd's Arms, when Nicholson pushed the deceased, who fell against the table and died instantly. Trris ASSOCIATED CHAMBER'S or COMMERCE of the United Kingdom met for their annual conference at Derby on Tues- day, under the presidency of Mr. Monk, M.P. A number of important subjects were discussed, and in the evening the delegates were entertained at a convers.aione given by the Mayor of Derby, at the Museum and Art Gallery. I JUST IN TIME.—At the Edinburgh Police Court, on Mon- day, George Farquhar, butcher, Cowcrate, was convicted of having, on the 26th ultimo, exposed for sale 821bs. of un- sound horseflesh. When the police made the discovery part of the flesh was being put through a mincing machine, pre- paratory to being madeinto sausages. Bailie Clarke imposed the maximum penalty of £2O, or 60 days' imprisonment. SAD DEATH.—The dead body of Mr. J. Bottomley,of the firm of Bottomley and Sons, Adelaide-street, Keighlev, was found on the banks of the canal, at Monk Bridge, 'Leeds, on Thursday, with two large wounds on the forehead and another on the back of the head. His watch was missing, but a gold guard was around his neck, and a purse containing money in his pocket. It was at first thought that murder had been committed, but later investigation pointed to an accident. .

THE NEW LORD MAYOR OF LONDON.—A crowded meet- ing of the citizens of London was held in the Guildhall, on Saturday afternoon, for the purpose of selecting the Lord Mayor for the ensuing year. The election resulted in the liverymen sending to the Court of Aldermen the names of Alderman Hadley and Alderman Fowler, and that court, after deliberating in private for half an hour, selected Alderman Fowler. The result was received with groans and hisses. AFFRAY BETWEEN VALIAN ORGAN GRINDEBS.—.It Birmingham, on Wednesday. Gereminz Orlando, organ grinder, was committed for trial for maliciously staliaing a fellow "musician," named Malveo Riozzi, on Sunday night. Both Men, together with several other organ grinders, were playing a game called "Mora," when the prisoner desired that cards should be introduced. The request being refused, the prisdner. as alleged, seriously stabbed the prosecutor in the side, and otherwise assaulted him, necessitating his removal to the hospital. The defence was that there was a general fight with knives and fists, and that the prosecutor got the worst in the affray. THE MYSTERIOUS AFFAIR AT PRESTON.—An inquest was held on Saturday, at Preston, respecting the death of Mrs. Elizabeth Alston, who was found dead in her house. The evidence of Mr. Garner, surgeon. showed that the woman had been attacked and dreadfully injured, and the jury re- turned a verdict to the effect that the deceased met with her death in a foul manner, but the evidence was insufficient to show by whom the violence was inflicted.—Thomas Riley, a stonemason, was remanded, on Monday, charged with having caused the death of Mrs. Elizabeth Alston, and on Wednesday he was committ-d to the assizes for trial on the charge of murdering the woman.

div.head: PERSONAL.
div.p: PERSONAL.
Lords Henry and Robert Grosvenor are staying at Eaton Hall. _ _ _

Sir Henry Darylll, town clerk of Windsor, died on Sunday night. Mr. Ruskin is at present the guest of Lord and Lady Reay at Laidlawstiel. The Rev. Dr. Begg, of Edinburgh, one of the leaders of the Free Church of Scotland, died on Saturday afternoon. Lord John and Lady Manners were present and spoke on Saturday at the opening of the Birnan Working Mon's Institute. _ . .

The Duke and Duchess of Westminster will arrive at Eaton Hall from Stack Lodge, Sutherlandshire, about the middle of the month. Mr. John Morley, M.P., has been invited to preside at the Parliamentary Reform Conference at Leeds on the 17th and 18th inst. It is understood that the Queen, accompanied by the Princess Beatrice, will leave Balmoral on or about November 20th for Windsor Castle. The Princess Christian and her family will leave. Scotland previous to the departure of the Queen, returning to Cumberland Lodge, Windsor Great Park. On Thursday night the members of the Liverpool Art Club entertained Mr. Henry Irving at supper at their rooms in Upper Parliament-street. The Right Hon. G. J. Goschen will deliver the opening address of the new session of the Philosophical Institution at Edinburgh, on Friday, the 2nd of November. Mr. G. 0. Trevelyan returned from Switzerland, on Satur- day, and after a visit to his father at Wallington will take up his residence at the Chief Secretary's Lodge, Dublin, for the autumn. Tuesday, October Id, has been fixed for the presentation to Sir Archibald Alison of a magnificent claymore, subscribed for by the people of Scotland. A banquet will be given in the evening in St. Andrew's Hall, Glasgow.

div.head: POLITICAL.
div.p: POLITICAL.
The Aberdeen Town Council have resolved to confer the freedom of the city on Sir R. Cross and Lord Aberdeen on 2nd of November. _ _

_ TORY RESPONSIBILITY FOR IRISH TROUBLES.—Professor Thorold Rogers, M.P., addressing a large Liberal meeting at Canterbury, on Monday, credited the origin of Irish violence to the rejection by the House of Lords of three remedial measures, at the instance of Lord Beaconsfield. Mr. Parnell clearly saw that as a political force the strength of his posi- tion was trebled by this action, and it was not too much to say that the greater pert of the Irish trouble Had arisen from the unwise rejection of these bills.. A REPLY TO MR. GIBSON, M.P.—On Wednesday night the Hon. Ernest Noel addressed hiS constituents at Anna". He offered some criticisms on Mr. Gibson's speech, and de- fended the Government from the charge of non-fulfilment of promises, saying that systematic obstruction had pre- vented them carrying several measures. The principal measure of next session would be the extension of the county franchise, and the Government must not listen to the demand of the Conservatives that it should be accompanied by a redistribution of seats. MR.BRADLATIGH, addressing a meeting on Sunday evening in Manchester, said that what would happen at the begin- ning of next session in regard to taking his seat would de- pend very much on the decision of the law courts in .No- vember. If the decision were in his favour, the courts of law and the House of Commons would be left to settle which was stronger. If the courts felt that the privilege of Parliament as between the House of Commons and one of its members prevented them from expressing any opinion, it would be his duty to act on what he believed to be the law.

_ SIR WILFRID LAWSON ON THE LIQUOR TRADE. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., supporting a resolution at a large meeting of Permissive Bill supporters, held at Glasgow, on Tuesday, spoke in favour of Mr. 3FLagan's Liquor Traffic Local Veto (Scotland) Bill, and said that at present magis- trates had the absolute power to put a stop to the liquor traffic, and the object of the bill was merely to strengthen the hands of the magistrates by giving the people the op- tion of saying that there shculd not be a public-house in a particular district. To thrust drink shops on any locality was what Sir William Harcourt would call grandmotherly legislation, but Mr. M'Lagan and his followers thought that the grandchildren were old enough now to take care of themselves, and to get out of the leading-strings of the grandmother. They wished to allow the people to say they Would or they would not have public-houses, just as they had the power of siying that they would or would not have public libraries. Mr. M'Lagan, M.P.. and Mr. Pease, M.P., also spoke in favour of the measure. 1 MR. GIBSON, M.P., AT GLASGOW.—Mr. Gibson, M.P. I addressed the Glasgow Conservative Association on Tues- day night at a great meeting in St. Andrew's Hall. He ridiculed the Government as one of great promise but small performance. Haying got the Tories out of office, the Liberals had increased the national expenditure, producing an apathetic indifference in the public mind en political questions at home, and stirred up discontent in India and the colonies. Retelling to the Government policy with regard to Ireland, he said that what Ireland wanted was not only rest from violent agitation, but rest from violent and disturbing legislation. The Irish crisis was not over. The snake was scorched—not killed. The Land League, thinly disguised under the name of the National League, was still organising and spreading itself. If the Government per- mitted this to go on, or if in the coming winter there was an increase of crime and return to the "no rent" programme, the nation would call them sternly to account. The Govern- ment had mismanaged business in every part of the coun- try, and on a fair consideration of their doings must arrive at the conclusion that they were no longer worthy to direct its affairs.

---„, YELLOW FEVER IN MExrco.—Yellow fever is prevalent to a terrible degree in several districts of Mexico. The cities of Guaymas and Mazatlan, where the mortality is greatest, have been deserted by the inhabitants, all trade and intercourse being suspended. In the former place scarcely a family has escaped the fatal scourge. ATTACK ON A TRAIN IN KANSAS—One Of the incidents of life in Kansas was reported on Tuesday. A gang of banditti "attacked" an express train during a stoppage to take in water. The driver was killed and the fireman badly wounded. The" cowboys" then sun °untied the car which contained the mails and specie, but were unable to enter it, and were finally driven off.

---PRI-N.JE—B-IS-3'IARCIC AND MR. GLADSTONE.—Prince Bis- mirck is said to have reassured one of his fellow-visitors of Gastein who expressed his fear that Mr. Gladstone was mak- ing dangerous agreements at Copenhagen as follows:—" not be alarmed. Mr. Gladstone is a man of cold blood and sound understanding, and I am sure be has lost neither the one nor the other, even in the highly dangerous'atmosphere of Hamlet." THE INSULT TO THE KING OF SPAIN—The French Government has decided that an official inquiry shall be instituted into the incidents attending the King of Spain's arrival in Paris on Saturday. According to a despatch from Paris published by a Berlin paper, the Emperor William has telegraphed to King Alfonso as follows :—" I sympathise with you for the insults offered to you in Paris. I know, however, that they were aimed at me far more than at you." THE KING or SPAIN, on his arrival in Paris on Sunday, was hissed and hooted as he passed through the streets to the Spanish Embassy. King Alfonso left Paris on Monday morning for Madrid. These was no further demonstration. The King of Spain, on his return- to Madrid on Tuesday, was received with grtat enthusiasm, the streets between the station and his palace being completely blocked by an enor- mous crowd of people. Reuter's Madrid correspondent says that so mach enthusiasm has seldom been witnessed in that city.

noticeable articles Were a child's cot, two beautiful doll's beds, wool-worked cushions, lamps, china ornaments, oleo- ! graphs, inkstands, the. Besides this was a stall containing a handsome vase of Doulton ware, gipsy ' tables, doll's bed, beaded tea tray, plaques, large doll, icreens, brackets, sofa rugs, perfumery, and a number of curiosities from Mr. Henry Rigg, of India. Superintending this stall were Mrs. Hatton, Mrs. J. Harding, Mrs. H. Rigg, Miss Kendrick, Miss Leach, Miss Lillie White, Miss Sybil Harding,and Miss Emiline Hatton. Close by was a small stall crowded with children's clothing, dolls, cosies, footstools, toys, original water-colour drawings, the,, and presided over by Miss Haynes, Miss A. Dobson, Miss L. Dobson, and Miss M. Dobson. In the centre of the room was a handsome flower stall, which added greatly to the general effect of the decorations. It was under the care of Mrs. Byrth Howson, of Wilderspool, and contained flowers contributed by Col. Blackburne, M.P.' and the Mayor (Councillor Crosfield). In one corner of the hall was a pen of live rabbits, and cages of doves and pigeons; while in the opposite corner was a fish pond, which proved a source of amusement to the visitors, and profit to the bazaar. Various other attractions were provided, and amongst them was the "Theatre Royal," in which performances were given each evening. As already stated, the bazaar was opened by Lord Win- marleigh ; and amongst those present were the Hon. Miss Wilson-Patten the Rector (Rev. W. Quekett) and Mrs. Quekett, the Rev. Canon Dodd and Mrs. Dodd, the Rev. Canon Whitley, Rev. Canon Heron, the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. ICarleton, Rev. S. and Mrs. Wilkinson, the Rev. F. W. Cory, Rev. A. M. Mitchell, Rev. E. D. Garven, Rev. E. J. and Mrs. Willcocks, Rev. F. and Mrs. Slater, Rev. J. Har- rison, Rev. J. G. Richards, Mr. and Mrs. Beamont, Mrs. Williamson, Miss Garven, Alderman and Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Don, Mrs. Mackie, Mrs. Peter Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. Stanton, Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. W. Sharp, Councillor and Mrs. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. Charles White, Miss White, Mrs. Broadbent, Mrs. Brabazon (Lynam), Mr. John Hatton, Mr. Haynes, Mr. William Owen. Mr. William John- son, kc. Theßev. E. C. E. CARLETON said they would all be aware of the occasion of holding the bazaar. They had had to suffer a great deal from the want of school accommodation in the parish for some time, and those present could understand the great drawback to the work of the Church in the parish for it to be lacking in mach an important matter. He ought to say that the origin of the bazaar was in the first in- stance to effect some renovation in the church; but that bad been changed by one whom they all knew coming for- ward and offering £5OO if the work could be begun. He felt with that effort the work of the erection of the school was really done, because he could go to other gentlemen with a strong claim, feeling sure that they would not allow so handsome a gift to be lost to the parish. He might say that he was not disappointed. He had met with a response on all hands which certainly far. exceeded his expectations. for during this last few weeks he had been really pelted with cheques and bank notes. (Laughter.) He could really fill a book with various pleasing incidents which had at- tended the getting up of this bazaar; but he was quite pre- cluded from mentioning names. Mrs. Carleton and himself felt deeply grateful for the assistance and encouragement in every possible way while the work in the preparation of this baz ear has been going on. Referring to their present financial position, he said the total amount of expenditure necessary for the cost of the building site, furnishing and other expenses might be put down at £2,300. With what they had promised and given he might say they had £1,550. That left about £750, and they expected still fur- ther to obtain about £lOO from the National Society, which would leave them about £O5O to obtain. We felt sure that more than that amount would be obtained, and they pro- posed that what remeined over-aod !aboye the arrmant npcel sary for the schools should be given to the renovation of the church. In conclusion, he spoke of the claims Holy Trinity Church had upon Church peolife; it being, he fancied, the second oldest church in Warrington. It stood in the centre of the town—at the old Market Gate of the town—and he should be very glad if they would respond and make it a monument of their liberality as they had already done the Perish Church. (Hear, hear.) Lord WINMARLEIGII said he attended that day to aid in maintaining the character of Warrington for joining in the great movement of education which was '°Ang on in the country. and in which Warrington had not been behind in former times. Ho felt perfectly certain it would'not be behind in the future. (Hear, hear.) He might perhaps re- mird those who were of the same age as himself of the state of education in Warrington in their early days. He recollected the time when they might say that the Blue Coat School and the Grammar School were almost the only schools of any note id the town. There were a few small schools, but there was no National School, no Heath Side School, no Wycliffe School, no People's College, no institu- tions at St. El phin's, or anything which could be called an educational establishment, except the two great schools he named first—the Blue Coat School and the Grammar School. But he was pleased to say that, since that period, by the exertions and the beneficence of the inhabitants of Warrington themselves, they had now got all the schools he had named, and others, afford- ing education for the great mess of people in the town. At the same time it was quite impossible for anyone to go Ithrough Warrington, as he did occasionally, without being aware that something more was wanted, especially in the Bank Quay district. They could not go through the streets of the town without meeting little wandering arabs, who, he supposed, had no place to go to, but for whom it was very desirable that the means of education should be pro- vided. And there was no part of Warrington which required education more than the portion over which their friend Mr. Carleton so worthily presided. (Applause.) He didn't know a parish anywhere in which a clergyman had more difficul- ' ties to encounter than Mr. Carleton had. He had a church at the very uttermost bound of his parish. It was within a few yards of Market-gate, and perphaps the most populous part of his parish was a mile or two away at Sankey Bridges. The increase of population had been so great within his memory that he was sure, if it went on as it had done, the parish must be again divided, as ft had been from the mother church of Warrington, some day or other. He was sure that the district lying west of the railway meet be formed into a distinct parish under Sir Robert Peel's and Lord Blandford's Acts, and when that time came Mr. Carle- ton's diffieulties would not be at all diminished. They would be increased in one respect, for unless he had a school provided for him now be would be left entirely without one in what would remain to him of his parish. That should be borne in mind by all of them. He did not hear 50 much as he used of what was going on in the way of education in Warrington, but he heard by repute that nothing could be more satisfactory than the schools which already exist here; and seeing the energy with which Mr. Carleton under- took everything in the parish, he felt perfectly certain that when the new school was erected it would not be behind others in the good it wkuld do amongst the population. (Applause.) As to the bazaar, he bad not the slightest doubt that if they looked well round the room thee would find woods that would remunerate them to a certain extent far your charit- able gifts. He should not indulge in quoting poetry on that occasion, but concluded by makiee use of an expres- sion they sometimes heard on a steamboat as they crossed a river, "Go ahead." He then declared the bazaar open, and wished it the greatest possible success. At that meeting certain resolutions were passed, out of which came the foundation of the normal schools both of Chester and Warrington, and he believed upon that came very properly the Act of Parliament which established the Privy Council. At that meeting there were present the Earl of Crawford and the late Earl of Derby, who made speeches on that occasion, and he believed Mr. Colqnhoun, whc then lived at Bewsey, was present also. div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Earl Spencer paid a visit to Portrush and formerly opened the electrical tramway from that town to the Giant's Cause- way, a distance of about eier miles. The Very Rev. Canon Donnelly, parish priest of Rathgar, has been appeinted assistant prelate to Cardinal M`Cabe, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin. A LADY SUED FOR BREACH OF PROMISE.—A suit has been commenced on behalf of the son of a major in the army against a lady„of rank in county Limerick for breach of promise to marry. Thomas Higgins, a Roman Catholic priest, was brought up at the Bray Petty Sessions, on Saturday, charged with obtaining goods and money by false pretences. He was remanded for a week. ASIRIRIAN INCENDIARIEM.—A.YoughaI telegram reports that a house, called "Red Barn," situate about five miles from that town, was destroyed by fire on Monday morning. The occupiers had previously been threatened. A CRUEL EVICTION.—At Blessington Petty Sessions, en Monday, George Tottenham, a Poor-law guardian of the Naas Union, was committed for trial on a charge of evict- ing a labourer in his employment, and turning his family out on the road side, without the requisite legal notice. A VERY Uerusuee CIRCUMSTANCE is reported from county Cork. At the quarter sessions for the west riding of that county, held at Macroom on S rturday, the learned chair- man was presented with- a pair of white gloves, in testi- mony to the fact that there were no criminal cases for trial; A FARMER SurroceTen.—A farmer named Jacob Rooney was on Saturday night proceeding from Westport to his home, about two miles distant, when the cart he was driving came into collision with a car. The cart was overturned, and Rooney fell into a ditch on the side of the roa.', where he was suffocated. A BALLAD SINGER SENT TO GAor..—At Limerick, on Wednesday, a ballad singer named Hynes was sent to gaol frr one month for tinging ballads praising O'Donnell for murdering Carey, and calling upon all Irishmen to act similarly towards informers. Other ballads were found in the man's possession advocating rebellion in Ireland. THE TRANSPORTED FFINIANS.—Mr, Michael Devitt pre- tided on Wednesday evening at a meeting in Dublin, which I was called for the purpose of raising funds to erect a monu- ment to some of the men who were sent to penal servitude in connection with the Fenian movement in 1867. There was a large attendance, and a censiderable sum was realised. A FACTORY BURNT Dower.—A large factory belonging to Mr. Mulcahy, of Ardfinan, near Calfir, woollen manufac- turers, was on Monday burnt to the ground; Mr. Mulcahy's dwelling-hoese, which adjoined the factory, being also des- troyed. The fire Ls supposed to have been caused by the friction of some engine shafts through the want of sufficient oiling. THE TRIAL OF JOE POOLE.—An order has been placed in the hands of the City of Dublin Sheriff to empanel a roll of special jurors for the trial of Joseph Poole, who has been indicted for the wilful murder of John Kenny, and also with being accessory to the act. Large sums have been collected by the members of the Irish Republican Brotherhood to fee counsel for the prisoner, who is a prominent member of the Fenian organisation. MRS. CAREY AND THE IRISH INFORMERS —Mrs. Carey, pending the trial of O'Donnell for shooting her husband, is allowed £2 per week for herself, and lOs for each of her children, by the Government. The Irish informers, Hanlon, Kavanagh, and Smith are, it is stated, to go to India, where James Carey had decided to go until persuaded otherwise by his wife. Carey, it is reported, had been offered the appointment of clerk of the works to the new barracks which are being erected at Kurrrachee. SUCCESS OF IRISH PAUPER EMIGRATION.—Captain Boyd, a member of the Soath Dublin Poor Law Guardians, who went out in charge of 80 paupers sent to Canaßa by the board, has returned, and at a meeting of the guardians on Thursday reported favourably on the arrangements at Que- bec for the reception of such emigrants and the, immediate employment obtained, the women being engaged as servants and the men on railway works. The boys were engaged by farmers. The board welcomed Captain Boyd, and passed a vote of thanks. SIR S. NORTHCOTE IN IREI.AND.—Sir Stafford Northcote received a very enthusiastic welcome on his arrival at Bel- fast, from Dublin, on Tuesday evening. At Portadows the right honourable gentleman received a deputation from the local Conservative Association, who presented him with an address, assuring him that their motto was "No Home Rule for Ulster." Sir Stafford Northcote, in reply, said he was rejoiced at the determination expressed in their address to resist any attempt at dismembering the empire. At Lis- burn a deputation waited upon the right honourable gentle- man, who, in reply to some observations, said he hoped that the people of Ulster would always stand up for the principle of the unity of the empire. On arriving at Belfast, the right honourable gentleman was welcomed by many thousands of the inhabitants, who cheered him lustily. When the procession passed the offices of the two Liberal newspapers, some persons in the crowd smashed their windows, and the police made several arrests. Sir Stafford Northcote was present on Wednesday at the annual meeting of the County Down Constitutional'Associa- tion and also at the opening of a Constitutional Club at Belfast. ' Addresses from Orange lodes and Conservative bodies were presented to him, and in the course of brief replies he commended the spirit prevailing there, and reminded them that as the next session would probably bring forth measures of the first importance, it was advisable that they should strengthen themselves for the approaching struggle.

REPORTED MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE OF AN EARLES- TOWN YOUNG WOMAN.—Last week paragraphs appeared in one or two papers stating that a young woman, named Uzzio Saunders, residing in Viaduct-street, EarlektTwn, had disappearei under circumstances of a mysterious and sus- picious character. It is true that the young woman left her home on the Monday, and mthing farther was heard of her during the next few days, and that the matter was placed in the hands of the police. The poiice officials in- stituted inquiries, and made a vigorous search, but they were unatle to ascertain the whereabouts of the missing female. On Tuesday morning last, however, her parents received a letter from her stating that she was staying with her relatives at Stockport. Thus all fears as to the young woman having met with an untimely end have been set at rest. •

div.head: TETE LATE MR. J. CHUBB.
div.p: TETE LATE MR. J. CHUBB.

FUNERAL SEILIEON. The Rev. Thomas Rippon preached a funeral sermon in Bewsey-road Wes- memory of the late Mr. Jacob Chubb, al: leyan Chapel, on Sunday evening last. The edifice was crowded, and special hymns were sung, Mt'. R. Wood Pre. siding at the organ. Taking for his text the words, For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain," the r4v. gentleman sketched Mr. Chubb' s career in the artily, and said :—Fur 42 years he served his Queen and country, and when he retired, 12 months ago, officers and men alike combined to do him honour. Colonel Bell, the chief of the Warrington and Liverpool military district, in a conversation with me I expressed his profound sorrow at the death of our friend, and spoae of him as a man most worthy and honourable. Colonel Mansergh' now in Ireland, in a letter to his widow deploring her husband's death, said had he known a day" earlier he would have crossed the Channel and followed him to the grave. His late adjutant, Colonel Godfrey, sent a beautiful wreath of flowers and a touching letter of sym- pathy to Mrs. Chubb, in which be says, "I feel I have lost a most faithful and devoted friend whilst his staff and old • comrades were unanimous in desiring his burial should be with military honours. As a soldier never a truer bore his country's colours. Chivalrous, obedient, faithful, with a high sense of duty, our brother served his country well, and showed the ancient spirit was not dead. As Englishmen we keep the memories green of Clyde, and Wolfe, and Wellington, nor would we forget the brava men they led to victory—men, some of them, who never won a stripe, and yet whose heroism was Line. Men like those who went down with the Birkenhead without parade, without display, as if it were the most natural thing in the world. Men like those of the Light Brigade—

Though some one had blundered; Theirs not to make reply, Theirs not to reason why, Theirs but to do and die. To this class of men belonged the subject of this sketch, and as Englishmen we thank God for his example, and pray that there may be continued to us a bright and long succession of such defenders of our hearths and homes. But Jacob Chubb was a Christian soldier. He was a Christian when he enlisted, and he always believed it possible to live a godly life. The peculiar temptations of his calling he turned to glorious gain. When he experienced the grace of conversion I can- not say, for the reason he did not know himself when God's spirit failed to move and inspire his life. But it was in China in 1845, and in his 21st year, he took a (1c1.10:1 stand as the Christian confessor and witness for Christ. From those who were with him in India, and knew him in- timately, is the united testimony given of his uniform Christian condact. He was known as the leader of what was termed a " pious band," and in camp, or barrack, on shipboard, or in lonely jungle, would he gather around him men disposed for prayer and Bible reading; and eternity will alone reveal the work done during those yearsin India What was said of Havelock, the godly soldier, might truly be said of our lamented friend—" It was his constant aim to adorn his religious professien and to demonstrate that spiritual mindedness was not incompatible with the ener- getic pursuit of a secular calling—that a saint could be a .soldier." As already stated, Mr. Chubb came to Warring- ton upwards of 20 years ago. The late Mr. John Martin, a local preacher, first gave him welcome. and introduced him to the class conducted by Dr. Smith, of which he became a member, and for some time was assistant-leader. In June, 1862, he became an accredited local preacher, and with much acceptance and profit to the several congregations in this circuit proclaimed the words of eternal life. His ser- mons were carefully prepared, being plain, practical, and delivered with much earnestness and fervour. He loved his work and the brethren with whom he was associated. His appointments were re- garded sacred, and he did his best to approve himself unto God, a workman needing not to be ashamed. As to the general estimate of his character, our friend was a Christian indeed in.whom was found no guile. Christ- lover, he sought to live Christ's life. Religion with him was a grand reality, and hence he doubted not. His hidden life was fed and strengthened by diligent study of the Holy Scriptures. Of him it might be said literally, "He was a man of one book." And his habit of prayer was a notable feature of him. His visits to friends were sanctified by earnest supplications. Quietly and unobtrusively "he served his day and generation after the will of God." Actuated by a predominant sense of duty, he did his work simply, silently, surely, and, as a consequence, it was deep and abiding and blessed. In demeanour he was modest, re- tiring in disposition, courteous and kind. Punctual, orderly and faithful, he went in and out among us without reproach. As one who knew him well says, "1 never beard him say one word derogatory of any member of the Christian church." Charitable in his expression of opinion of others, he never sought to raise himself by planting his foot on the prostrate reputation of his fellow. He spoke evil of no man. Cheerful and contented, he found religion's ways pleasant, We had hoped his life would have been prolonged for many years, and he hoped himself, beim; free from-.secular cares, to spend the rest of his days in the service of Christ, whom he loved so well. But it was otherwise ordered. For several months he lacked physical force, but we little thought his end was near. On the Wednesday before he died I en- joyed with him a solemn talk about eternal things. Speak- ing of his sickness, he said "It is all right. Let it be life er death: if (3rod will lam ready. All is well." Dnring the remainder of the week he suffered mi1(.11.2 physical pain, and to all appearan6A with but slight intervals, was mentally unconscious. In the grey dawn of the Sabbath, two weeks to-day, God called him home. The light of the eternal and unchangeable broke up the shadows of the border land of darkness and storm, and a still small voice, which the stoop- ing ear of loving watchers cent(' not catch, told him he must die. Opening his eyes, looking upward, and lifting his hand, he said, as if answering the roll call, "I am here. I am coming Lord," and all was over. Mortals cried, " A men wee dead ;"
Angels sang,
"Achild was born."'
At the conclusion of the address the choir s tng " Vital Spark," and as the congregation left the Ich ipel the Dead March in "Saul" was played upon the organ.
GRAPPENTIALL REVISION COURT.

Mr. W. L. Foulkes, revising barrister, held a court at the Barry Arms, Grappenhall, on Saturday, for the annual revision of the Parliamentary lists of Grappenhall and dis- trict.—Mr. Pattinson, Liberal agent for the Mid-Cheshire division, and Mr. H. Roberts, Liberal agent for the borough of Warrington, represented the Liberals, and Mr. Bentley, Conservative agent for the Mid-Cheshire division, repre- sented the Conservatives.—Mr. Pattinson objected to Mr. Albert Thomas Nuttall Royds, of Rochdale, who said he had owned land in Stockton Heath since 1874, and had never been on the register. Mr. Royds added that this year he had come from Lytham, and had already expended a guinea, and for some reason er other he had always been objected to. —Mr. Pattinson: But hasn't your father a share in the pro- perty ?—Mr. Royds: No, he hasn't. My father gave me the property in 1874, but somehow my name was not put on the list.-1 he vote was ultimately allowed.—Mr. Rovds said lie claimed hie expenses, £1 3s, adding that he 'had lost £2 103. last year.—The Revising Barrister: We cannot deal with last 'rear.—Mr. Royds: But I think I ought to have more. lam a member of the Honourable Society of the Middle Temple, and I think that entitles me to two guineas, doesn't it ? (Laughter.)—The Revising Barrister : Sup- pose I make it into £1 10s. ?—Mr. Royds : All right, I'm agreeable.--Dani.el Jones, for whom John Warburton, his partner, appeared, was objected to by Mr. Pattinson.—Mr. Warburton said he and Mr. Jones were joint owners of some works inWildeilpool Causeway. They let a portion of the land off. The works were worth between £2OO and £3oo.—Mr. Pattinson said his objection was based on this ground: that Mr. Jones and Mr. Warburton occupied the shop, and were therefore entitled Co a vote in the borough of Warrington.— Mr. Bentley : But. he hasn't got a vote in the borough for these premises.—Mr. Pattinson: But he can have.—The Revising Barrister : Have you a vote for these works in Vte borough ?—Mr. Warburton: No, air.—Mr. Pattinson: He coul 1 have a vote in the borough if he liked.—The Re- vising Barrister: He is entitled to a vote for property for which he hasn't a vote in the borough.—Mr. Roberts and Mr. Pattinson contended that such was not the case, the former gentleman saying that the question had been decided over and over again.—Mr. Pattinson: It is enacted by the 24th section of 30 end 31 Vic. that no person shall be en- titled to vote for the connty as a freeholder in respect of any house, land, Arc., in his own occupation if the premises would entitle him to vote for the borough, and that whether he has actually acquired the right—that is, by being registered or not.—The Revising Barrister after read- ing the section of the Act referred to, said that Mr. Roberts and Mr. Pattinson were right, and the vote was disallowed.

THE LISTS OE JURORS.—On Saturday, at the Newton Petty sessions, the Assistant Overseers for the various townships in the Newton Petty Sessbnal Division, sub- mitted their lists of persons qualified to serve on juries during the ensuing twelve months. There was only one objection—by a man named James Craik, residing at War- rington, who claimed to be exempted on account of being over-aed. Mr. Craik was accordingly struck off, and the other lists were approved.

(eliairm Mr. Cooper (vice-chairman), Major Cartwright. and Messrs. Blackhurst, Jolley, Darbrihire, Appletim, Grange Hind, Bonnell, Brown, Greenall, Foster, J. Houghton, 'Gibson, Jeans, and W.
