B. Prescott, for the flowers and fruit he sent them ; also Mrs. Carleton for a similar present." There were in the house 288 inmates, as against 515 in thocor- responding week of last year. During the week 61" met), 181 women, .and seven children vagrants had been relieved. There were 24 boys and 30 girls in attendance at the Wprk- house school and 12 boys receiving industrial training. ! THE WORKHOUSE COMMITTEE. • The committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Wm. Gandy, for clogs, and that of Messrs. Unsworth Bros., for cordu; oy and-lining, be accepted:— The committee alsci re- commended that the tender of Messrs. Nunuerly and Co., Limited, for 50 tons of sleepers, be accepted. Under date 22nd September was the following entry :-" 1 have inspected this workhouse to-day and shall report to Mrs. Came upon it. With the exception of one or two minor matters, with w Web - the master will deal, 1 find the house in a good state ars order." Nurse Watkins applied for an increase of salary of X 5 per annum, and the committee recommended the ad- vance.--The minutes were confirmed, the CHAIRMAN ob. I

serving there were three cAses of typhoid fever in. the house. ' PADGATE SCHOOLS: DISGBACEFUL TREATMENT OF THE CHILDREN BY ONE- OF THE OFFICERS. 'The Schools Committee book contained the following : —" Annie Dowd, Mary A. Buttress Martha A. Bowden, Bridget Watton, Mary Hurst, Isabella Flanagan, baying complained of Mr. Bailey, handicraftsman, severely beating them, the committee have seen the girls and have come to the conclusion to suspend Mr. Bailey at once for this and other reasons."

Mr. DARBYSIIIRI3. in moving the confirmation of the proceedings of the committee, said there was nothing particular in the minutes except that referring to the beating of some of the children by Mr. Bailey, the handicraftsman, and the husband of Mrs. Bailey, who had charge of No. 3or Na. 4 home where 50 girls were kept. The superintendent had reported to the committee that Mr. Bailey had flogged several of the children severely. The girls It was found upon inviry had retired to bed at the usual time 1. on Monday evening, after which they kept talking and laughing for some time. Mr. Bailey sent a message to them to be quiet, but they did not desist, and he said he went up to them himself five times, still they continued talking and laughing, and at last he took up a cane to them and thrashed them all round. One of the girls was cut in three places, and blood must have flowed from the strokes; another was cut across her knees and again behind, which latter cut had been inflicted in turning over, and these blows where they had not been relieved by blood flowing were very black indeed. The committee were se disgusted, seeing Mr. Ba7ley had no right in the be,droom, that they marked their disapproval of the whole proceedings by telling Mr. Bailey he would be sus- pended. Some of the committee thought of discharging him altogether; and he must say if the Case had been taken before the magistrates, the man would hare been com- mitted. If it had been merely a correction, the com- mittee would have thought nothing about it, but it was downright cruelty on Mr. Bailey's part, the dictates of whose heart ought to have told him that he ought not to treat children in the way he had done.

Mr. BLACKIIIIRST said the way in which Mr. Bailey had treated the girls showed be was totally unfit to be about the place altogether. He had no right to go into their bedroom, turn the clothes down, and flog them as he bad done. His own sense of humanity ought to have taught him better. It was altogether very improper to allow a maa to go into these children's beelroom.

Major CARTWRIGHT: I cannot conceive why he was up there at all. Is this the first case that has occurred? Mr. BLACICHURST : I do not think it is. Mr. DAREYSHIRE : It is the first that has come to the knowledge of the committee.
Major—CenTwalGHT: What explanation does the superin- tendent give of the transaction.
Mr. BEACKHURST: It seems that when Mrs. Bailey has been away on the bath nights- The CHAIRMAN here requested Mr. Blackhurst not to proceed further with that matter.

Mr. DAftsysmax said Mr. Mines had stated to the com- mittee that this flogging was done at bed time on Monday, but it did not come to his knowledge until the following morning. Mr. Mines had stated that he had to correct a Mr. Reynolds for boxing a child in the presence of the other industrial trainer, and also in the presence of Mr. Bailey himself, so that Mr. Bailey knew he ought not to have flagged the children. Mr. JOLLEY said he was somewhat_ shocked and startled by the report, and it was a very serious matter for them as a Board of Guardians. His own feeling at the first blush of the thing was that the action he would take would be to take the man before the magistrates, and not hush up the thing at all; but perhaps he would not be supported in that. If they did not make an example of things of that sort in that new establishment, they did not know where it would end.- Ile thought it was a most shocking thing to turn the children's clothes down and thrash then) on their naked flesh.

The CHAIRMiN read the regulations of the Local Government Board to the effect "that no corporeal punishment shall be inflicted on any female child, and on no in ls child except by the superintendent or schoolmaster."

Mr. MINES (the superintendent of the schools), on being called into the room, said the offence seemed to have occurred about rive or ten minutes past nine. The girls were talking in their dormitory, and Mr. Bailey sent word Ipy a messenger for them to be quiet. He subsequently went up himself seeing that they continued talking, and ultimately, as they did not desist, he went up in a tit of temper with a cane and whipped them all round. Major CARTWRIGHT : Who was the messengcr ? Mr. MINES: One of the girls in the home, He heard nothing during the night, but next day one or two of the girls who were flogged DA:110 to him and showed their marks. He considered them brutal and cruel, and he felt it his duty to place the matter before the committee the same afternoAl. The strokes were chiefly across the thick of the legs, behind, and on the buttocks. One girl had received two stripes across the higher part of the back. A GUARDIAN: Was there any blood on the night clothes? Mr. MINES: I did not examine the night clothes. Major CARTWRIGHT : Had the skin b?en broken? Mr. MINES: In two instances. The girl Watson showed marks of the skin having been broken. A GUARDIAN: It is cruel and disgusting. Mr. MINES: I had cautioned the industrial trainer before . Bailey about using the hands. Mr. BhowN Did you read tbe rule the Chairman haq read verbatim ?

Mr. Mss; I told him the contents of these rules, and I read them verbatim to Mr. Reynolds himself on another occasion. Majnr CARTWRIGHT : Did Bailey make any excuse? Mr. MINES: He made no excuse only the girls were talk- ing. He asked them to be quiet, and they would not obey his orders. He was down stairs in his sitting-room, and I suppose he could not do with the noise. Major CARTWRIGHT : Where was his wife? Mr. MINES: Downstairs with him ; but I an not sure whether she was not out that night. he CHAIRMAN here asked Mr. Mines to tell what he had beard about the bathing to which Mr. Blackhurst referred. Mr. MINES then said that on Thursday night Mr. Bailey sent to him for two girls who were employed in the house to go and get bathed. He (Mr. Mines) knew Mrs. Bailey was out, and he also knew it was her duty to attznd to the bathing. He, therefore, immediately inquired what Mr. Bailey wanted the girls for, and they told him that Mr. Bailey was superintending the bithing, and that he fre- quently did it. He than went and told Mr. B ailey he should report that matter to the committee, and he (Mr. Mines) re- fused to allow the girls to go over until Mrs. Bailey came home. _ _ _

A GUARDIAN: What were the ages of the girls? Mr. MINES: Thirteen or fourteen years of age. One of the girls told me that the Thursday evening previous, be- cause she did not go to get bathed, or refused to do so before him, he went to the home at night and stripped her clothes from her. The CHAIRMAN: She refused very properly. Mr. Bnacxunasr: This is abominable. In answer to Major Cartwright, Mr. MINES said that to his knowledge Bailey had never previously interfered with the children in their dormitories. The fact that be went into the bath-room to lath the children only came to his know- ledge on Thursday night last, and that quite by accident. lie could not himself tell whether Mr. Bailey was there, because he was never there himself. It was Mrs. Bailey's duty. It was usual when one mother went away that another was called in to perform the duties, except in the eAse of married couples, the home in that case being left in charge of the husband. Mrs. Bailey returned about 90 minutes past nine on the Thursday evening when she was out. Major CARTWRIGHT : It may be that this Bailey has per- formed this bathing duty for some time. That is what I want to get at. Mr. MINES said he had never known Mrs. Bailey to be away on a bathing night before, and he could not say whether Mrs. Bailey was present on the evening the flogging took place.

_ Mr. BROWN: Are you aware whether the matron has ever been present when these children have been bathed? Mr. MINES: No, I think not. Mr. BROWN: Don't you think it would be quite as well if the matron did occasionally superintend the bathing of the children in the pres.enca of the mothers of the various rooms?

It was a very improper thinztcr Reirry to L!‘) up into the bedroom of the girls, at the s,prce i rnt he sh )nid not go to the extent of dimissal,.joecause the roah bad been punished already, and to ditniss hint woad i he pgniehing his wife. Mr. COOPER said his sympathies were entirsl", with committee. The inAitution hadgot a stiong hold upon "ke. people, it was not so repugnant to many as the Workbouss.,, and he thought they should take care that the 7 prq'.a,-srop. to conduct of this description. Mr. A.PPLEroN expressed himself in favour of Mr. Jor.LEY here said that afr what had I.een- ssid ho. would withdraw his remarks about prosecuting. The Cnernatert said the matron ought to have the super— intendence of the whole establishnymt. It ought t.,e•lanown to her when a mother leaves the house, and it aught to be the matron's duty to see there was somebody appointed to. look after the duty of the absent one. This was.an abom— inable and disgusting piece of business. (Mr. 1e..-PrErrpx•:. It is an outrage.) When a girl showed her regugnance to • be exposed to a man, and that man insisted unort,her being stripped—notwithstanding the girl:in ,her modeot,,,,sho,ed a decided objection—he thought the man a through ard complete brute, and the sooner he was diechargelthe better. Had he (the Chairman) been rxeeent at the committee- meeting he should have sent fot• a policeman and given Bailey in charge there and then. That would not have been a bit too severe.

Mr. DartsYsstax, alluding to :be remarks w1y!..11 hai been made respecting the matron, said that so far as the commit- tee were concerned they were thoroughly satis.fted with the manner in which she discharged the duties which devolved upon her. Tile matron could not be in all te homes at once. When this matter occerred she was in bed and was still in bed; and he had noAloubt that so- far as in her Jay she would attend to the wants and contorts of the children. He hoped, therefore,that in this dbaussion mem- - bets would refrain from castingreflection upc.n the matron. Mr. JEANS observed that what be ,hnd raid was no re- flection upon Mrs. Mines. All that he advolaged was some. general supervision over the establishme3t, and if one, inferior officer happened to be away, then that her place should be supplied during her :ternpora2y absence by another.

Mr. Bailey was now called into the tvorn, and on his. entering, The CHAIRMAN explained the charges which had been preferred against him, told him of LSI "brutal " and "abominable," conduct, and added that it cauld not be tolerated by that Board or anybody. The Board, however, would be glad to bear what he had to say in his defence.. Mr. BAILEY said he was exceedingly sorry that he had marked the girls, but he bad cautioned- them several. times before chastising thent. When be spobe to them the biggest and the least only laughed in his face. He ha -t hitherto behaved well to them, and the girls Lad cried like to break their hearts when they knew he and Mrs. Bailey were likely to leave them. With respect to ba.;:bing, he bad, only gone as far as the door when one of the oldest girls was bathing, and that was because Mrs. Bailey could not persuade the girl to leave the bath in which shobad been playing half-an- hour. He could assure them be Cfal not go into the bathroom unless it was a case of neceasity, nor into,the bedrooms. either. He should quite willingly submit and conform to'iilL rules, but be added he never b...isu7d any read. • The CHAIRXAN here asked, Mr. Mines whether he had at any time communicated aay information. to Bailey as to what his duties were.

Mr.:slrsEs said he had :lot cornmunicat-ed anything about the girls. That was utrecessary, because he had nothing to do with the girls. Ho bad, however,..:eacl the regulations in Bailey's presence. Mr. BAILEY said hr., supposed be was a father for the home; and he had tried his hest to to a father to eyeryone of the children. Only a short tirse since Mr. Mines con- gratulated him and Mrs. Bailey cr.: their treatment of the children and the behaviour of the children towards them. In reply to further questions Bailey flatly denied ever attempting to undress a girl, big or little, or threatening the girl with a Cane if she did not undress in his presence. He had once thrown some cold water on a girl. who wtuld not leave the bath.

Mr. JoLLEY: Your common setre ought to have told yon you had no right to do such a thing. Mr. BLACKIICRST (after Bailey had retired) said there was no jastitica'.ion forley's conduct, and he should be sum- marily discharged. Major CARTWRIMIT said ho thought there was a little ex- cuse for the man, for he had evidently acted in ignorance. He had no right to strike the children, but he was of opinion the man was improperly instructed as to his duties. He thought be had the power to chastise. Mr. JEANS said he also believed the man thought he had ! a right, if neceesary, to give a little punishment, though of course he did not justify B tiley marking the children. He • was not going to move an amendment, but Mr. Bailey seemed a decent sort of man, and he (Mr. Jeans) suggested they should look over this matter now, and have every ! officer thoroughly inWuctel 29 to their duties and tho rules to be observed in each dwelling-place. Mr. JOLLEY SAICI he had " not so much of ths milk of human kindness " in Lim as Mr. Jeans seamed to have.

Major CARTWRIGHT : Well, you ought to t;a-ve-o;-Count of your age. (Laughter.) Mr. JOLLY: The man ought not to be allowed to put hi 9 j he prernics again. Mr. BnowN thought if the man was diecharged he should have a month's salary. But he did not think the man knew his duty, nor had he received proper instructions.

Major CARTWRIGHT said he should be glad if the chair- man of tfla committee could see his way to ths matter being referred back for reconsideration. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE said he was on the side of forgiveness. Pretty nearly all the committee were against Bailey ; the only question was whether he should be suspended or discharged, and the committee left It to the Bard to say whether he should be discharged. He should himself be satisfied with forgiving this affair. Mr. BLACKHURT : I shall not be a party to it. Mr. DARBYSHIRE (continuing) said he should do so be- cause he had not lost faith in Mr. Bailey. He did his other duty well, he felt sorry for what he had done, ami he thought the children liked him.
Itlr. J. HOUGHTON suggested the man should have another trial. .

Mr. B.r.AcKuunsr thought the man was totally unfit for his post, and if he had tmen taken before the magistrates he would have been sent to prison. He therefore moved Bailey be summarily discharged. Mr. APPLETON seconded the resolution. If the man was so depraved as to intrude upon a bath-room when these children were bathing, he was totally unfit for his pz,sl- - Mr. FOSTER bOieved there had been some laxity in this matter, and as the committee were divided he thought the question might be referred back for their reconsideratiou. Major CARTWRIGHT subsequently moved an amendment to Mr. Blackhurst's resolution, the amemitneut being to the effect that the question be referred back to the committee for reconsideration, the suspension of Bailey tinning. still con- Mr. FOSTER seconded this amendment. On a division, nine voted for the amendment and six against—Mr. Darbyshire declining to vote. The amend- ment was therefore carried, and Mr. Bailey was callA into the room and told the decision of the Board, the Chairman telling him among other things that be ought to have ben taken before the magistrates. The matter then dropped. _ SALARIES OF OFFICERS.

The following letter was read:— To the Chairman and Guardians of the Warrington 17 Jon.— Gentlemen, —ln accordance with your arrangement that the salaries of the officials wre to be considered only in October of each year, I beg respectfully to submit my case to your notice. In May, 1673-10 years since—the Board increased my salary £5 per annum. making it £45, and although 1 was promised a further increase in the following wizter the promise was not fulfilled. In 1877 I again applied. Some of the members of the Board said that I was n,,,t paying for my children; so that, in lieu of the increase, it was decided that I was to understand that I was in reality paying at the rate of £5 per annum for each of them. To this arrangement I consented, and until lately thought the matter was considered arrangedand sealed. Seeing that I am now paying for the chiidren directly out of my own salary, and that I have been in your service 16 years, I feel I have a claim ou your generosity. The House Committee and Local Government hoard inspe,ctor have invariably re. ported favourably of my department ever since I took charge; and I can truly say that no officer can perform her duties more f i'tlifolly than your obedient servant, S. A. 3,IAcKEr, gatron. —September 29th, 183. After a short discussion, it was decided, on the proposi- tion of Mr. DARBYSIIIRE, to defer the consideration of sip- Mications for increases of salary until the eld of the month, when a special committee, the appoiutment of which notice notice was given by Major CIRTWRIGIET, WOD.II tako them into consideration. This concluded the business. •

COLLECTOR OF POOR RATES WAXTED.—The Guardians will at their meeting, to be held on Wednesday, the 17th instant, proceed to the appointment of a Collector of Poor Rates for the Township of Warrington, in the place of Mr. John Pilling resigned. Candidates must be above 21 years of age, and thoroughly competent to keep the booke and accounts prescribed by the Local Government Board. The Eovson appointed will be required to submit monthly to the uterk to the Guardians, at his Offices, Bewsey Chambers. Warrington, statements of the sums collected in the previous month, and other particulars thereon; he will also be required at the close of each quarter of the year, and when otherwise re- quired, to submit his booka and accounts duly posted up and balanced for examination by the Clerk to the Guardians at his offices aforesaid. The waxy win be £250 per annum, paid quarterly. Applications to be sent to me at my Offices not 3'. the 16th instant. Canvassing later than 4 o'clock on Tuesday, the Guardians by or on behalf of any ce.ndidate will be deemed a disqualification.—By order. JAMES 0. BUTTON. Clerk to the Guardians. div.p: THE EXAMINE&
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 1883.

THE mm of "light and leading" in the Conservative rank 3 are now on the stung): They have this week inaugurated in earnen the political campaign of the recess, aril though so far they have pretty well had al` the talking to themselves, they can scarcelie expect to enjoy this luxury long. One d' their own organs in Liverpool has, uninten: tionally no doubt, done these men of "iigb and leading "an injustice. "The Conserva- tives," it says, "do not take cordially to the policy of agitation ;" and it adds, " hereM, they differ from their opponents, who tre.al agitation as a fine art, and practise it persil; tently from the highest to the lowest ranks. We have only to look to the pages of our daily papers at thepresent time to discover ha/ much our Liverpool contemporary wrongs the leaders of its own party. Why, within the past ten days Mr. CROSS has been buoying up the depressed spirits of the Conservatives at Penrith ; Mr. GIBSON is now making a tour of some of the Scotch constituencies, in the, hope, no doubt, of converting one or more C"' them to Toryism; Sir S. NORTHCOTE is exe.r° cising his persuaEive eloquence on Ireland' and wc are told that c,ther prominent mar bers of the late Cabinet will soon take the field. To say that the Tory leaders do 11°t take cordially to agitation is absurd; thei glory in it. Our Liverpool contempoiary ha's conse4uently very little, if any, cause to eg" hort its party to greater ac ivity ; on the other hand, we think Liberal organs have reason t° complain that the assaults of the enemy ail not energetically resisted. div.head: tilt editor.
div.p: tilt editor.
THE SALVATION ARMY.

Sir,—Yeur correspondent, "High Ranger," rides the high horse and runs tilt azainst the Salvation Army in the style of a new-edged Cardinal. He objects to their parading the streets with music and singing, and especially does he object to this on Sundays. I wonder, as he seems to have such sensitive ears, that he does not denounce the jingling and clanging of the discordant Church bells. For my part, being w.thin hearing of these instruments of torture from . live different churches, I am distracted for the time being; they don't sweetly usher in sweet hour of prayer" for me, nor do I understand how they can for anyone else. This melancholy olla podrida of clashing sounds is worthy only of heathen lands. But if my neighbours like it—many I know don't—l am comforted; why should I growl at their delights? No—give and take; that is my idea of being a good citizen, not insisting upon one's own infallibility, or clamcuriez against what does not square with one's tastes. " High Ranger" must have seen in the same column that his letter appeared from whence the real turmoil comes; another correspondent saying, "By the odious disquiet that is occasioned and the malicious wranglings that incessantly prevail in the Church of England, not only is night made hideous, but the glorious sun-lit day not passing over the blessed Sabbath either." Now I think the band of the Salvation Army in the quiet of Sun- day mornings very stimulating and pleasant, especially accompanied as it is with voices singing w.hat I take leave to describe as very pretty melodies. If they took up a fixed position before the house of "High Ranger," I could under- stand his vicious growl; but they are on the riArch. And then I think they do no little good by awaking the sluggard and the indolent to the pleasant remembrance of his holiday Sunday rest; and if he turns out the sooner all the better. There is a wonderful deal of real Sabbath breaking by lazily lying in bed until the sun is well up to the meridian on Sundays—this is wastefulness find em n of a culpable order. Your correspondent denounces the teaching of the Army— why, he must be ignorant of what orthodox teaching is; the Same he will hear in every church in the land, But he would go in for another regions altogether, and sweep others away as well as the Salvationists. He seems surprised to find that these people teach hell firs to children, as though there was no such teaching in any other church. Where has he been hybernating I give for his information a specimen of orthodox denunciation from a book of poetry published by the eminent firm of Blackwood—it is from an Address to 0, Unitarian preacher " And lest we shall uneasy feel. Ye tell us plainly there's nae deil, 15 or endless fire where sinners squeal In desperation : If 00, thapks t' ye, dainty chiel, Forth' information: But maybe 1 mlstook mysell, And ye just only meant to tell Ye ins incarnate: Nick yersell Wandrin' about ; And troth that ye come straight frae he:l, I dinna doubt.

In the preface the amiable writer of these tender verses says he "has not intentionally written anything inconsis- tent with christian morality." There, now, is not that the received doctrine ?" The Army's ways don't suit the deli- cate taste of "High Ranger," but they are not outrageous to the class who share in them. Can he measure the dis- tress, the prickings of conscience of the devotees who are thus stimulated to these manifestations? As to the selling of "War Cries" at a holiness meeting, I see no harm in doing that. I wonder what his opinion is about the an- nouncement on bills of certain great churches—" Silver will be expected." That is very bed, very had form, is it not ? That does shock me. B2sideS, and remember, there are no business paid-for advertisements in the "War Cry," which, I think, an approbrious and mercenary element in religions magazines and periodicals. Don't strike at the poor and ignorant—their religion will die out if it is built on the sand. LOWLY RANGER.

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to say a few words in reference to "High Ranger's" letter in reference to the Salvation Army. As I have been a member of society for 14 years I don't like to hear any religious denomination criticised. In consequence of what " High Ranger" said I. for curiosity sake, went for the first time on Tuesday night to a Salvationist's meeting, and, my opinion is, quite the reverse of "High Ranger's." I was very much pleased with their form of worship. "High Ringer" wants to know the reason, our paid ministers cannot reform these illiterate men and women. First, because they would not understand what a paid minister was preaching on account of his college gram- mar ; whereas these people give their experience in a rough, straight-forward manner so that they can be understood.and, as a sample, I will give him two cases which occurred on Tuesday night. A man told how his children were barefoot and his home neglected when he joined the Army; but now he has clothed them, and what money he owes he will pay —I thinte that is justica. Another said that if a man struck him on the cheek he would not return the blow. That's mercy. It their religion will do that for these two men surely it will do for all. "High Ringer" goes on to speak of the women selling the eke" War Cry's." I hope he will understand that no religious cause can be carried on without money; but he puts me in mind of the woman the Rev. C. H. Spurgeon, of London, spoke of in one of his ser- mons some years ago. She was going through the market and she saw a barrel of fresh herrings. Thera happened to be one stale one on the top, and when she smelled it she said to her husband "Come along, they are all bad." "High Ranger" seems to condemn the whole Army for the few. And, again, he says if their teaching were looked into it would be well. If he would look in the, 3rd chapter of John, and 15 and la verses, he would flail there the funda- mental doctrine or teaching is repentance towards God, faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, and holiness of heart, justice and mercy; and if be can find anything better than these I should be very glad. I think people should be very careful what they say about any denomination. People who live in glass houses should not throw stones. He that's without fault let him cast the first stone.—Yours, Warrington, October, 1883. FAIR PLAY.

div.head: EARLY CLOSING MOVEMENT.
div.p: EARLY CLOSING MOVEMENT.

Sir,—The movement in favour of closing shops at an earlier 'hour than at present, has had little or nothing said about it in St. Helens. The keen competition between tradesmen and the consequent desire to catch the late as well as the early worm, leads yearly to the extension of the hours of business among the retail tradesmen in so alarming a manner that the unfortunate assistants, male and female, who have nothing to gain by this lengthening of the hours of labour, are so closely confined that they have positively no time whatever for that healthy recreation which is so 'essential for the recuperation of their physical and mental powers, which must, sooner or later, succumb to the unrea- sonable and unnatural strain. Now, sir, I think if an assis- tant were to go round with a list of those of his own trade and endeavour to induce others to sign their names in favour of the movement, something would be done speedily to the purpose.—Yours, REFORM. October, 1883.

- REVISION COURT AT LIMN. The court f.or the revision of the Parliamentary lists of Lymm and district was held in the Plough Hotel Assembly- room, Ll'm!n, on Saturday M r , before r. W. L. Pattinson objected to Mr. Hugh Warburton being on the list.—Mr. Warburton said he had occupied a house in Rush Green, Lymm, far three years, at a rent of £2O per year.—Mr. Pattinson : Does this house belong to your sister? Yes.—Does she live in the house? She, does.—Do you live with her? No, she lives with me. (Laughter.)—Mr. Bentley : Your sister owns the house? Yes, and lam the tenant.—Mr. Patti. 20n :Do you pay any rent to your sister? Yes.—£2o a year? Yes.-e--Allowed.—Mr. Bentley opy ct , ,d Peter Warburton, who Said he had occupied a house in Booth's Hill since 1875.—Mr. Warburton said, in answer to Mr. Bentley, that his father used to be the tenant, but he ceased in 1874, and he (Mr. Warburton, jun.), had been the actual tenant ever since, and paid LGO per year to Mr. Brough.—The Revising Barrister: Well, you'll be allowed a vote.—Mr. Bentley: But you see, sir, his father is a voter as occupier of the same premises. He has been living with his father since 1874. and his father has been regarded as the tenant, and his/ father's name is on the rate book. The consequence is flak two will now be on the book as oc- cupiers of the same premises.—Mr, Pattinson : But his father occupies another place.—The Revising Barrister said that as tenant of the premises referred to Mr. Warbur- ton, junr., would be allowed a vote.

div.head: ROBBING PETER TO
div.p: ROBBING PETER TO
PAY PAUL.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of "HIRELL ; OR, LOVE BORN' OF STRIFE," "ABEL DRAKE'S WIFE," " ISRAEL MORT, OVEMIAN," &C., &C.

CfI&PTER XXII.—MISS VANDELEUIeti LITTLE COMEDY. That some sort of understanding bad long prevailed in the family, favouring the possible marriage of the young heiress with the present Earl, Stephen knew perfectly well ; before the Countess had refemd to the matter in their late interview ; in order to show him she had set Miss Vandeleur perfectly free on her entrance into Harlaxton
Reuse. The knowledge had for a time prevented him from considering her in any other light than as one destined fer his brother—supposing they were themselves disposea

that way. But when first Miss Vandeleur cams from abroad and joined the Harlaiton circle she was still but the school girl, attractive, wilful, and undeveloped; and therefore produced no effect on Stephen calculated to make him overlook or care for the barrier that was tactiv :assumed to

exist. His own life and occupations at the slaw time had no yet ceased to be. pleasant. Ile was a favourite among men, for his manly demeanour, his love of sports, and skill in them, quite as much as for the incisive character of his talk; generally full of well-aimed satire, but rarely of that kind in which one feels there is more or malignancy than humour, as is too. often the case with professed satirists. But it cannot be denied that he was at the same time in- dulging himself in lees innocent ways; had many acquain- tances—male and female—of which at the beginning he could not feel proud; and of whom. as nutters progressed he WAS unable at last to conceal from himself, he was heartily ashamed. And then he began to think and look into his own position and doings, and see the frivolous character of his daily life; and to become rapidly dissatisfied with himself and with his mother, who seemed to have encouraged him in the paths of an aimless existence; though why, he could not for the life of him discover, since he was compelled to acknowledge she was exemplary in all other relations. And just as that discontent le!gan to simmer perpetuelly in his brain, Miss Vandeleur, who had in the me intime grown up amazingly in stature hoth of body and mind, who had in a word ceased to be the girl and become the woman; began to appear to him in a new light, and to interest him, while he outwardly seemed unchanged. And at last she so fascinated him alike by her faults, merits, and charms, that almost without the intention he dropped one after another his evil or dangerous associates; till only one remeed— Gentleman Jack; and at last he was cut in the streets, as he complained to Stephen, in a previous chapter. The. scene with her in the billiard room moved him deeply; even while through it all he still kept up his light I bantering satirical style of talk,so that she might not perceive what was passing within him, but proceed in her own way, and in accordance with her own tastes and inclination, to so speak and aet that he might judge if the growing seri- ousness in his own character was likely to find any answer- ing chord in hers. Failing to satisfy himself on that, he found at the same time that, taking her as she was, she was infinitely de- lightful to him ; and the close of that scene left him more impatient for a fresh opportunity. "But what was the good ?" he asked himself. Apart from his own secret mental dissatisfaction with her, when he was not actually in her society, and therefore could calmly and severely reflect; apart too from his fear that the idea of a coronet was probably as attractive to her as to most other women similarly situated, and that her present intercourse with him might only mean her love of amusement, to which she gave way with all the more zest, pending the -serious issue that must take her finally away horn him. Apart from all this his brother's attentions to her were so marked that there could be no self-deception as to what he wished and intended, in Stephen's mind. He resolved to go more vigorously than ever into athletic sports; though conscious that any going back to what was inneeent might lead him also to revert to what was not, through the close personal links that hound the one set of influences to the others in his past. And though, as a matter of course, he SAW, as every man in his position would, how advantageous would be a manage with her, if only the way were open, he must be credited for the honour, the good sense, and the manly independence of character, that made him determine, almost fanatically resolve, to givesway to no temptation while these doubts remained. Such were the relations of the hero and heroine up to the period, and the incidents now about to be described. A day or two after the fancy fair, when the illness and soreness evoked by it had passed away, the Countess sought Stephen to say to him that Miss Vandeleur had been taken out on a shopping expedition by Lord Harlaxton; and, as the Countess believed, against her own inclination. "My dear boy," continued the Countess," "don't mis- take anything I said to you in. cur long talk together the other day. I guess the causes of your .hesitation regarding r Miss Vandeleur, and respect them. You have doubts about her, which you do right to be eatiefied upon before com- mitting yourself." "That is not the only difficulty," answered Stephen, with a smile. "Such doubts as I may feel regarding ene of the proposed contracting parties, were they confined to that one, 'eight perhaps be taken silent note of to be encountered and dealt with after marriage; but it is very awkward, if my doubts also extend to the other—that is to say—to myself. I However, we shall see." "And in happy time you can now make the trial. Listen. You shall not go to her a pauper. If you marry her, all my fortune except a bare suffic,ency for my personal wants while I live shall be settled on you. She is half won ; and if you will but threw yourself cordially into her moods, and try and draw out that which you want to see in a sym- pathetic spirit, you will, I doubt not, at one and the same moment win her wholly, and see how richly she deserves to be won. Hush! They are here." A peal of bright music tl laughter again heralded Miss Vandeleur's approach ; and Stephen could not help thinking ironically as she entered with Lord Harlaxton, it was a pity to interfere with what looked so premising a state of things. However, he had given a promise. That promise he was bound to fulfil, and the more carefully seeing how serious .was the step he had decided on if the experiment failed. But such thoughts were promptly arrested by the young lady's contagious mirth. "Oh, my dear Countess," she said the moment she entered, "I can scarcely speak for laughing. lam ill with laughing. I shall die with laughing, if you don't all stop me." "What is it about, Frances?" asked the Countess. "We have been innocently eaves-dropping at a fashion- able milliner's—" here she again broke out with such hearty irresistible enjoyment that not only was Lord Har- laxton unable to help joining in, somewhat to the detriment of his habitually serious dignity of manner, but Stephen himself forgot the jealous impulses that had moved him, and began to study her bright, fair, happy face, in the very frame of mind the Countess so ardently desired, and now in her watchfulness saw, and was greatly comforted by. "Now, do not, Lord Harlaxton, set me eff again," the young heiress cried, as after getting quiet, she found her- self once more in danger of exploding. "Come, then," said the Countess, "tell us all about it. Stephen and I may benefit by your mirth, since we appear to have so little of our own. Come, let us sit down." As they took their seats on one of those convenient lounges that afford places for four persons, so contrived that all can in luxurious ease share in a common conversation, Lord Harlaxton took care to be next Miss Vandeleur ; and managed, perhaps intentionally, to suggest to Stephen a query whether by his behaviour to her matters had not already gone too far to render possible the trial he had promised to make. Lord Hallaxton could have done nothing more injudi- cious. Provocation was just the one thing to rouse Stephen. prom that moment he shared, or appeared to share fully in the general enjoyment of Miss Vandeleur's piquant nar- rative. 'While zig-zagging, butterfly-like, from one place to another, as I suppose Stephen would say, now hovering and humming over this attraction, now hurriedly and discon- tentedly flying away from that, I happened to admire la locket in a jeweller's window; and nothing would satisfy , my lord but buying it, and despotically insisting on my re- ceiving it as a gift. " Chancing next to admire a hat, he inveigled me into the shop on false pretences he wanted a pair of gloves, which they hadn't got, and didn't sell. Then I thought I would try on the bat on my own account, which pleased me, but required some little' alteration; so we were shown by an assistant into a little ante-room to wait • and then became the sole spectators, or rather auditors, of a most piquant little comedy. Oh,ethat I could give it you as I re- ceived it ; but I c nnot, particularly before a critical audience." And then was shot a Parthian glance at Stephen, which duly penetrated, and did its work. " Mother, believe me," said Lord Harlaxton, " she acts it inimitably. It is I who have had to plead to be left in quiet all the way home." Well," continued Miss Vandeleur, "the characters are the mistress of the show roots, several assistants (whom I must, compress into one), and a Lady. Presently the mis- imtresmseedaybeme gtoan; adesk close by the half-open door of our little ear-hole, and knowing nothing of our being there, the which we liked all the better for the per- feet unconsciousnese of the performers that they were comedians The mistress had a rough loud voice, which con- t r aAs tuedd 3wiiitstes vt haenaduebtemnirs: o a richlyietone d humorouslyoafoeachassistant."imitatedflamethe burst, perhaps enhanced this rough loud voice all through her narrative, any needetas, laughter theter very fi first sound withoutsou n d produced in which the Countess felt it a real delight to be able to Mistress : Miss Gentle, what did that lady in the green velvet buy? - Assistant: Nothing, ma'am. Mistress: Nothing! We can't give you forty pounds a year for nothing. The rule here is everyone who comes I buys! " Wasn't that delicious to begin with ? " Miss Vandeleur asked her audience; "and for me, a pupil panting to dis- tinguish myself at some future fancy fair?"

div.head: EX AMlNtit, F
div.p: THE EX AMlNtit, F
And then there was another Parthian glance at Stephen, to remind him that if she had condoned she had not forgot-
ten his offence; and he had better be cautious for he might

else guess what impended. "As to Lord Harlaxton, he looked as scared as if he thought the rule might be inforced on him, and he be obliged to carry home heaven knows what !" Amid the general laughter this caused, Lord Harlaxton protested that he was only listening for, and afraid of losing the next good thing. "Tne audience waits!" remarked Stepnen. "Beware of catcalls." So the comedy was resumed Assistant: Mrs. Gri:athead, ma'am, says you have put the rose on the pretty side of her face. Mistress: Shift it then to the ugly one! Assistant: And please, ma'am, Miss Diffident wants to know what colour will be most becoming to her as a generally useful bonnet. Mistress: Generally useful! That means one bonnet do- ing duty for six. There's a Terry velvet in the No. 4 drawer that will just suit her. It was a delicate violet in the summer, is now settling into a comfortable winter-red, and most likely will emerge a primrose with the advance of spring. Ha! ha! ha! Stimulated by the increasing enjoyment of her audience, Miss Vandeleur perfectly revelled in the fun of her recollec-

tions, as she went on— Assistant: A. lady, ma'am, wants something very choice and fashionable. You needn't sh9w her anything else; she Itn mys what's what as well as ourselves. Mistress: If she did she'd make less fuss about it. her with the Nlethusaleh. " The Methusaleh, Frances? " interposed the amused Countess. "That's just what the wondering girl said," respouded Miss Vandeleur.
Try

Assistant: The Methusaleh, ma'am ? Mistress: Oh, you're the new-corner! The Methusaleh, my dear, is alway the oldest inhabitant of the show room. Quick! The brown satin, in the same No. 4 drawer ; you're sure to know it. Miss Vandeleur did not wait for the renewed laughter of her audience, hut herself led the way, and they were ir- resistibly obliged to follow, as captives in old times were obliged to follow—but in a very different mood—the car of their conqueror in a triumphal procession. Sobering a little she said— • " There was now a pause, and I began to think the comedy was over; but it soon began again." Assistant: Mrs. Sly's bsnnet, ma'am, one pound fifteen. Mistress: She didn't haggle about price? Assistant: Oh, no. She never does. he has paid the fifteen shiltinga, and the bill for a pound only is to go to her husbaud. Mistress: An excellent wife—and—ahem—an excellent customer. Oblige her by all means. She is so anxious to convince her good man that he pays less than the ordinary price, that she doesn't mind our really getting a little more for the accommodation. "That's capital," here interrupted Lord. Harlaxton, "but my conscience compels me to say the last remark did not reach my ears." "Oh, Frances! Frances! " exclaimed the Countess. "Fairly caught! The true dramatist is unveiled at last ! " "Now, does anybody think I could even hops to refine such very fine gold?" demanded Miss Vandeleur, with prompt audacity. "I coufess only to being a sympathetic reporter." " Well, we are warned," rejoined the Countess. "And watching!" added Stephen. Miss Vandeleur seemed to grow fully conscious of her new responsibilities, and to gather herself together for the occasion: "Now comes a change. A lady walks up to the desk and begins: " Lady : Mrs. Decker, how could you send me such a vul- gar dowdy of bonnet? I should never have forgiven my- self if I had worn it. Mistress : Very sorry, ma'am, if the bonnet does not please you. It is in a remarkable style certainly; but what people call good taste is so common now-a-days, that I thought something more recherché. Yes, I did think that you ma'am Lady: Oh, I agree with your principle, bet this is so very outré. Mistress: The very thing that won her Grace's heart! Lady: Her Grace! Mistress: Yes, the Duchess of Battersea. I intended this bonnet to have been all the rage next season. I knew you, ma'am, could make it fashionable at once, but I felt the awful responsibility, so I ventured to ask her Grace's opinion, and she ran Off with it directly, saying I must make you. another. Lady: Indeed! Really! Well, though i Ssin't say I quite like it myself I own there's something about it,— Mistress: Distingui, ma'am? Lady: Distingui truly; was the answer. Mistress: Ab, ma'am if all ladies had but your dis- crimination! Lady: Nay, Mrs. Decker, if all milliners would but learn from their customers as you do! Good morning! I shall recommend the bonnet everywhere. How Stephen had enjoyed the separate hits of what Miss I Vandeleur called her little comedy, may be readily imagined; and with what, delight he had watched, in his , quiet way, the face, and occasional pantomime of the fair speaker. But the accumulation through the double process became at last too much for him. He fairly roared again before she could establish silence to say, with a show cf melancholy, "The best things will end, and se I found presently, as I came to the last scene sf the milliner's show-room: " Assistant : Mrs. Pious, ma'am, wishes you to send some one for orders. Mistress: Certainly. Send at once. Good sensible old lady! As she says, since we are made in the Almighty's image, Mrs. Decker, what a duty to set off that image to the best advantage ! Miss Vandeleur bowed from her imaginary stage in acknowledgement of the ranturops cheers from her small auditory, bowed from side to side as if they might be three hundred instead of three, and then removing her chair, sat down by the Countess; and began to talk of some totally different and perfectly uninteresting topic, leaving, heweyer, a fresh and distinct impression on the minds and hearts of those present of a new power they had not hitherto antici- pated, and which each one might have to reckon with, in regard to his or her own particular desires or movements. CHAPTER xxim-rHE PORTRAIT.

The succeeding minutes were embarassing : Stephen waited for Lord Harlaxton to go, and Lord Harlaxton was equally solicitous for the departure of Stephen; while the Countess watched both with a sense of annoyance, not at all shared in by Miss Vandeleur; who, fully appreciating the position, felt she was monarch of all she surveyed, the arbiter for the moment of the destinies of her two lovers. She looked, moved, and spoke, with a demure but rich enjoyment of the scene, half thinking to herself here was to be the preparation of a denouement for a little comedy, that might contain a serious element. Suddenly she started and cried aloud, while her hands became busy in search about her dress, 'Oh, where's my locket! I have lost it—Lord Harlax- ton's kind gift—or left it behind at the milliner's! " "In payment, no doubt, for your entertainment ! " ob- served Stephen, a little audacionsly. "I remember, now." continued Miss Vandeleur, "I laid it down while trying on the hat, and I suppose thought I had taken it up again. Oh dear. lam so sorry." She looked so sympathetically at Lord Hirlaxton that he could do no less than offer to go back to the place in search. Miss Vandeleur at once accepted his kindness, and was profuse in her thanks; a little too profuse thought the Countess; as she considered this was the kind of thing that probably influenced Stephen so unfavoarably, and made his judgment of the young lady so harsh. However, Lord Harlaxton hurried away. The course was clear, and the face of the Countess brightened with animation and hope as she rose to go. took Stephen's arm, and whispered to him before parting at the door— " Now is your time. Again I say throw yourself into her oods !"

A moment after Stephen and Miss Vandeletit were meet- ing face to face, and this was the mutual salutation: "Well, General Moth !" " Well, Lady Butterfly !" "A truce to warfare. kind ?" "That depends." said Stephen, "Depends ?" cried Miss Vandeleur. "Yes, on the reward he may expect." "Come then," she continued, "help me to think of some- thing suitable as a return gift." "You are clever with brash and pallete responded Stephen, "paint his portrait. He would like that. And considering the sort of gods we place now-a-days on the Social Olympus, he would make a very creditable object for female idolatry. Try." There was something very like a sly expression came over Miss Yandeleur's face; merging, however, quickly into one that showed her secret bat strong desire to hear how he would answer, as she asked,— "And may I recommend a similar process to you and the lady—whoever she may be—that no doubt pre-occupies your thoughts and time, and takes you so much away?" "I don't paint," was Stephen's brief answer to the young lady's insidious question. "0 yes, you do—in words. So no evasion. lady we all know." "And you want me to paint her portrait?" "Well, it might interest me, and serve you to pass the time."
Tell me, isn't your brother
There is a

"Queen's command, subjects have only to obey. I am ready." And a certain sparkle in Stephen's eyes seemed to show he liked the prospect. "But will it be true ?" demanded Miss Vandeleur • her mind fluctuating between hope and fear as to a different denoue2nent of her little comedy than the one she had so fondly anticipated a few minutes ago. "Will it be life- like ?" "If I have the skill to make it so," responded SteO•en. "Perhaps you can draw from the heart ?" taid Miss Vandeleur. "Perhaps," was the reply. "Begin!" " Well, her hair is bright, golden, glittering, fresh as from Venus's own hand, who seems to have shard it in delicate tiny waves, reminding one of the dancing billows of her own natal morn." "One might almost suppose you were on the beach to see. Preceed. Her eyes— ?" "Are hardly the same in their different moods. Now, in their blue depths you see whole universes of thought open- ing upon you, and now they are so fraught with the by Cupid's own naizchievousneas that you cannot meet them

ues e, with safety—yet are unable to fly. SOMr theytteem ...-". to share your owe confUSion, and you vontao aP":1 .10 challenge their power, but only to feel that in eVarY glioce lurks a delicious death." "Oh that I were a man !" exclaimed Miss Vundeleur, with well-feigned enthusiasm, "to show how I apprecidte so exquisite a creature!" But Stephen noticed that the little feet were (quite um consciously to their fair owner) tapping the floor irritably, and threatening an explosion. And, truth to say, he went on with increased zest in his artistic labours, for that very reason. " Ah, but her cheek!" he said, as though revelling in the contemplation of it. "Is that so very wonderful ?" " Yes, though faulty : too richly red, as though the sun that coloured it loved. it too well to leave it."' 'So even her imperfections increase her charms !" said Miss Vandeleur, with a perceptible increase of sharpness in the tone. "Have you done f" " Done!" exclaimed Stephen. "Why, I have only just got to her lips." Miss Vandeleur's instinctive love of wit and humour pre- vailed for a moment over all else that was in her mind and heart; and it was with difficulty she restrained her laughter, and managed to say— " And may I ask how long you propose to stay there ?" Only while I note her teeth, those ivory crates of her soul's mansion ; her lips like fairy rose bank's before, so round and rich, and so overcharged with sweetness—no wonder the worqs that pass between them steal a more than mortal influence, and almost make one forget the pure, noble and maidenly thoughts they convey." " So masterly a portrait should not remain unfinished,' said Miss Vandeleur, in tones of stifled emotion, after a strange pause on Stephen's part. " Who- could do it thoroughly ?" he responded. "You are too modest! You do it very well indeed. Wonderfully well! One would think you had never done, or cared to do anything else." "I fear to tire you, although it is a subject I never weary of."

"Of course not," rejoined Miss Vandelenr, putting a strong pressure upon herself to be careful of her words, and avoid anything approaching to an outburst. "Else," cmtinued Stephen, "I would speak of her form so perfect, so full of grace, and so suggestive of the yearn- ing for another's support, that even the arms, like delicate tendrils, seem waiting but to twine." " Around his neck, I suppose," was the inward comment of Miss Vandeleur as she turned away, in fear of showing by her face how deeply she was moved. "But I must stop," said Stephen, with cruel enjoyment. "I am dazzled with the encirc!ing splendour. One must shade one's eyes to look at all." "Why not take her. then—l would !—if she would have you ?" burst out Miss Vandeleur in excited tones. And then what a Change came over her, as Stephen caught her dress, knelt before her, his eyes, face, manner, in an instant full of tender respect and earnestness, and mur- mured in a thrilling, yet strong, manly voice: "Do you say so? Do you not yet,know that if I have succeeded in my portraiture it was only because I drew in my own fashion from the sweet original before me ?" The Countess. who had been waiting near in • extreme anxiety, as seeing that on this opportunity de- pended probably the success or rain of her scheme, seemed to understand what was passing; so came into the !room just far enough ta see the attitude of the lovers at the critical moment; and then clasping her hands and turning her eyes heavenwards in devout thank- fulness, she passed away in silence unnoticed. "Oh, Stephen. do you speak truly ?" was all Miss Van- deleur could murmur, for her whole heart seemed to flow into these few words, when they were interrupted by a voice from the outside saying: "I will come to you presently." It was the voice of Lord Harlaxton ; and it sufficed to make Stephea leap to his feet, and toss the billiard balls about; and send Miss Vandeleur to a side table for a book; with which, and a throbbing brain, she sat down, and appeared to be reading, as the Earl entered.
(To be continued.)

WARRINGTON -POST-OVFICE CLERK.
BAIL REFUSED.

Samuel Higginson Worrall, a respectable-looking young man, of 5, Museum-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, with stealing from the Warrington Post-office, on Tuesday, a letter containing a half-sovereign, to sixpences, and 24 penny postage stamps, the property of H.M. Post-master General ; further, with stealing from the same rlace, on the morning of the 30th, ult., a registered letter containing a half-sovereign, also the property of H.M. Post-master General.—Mr. William Edwin Howson said he was a clerk attached to the Confidential Enquiry Office in connection with the General Post-office. The prisoner had been a sorting clerk in the Warrington Post-office for about five or six years. In consequence of numerous complaints of the non-receipt of letters containing money and other property- which ought in due course to have passed through the War- rington Pest-office, he was instructed by the Post-office authorities in London to investigate the matter. On Mon- day at 9-20 a.m. he handed a letter to William Smee, of the Detective Department, Scotland Yard. The letter was ad- dressed to "Mrs. Chantler, Higher-lane, Lynam," and con- tained a half-sovereign, two sixpences, and 24 penny postage stamps, all of which were marked. The envelope was securely fastened, with the addition that some gam-stamped edgings were pasted to it. He gave instructions to Mr. Smee to go to Birmingham to poet the letter. The letter was taken there and posted, and in due course it would have reached War:ington about 1-50 a.m. the next day, and the prisoner should have despatched it to Lymrn sub-post-office at 0-10 the same morning. He received information that the letter had failed to reach Lynam. Consequently on Tuesday morning he went to the prisoner's residence in Museum- street. He told the prisoner he was from the General Post- office, and asked him if he was on duty at Warrington Post- office on the previous night at 12 o'clock, and from that time until seven o'clock that morning. Prisoner replied that be was. He then asked prisoner if he opened the mail bag from Birmingham that morning, and h said he did; also if he despatched the letters to Lymm, and he again re- plied in the affirmitive. He further asked the prisoner if any- one handled the letters besides himself, and he replied that no one had done so. Witness then told him that a letter directed;to "Mrs. Chantler, Higher Lane, Lymm," had failed to reach , that place, and asked him if he knew anything about it. Prisoner said "No." Mr. Smee then searched the prisoner in his (witness's) presence. In prisoner's pockets were found the two marked sixpences, the 24 marked postage stamps, and some other money. Witness asked the prisoner if they were his, and he replied that they were. Witness than told him that he could identify the sixpences and post- age stamps, and charged him with stealing the letter. The prisoner made no reply, and was taken to the police station, Iwhere he was • afterwards charged with stealing the other letter. Witness asked for a remand, as there were several ladditional charges to be made, and time was required to make enquiries. The prisoner was accordingly remanded until next Wednesday. . —The mother of the prisoner then came for- ward and asked that her son might he admitted to bail as he had very delicate health, and was now under the care of Dr. Smith.—Mr. Howson said that it was a very serious offence, and that it was unusual to allow bail.—Mr. White (the magistrates' clerk) said it was unusual to allow bail under the circumstances, but the prisoner could be sent to Liverpool and attended to by the doctors there.—The Bench, in remanding the prisoner, decided to give the prisoner the option of staying at Warrington with the privilege of being allowed the attendance of his doctor, or going to Liverpool, but said that they did so in consequence of the representa- tion of the prisoner's mother, and that under ordinary circumstances it would not have been done.—The prisoner decided to stay at Warrington.

FRIENDSHIP'S RETURN' —On Weinesdav, at Warrington County Petty Sessions, James Barker, a brickmaker, of Newton-le-Willows, was elargsrl with stealing 53 6,1 from the person of Samuel Brown —On Saturday the prosecutor went to the vaults of the New Market Inn, Earlestown, and the prisoner, who was there, asked him for some money, saying he had been out of work. As he was a " mate "of prosecutor's he gave him some money. Subs4coently prose- cutor fell asleep, and while he was in that state the prisoner was seen by a.lnan named Robert Hall to take the money out of his pocket, and after looking at the clock,to leave the house. Hall did not say anything about the matter because the two men were friends, and he thought it was a joke. The prosecutor went to the prisoner's next day and asked for the money, but he refused to give it up, saying that he knew nothin?' about it.—The prisoner, who said he was drunk when he took the money, was fined 103 and costs.

- THE LANCASHIRE TRON AND COAL MADES.—The iron trade of this district continues only very dull, and at the market on Tuesday there was an absence of any business of weight offering. Lancashire pig ken makers would be open to book orders for foundry qualities at a little under their quoted rates, and in district brands there is some undersell- ing to secure business, bid 90 far as quoted rates are con- cerned they remain at 45s to 453 ad for Lancashire, and 44s 101 to 45s 101 for Lincolnshire forge and foundry qualities, less 2i delivered equal to Manchester. Finished iron makers are kept busy with present deliveries, and are firm in their prices, but the absence of orders for forward delivery is en- couraging merchants to "bear" the market, and for delivery into next year there are sellers at under the current rates of .£0 2s 6d to 5s for bars, £6 123 01 for hoops, and LS 5s to £8 7s 61 for good qualities of sheets delivered into this dis- trict.—As anticipated in our last report, there has been no further material upward • movement in prices this month. With the exception of an advance of 10d per ton announced at some of the Bolton collieries, quoted rates are unchanged, but for all th.=.criptions (Cf round coal prices generally are very firm and the tendency is to harden. Best qualities of Wigan Arley coal are firm at 103 per ton at the pit, with other descriptions of best coal averaging 9s 6d per ton, seconds. 73 91 to 8s 3d, and common round coal 5s 91 to 63 63 per ton. Engine classes of fuel continue bad to sell; burgy moves off only indifferently, and the commonerquali- ties of Slade are so great a drug in the market that to force sales very low prices have to be taken. Burgy at the pit mouth averages 4s 61 to ss, good slack 33 61 to 4s, with common sorts to be bought at almost any figure from 2s 6d per ton, upwards. A fairly active demand is kept up for shipment, with steam coal fetching about 78 9d to 89 per ton, delivered at the high-level, Liverpool.
