div.head: LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY.
div.p: LIVERPOOL UNIVERSITY.

The MANOR said he had received a letter from Mr. B,a- mont, which he thought he ought to read to the Council. The letter was as follows := Orford Hall, Warrington, September 29, 1881. Dear Mr. Mayor.—l attended this morning the yearly meet ing of University CAlege, Liverpool, as the governor appointed by yourself and the Town Council of Warrington. The enclosed papers will show the business that was to be tran- sacted. The Right Honourable the Earl of Derby was in the chair, and the report of the progress of the College and an account of its finances were read. The report showed that the number of students had increased but very slightly within a year. but perhaps a steady increase, if but slow, is a more healthful omen of success than sudden growth to maturity. Animals that are the longest lived take the longest time to at- tain their full age, and our great river, which was a runlet at its rise, bears is navy 01. its stream before it reaches the sea. .

- The funds of the University are steadily increasing, like the number of its eudents, and at present it has a balance in hand besides the funds invested for cirrying it on. It ' strikes me that Warrington, equidistant from the two great cities of Liverpool and Manchester, each of which places have a flourishing college, is advantageously situated for the education of her young men, for at one or both of these col- leges there is certain to be able instructors both In literatu• e and he professions of law and medicine, and out of the various , teachers each student will be able to choose for himself the best. With regard to the medical profession, there is an ex- cellent school at Liverpool, and I believe an equally excellent behool at Mar.chester ; but the latter either has already or will soon be able to grant degrees in medicine without requiring the stuient to proceed either to London or elsewhere to com- plete his medical education. Liverpool Uoiverslty College, I believe, will have the same advantage as Matchester when fully incorporated with the Victoria University. Thm Man- chester will have the advantage of being more accessible from Warrington. the trains taking up a shorter time. On the other hand, however, I perceive that lectures on law are to be given there, which I think have not been introduced at Manchester. Having thought it right to send you this information for the use of the Town Council, I remain, dear Mr. Mayor, yours truly, W. BEANIONT. The letter was ordered to be entered on the minutes of the Council.

div.head: WIDENING OF BRIDGE STREET.
div.p: THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE STREET.

Councillor MONKS said he would Hie to know if the Mayor had any communication to make with reference to the cost of widening Bridge-street. They woulA remember at the last Council meeting an assurance was given that an estimate of the cost should be put upon the minutes in such a form that it could be referred to heeafter. He found, however, that no reference whatever was made to it in any of the minutes, and as he did not want the thing to pass into oblivion, he would like to know whether they had any communication to make, because he thought that was the time to make it.
The MAYOR: The Town Clerk informs me that there has not been a meeting of the Street Improvement Committee yet about that. THE FIRE BRIGADE AND THE RECENT TIRE: THE WATER SUPPLY.
The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee. Alderman HARRISON seconded the adoption of the
minutes

Councillor WALLINGTON asked if tbe committee were able to do anything to prevent the discharge of firearms and. •,e6 making of bonfires in various parts of the borWagh. The danger was that there WAS no water--esr very little—to ex- tinguish fires. He would he glad tO now k '1 ,t 1 could • e, amg be done to put a stop to thie, Councillos. Apezers questioned the estimates of the fire e- eogine department of the Watch Committee; and drew attention to the fire which occurred at Mr. Wright's pre- mises some five or six weeks ago. He thought the matter was one which required the careful consideration of the Council, considering the immense amount of property that lay at the risk of that department. It was all very well to say that they were short of water; but he contended if what he had heard was true that the best use of the means they had was not made to the advantage of the property and the credit of the fire engine department. He believed it was a fact that for nearly half an hour the fire brigade made little or no attempt to save the property ; that the fire engine with the horses yoked to it stood in the fire engine-house, and that no amount of remonstrance could get them to move it, mainly on the ground that they had no in- structions from a certain official. He thought the best plan would be for the Council to have a committee of inquiry into the whole subject—(hear, hear)—:l be was prepared to give the names of gentlemen who would appear and say exactly what he had stated. He would not mention any names at present. The MAYOR: I think you might state the names, Coun- cillor Monks. Councillor MONKS said he had not permission to do that, but the persons were quite willing to go before any com- mittee of investigation the Council might appoint. It was not confined to the fire at Mr. Wright's, for he believed there was an equally disgraceful condition of things at the fire which occurred at the Wharfe Meadow Mill. In that case the brigade could not by any possibility be short of water as the river ran within a short distance of the place. What he had stated pointed to an inefficient fire brigade, lie did not wish to question the organisation, but it appeared to him—and it was a serious matter to those who had property in the borough—that they ought to have some better or- ganisation than they had at present. The sooner they had the better it would be. (Hear, hear.) If the Watch Com- mittee would take the matter up he. thought they might leave it in their hands, but if they weuld not he Was pre- pared to move that a committee be appointed to investigate the matter. He noticed upon the minutes that the sum of £29 6s. was to be paid to the men as wages. He did not know what their system might be, but it struck him as quite inadequate for wages to men who might be called upon any time of the day or night. It seemed to him that they were starving a service which was one of great importance to the borough. He would like to know whether the Watch Com- mittee were satisfied or dissatisfied with the state of things at present. ' Councillor FRANCOMB said it was an utter impossibility for the fire brigade to work without water. It was a shame to put upon any portion of the members of the Wa•ch Com- mittee the blame that they were responsible for fires: yet at-, the same time after every fire they were simply held up to the ridicule of the town. Mr. Wright was the gentleman who ought to feel the most aggrieved, but he had told him (Councillor Fi ancomb) personally that the members of the ' fire brigade did all in their power to put out the fire. He was sure the firemen, from the superintendent downwards, were most anxious to do their duty—(hear, hear)—and he believed the men would risk their lives to save the property of the town, but if at the same time they had no water, how could any man have a heart itiworking ? The Watch Com- mittee and the Council should be in a position to let the men do their work creditably or give it up altogether. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PeearTs, as the convener of the Fire Engine Sub-committee, said he would be glad to accept Councillor Monks' suggestion, and he hoped it would be carried out. He would like to see the fire engine department made into a separate committee again, as it was before, and he would ha glad, if Councillor Moeks had the superintendence of that department. The state of things which existed with regard to the supply of water was something disgraceful, at all events to anybody connected with the Waterworks Com- pany, because they were the parties to whom they had to look for protection against fire. He thought the matter about Mr. Wright's fire was fully explained by the Mayor at the last Council meeting. A letter from Mr. Ross had appeared in a local paper, which he (Councillor Platt) thought was utterly misleading. It might be literally cor- rect, but he thought the whole intention of the letter was to mislead those who read it. Mr. Ross evidently wanted the inhabitants of the town to believe that there were no hydrants near enough to the fire, but there were three hydrants within a very short distance of the tire. All three were utterly useless, and nearly an hour elapsed before , there was any pressure of water worth mentioning. He had reason to believe that no fire brigade in the world could have done better than theirs did under the circumstances. His opinion was that they had done their duty, and done it well, but if there was no water they could not extinguish a fire by a mere presence of hose piping. Something had been said with regard to the unfortunate fire at Wharfe Meadow, and the length of time before the engine got there. He did not know whether Councillor Monks had taken pains to know the reason of that. The man who discovered the fire instead of going to the Fire Engine Station ran over War- rington Bridge and up Leitchford to find the foreman— (laughter)—and after going back to the fire sent for the fire brigade. The fire brigade was on the spot in a very short time, but when they arrived the place was in fi Imes. Owing to the very inflammable nature of its con- tents it was almost impossible to ewe anything because thsetime had been wasted before sending for the fire brigade. They had literally done all that it was pos- sible to do. As the matter stood at present they were entirely at the mercy of the Water Company, and the sooner the question tva; taken in hand the better it would be. The matter would be gone irto by the committee to be appointed, and he would be glad to do his part, which he had dens so far.

Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT said the question which had seemed to occupy a great deal of attention lay in a nut- shell. It was a question of the supply of water. (Hear, bear.) The fire brigade seemed to be efficient, if they had only materials to work with. Where had the great pressure of water gone to that they formerly had from Hill Cliff e ? A great number of the inhabitants of the town were once summoned to see the pressure of water in Sankey-street, and he saw the water thrown over Trinity Church vane. 'lle question was where was the pressure now? Was any being kept back which they ought to bays? Councill)r BURGESS thought it should be understood that the amount mentioned to be paid for firemen's wages was not all that they received. It was the standing amount paid to them whether they had to work at fires or not. There ,was an extra amount allowed to them for each fire they attended. The MAYOR said the fire brigade on the occasions in question did their duty as well as any fire brigade in the kingdom c)uld have done. The simple fact was, as Coun- cillor Pierpoint hal just remarked, the fire brigade was of no use wit-tont water. The Town Clerk and himself (the

Nttyor) had been to the Waterworks' people; and had .bad two hours' argument with them, but he was sorry to sal, that they could make very little impression. (Laughter.) The Water Company admitted what Councillor Platt had }List stated, that a bydrant on a three-inch main was weless for extinguishin! fires. He thought the answer they gave them wa, that they might put‘down—if they chose—their own pipes—nine inches in diameter—and they would undertake to see that there was a pressure of water kept in them. As regarded the Hill Cliffe water, he believed that the water had stopped coming into the town entirely, and that was the reason why there was no presture upon those pipes. Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT Winwick is on a much higher level than Hill Clitfe, I think, and we might have the water from there.

The MAYOR thought it was, and Winwick was much better water to have in the town. He did not think they had any resource left but to go to the Local Government Board—(hear, hear)—represent to them the condition the town was in,and get powers to remedy the state of things. (Hear, hear.) He would not object to a committee of in- quiry if he_thought it would do any good, but he did not think it would do any good at present, especially after what Councillor Platt had stated that as far as he could judge the lire brigade did their duty as well as any men could do it.

Councillor MONKS subsequently moved that the minutes of the Watch Committee be confirmed with the exception of the estimate for £225 for the Fire Engine Department. Councillor WRIGHT said that as far as the fire at his place was concerned he felt, in justice to the men, that he should say he was satisfied with the way in which they did their duty. It was something wonderful that they saved the amount of material they did with the kind of apparatus they had at hand. He agreed with Councillor Francomb, that, considering they' had no water—the men did their duly well, and he was satisfied with them. (Hear, hear.) Alderman KEAN said the charge brought by Councillor Monks was one of indolence, inattention, and delay on the part of the fire .brigade, but they had a letter from the Wharf Meadow Mills congratulating them upon the activity of the men and the attention they paid to the fire. Now they had Mr. Wright's testimony that the men did their duty, and as Councillor Monks had made the charge they ought to put the matter right at once. Councillor SUTTON a-ad there was no doubt that the general opinion throughout the town was that there was something very seriously wrong in the management of the fire brigade. He thought Councillor Monks was perfectly justified in bringing the matter before the Council, -and in recommending that a committee be appointed for the pur- pose of investigating the question. That should be done in justice to the lire brigade, because it was the opinion that it was their fault, and that it was their mismanagement. The MAYOR: Do you second Councillor Monks' amend- ment ?
Councillor SuTTos: No; I say it is not necessary. The MAYOR: Then it falls to the ground. Councillor MoNics observed that he was just going to withdraw the amendment.

The MAYOR said the root- of the evil was the want of water, and the only way to put it right was to go to the Local Government Board and represent ,to them the condi- tion they were in. The Town Clerk thought it would be no I use going at present, as Sir Charles Dilke was away, but as ' soon as he returned they conld go and explain the matter. Ceuncillor SurroN; And in the meantime have a corn- mittee to enquire into the matter. The INLeaoR : A committee would do no good whatever. Councillor WALLINGTON asked if bit, question could be answered, as to the prevention of the discharge of firearms? Alderman KEAN hUnnUrOUSly observed that that question meant,—Could ty hang Guy Fawkes? (Laughter.) The YI.AY011: Directions are given to the Chief Constable lina the police to put them down as far as they possibly can. We cannot do more than that. The minutes were then passed. STREET IMPROVEMENT AND LIGHTING COMMITTEE.
Councillor PLATT moved the ad ption of the minutes of this committee.
Councillor WRIGHT seconded the motion, and the minutes were passed.
PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMDIITTEE.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of this committee, Alderman KEAN drew attention to an estimate set aside for macadam, which, he said, was a costly and a very dirty thing. The committee were of opinion that the sooner they had powers to borrow money to pave the leading streets with sett pavement the better. (Hear, hear.) They were quite prepared to believe that by so doing they would be saving the capital of the ratepayers. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the motion. The MAYOR said the Council would be very pleased to shi that the Committee had decided to try the experiment of wood paving in Sankey-sired. He hoped they would take care and see that it was done properly and by a competent person. Alderman HARRISON thought if Marketgate were paved with wood it would be better tested than in Sankey-street alone. Alderman BURGESS hoped they would soon have a large extent of the town paved so that they could get rid of the offensive matter known as macadam as soon as possible. He thought the removal of the macadam would be a great sav- ing to the ratepayers. Councillor WOODFALL observed, that some years ago Marketgate was paved with wood, bat there was an obj?c- tion to it on account of ifs noiseless character. Councillor LtrroN said the wood pavement in Liverpool seemed to stand remarkably well. The minutes were passed. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.
Alderman WEBSTER mm'ed the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attend Alice Committee. Councillor WALLINGTON seconded the Motion.—C.trried. MUSEUM, LIBRARY, AND ARTS COMMITTEE.
The minutes of this committee were confirmed, on the motion of AldermAn WEBSTER, seconded by Councillor BunctEss.

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
Alderman Trinwr.ts moved the confirmation of the minutes, and A!derman liannisoN seconded, and the motion was carried. , •
TOWN HALL, PAM, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. DAMAGE TO THE PARE PALLSADINGS.
The MAYOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee. The EX-MAYOR seconded the motion.

Alderman KEAN called attention to the destructive way in which the boundary wall of the Parkin Crosfield-street was being treated, and the wilful damage that was being done. It wanted looking into, as it was becoming a very serious matter. Large pieces of stone had been pulled away, and the iron palisadings had been bent very flinch. It was really shameful the way the wall was treated.

Councillor SUTTON was pleased to see that the receipts from the Baths were on the increase. He thought it was attributable to the fact that there was a Swimming Club in connection with the Baths, and he thought the Baths Com- mittee ought to encourage the club, because it caused d good many more persons to take advantage of the Baths than there used to be.
The MAYOR: I am glad Alderman Kean has called atten- tion to the boundary wall, and we will make a point of telling the Chief Constable and the police to be on the look out for the offenders.
The minutes were passed. MISCELLANEOUS.
The minutes of the Markets, Sanitary, Gas, and Finance Committees were confirmed without comment.
THE NEW TOWN CLOCK: THE PUBLICATION OF MR. BARRY'S
REPORT.

The MAYOR moved, and the EX-MAYOR seconded, the confirmation of tke minutes of the General Purposes Com- mittee, which contained Mr. Wolfe Barry's report on the navigation of the river between Warrington and Runcorn. Alderman DAVIES observed: Before the minutes are passed, I wish to formally thank the Mayor for his hand- some gift of a clock to the town. (Hear, hear.) Not many of us could assemble in the steeple to thank him, but I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to do so. I know the Mayor does not want many words said about the matter, but we do all most heartily feel indebted to him. (ilex-, hear.) Alderman KEAN: I think Alderman Davies has expressed the feelings of every member of the Council, and also of the whole of the inhabitants, for it is a great advantage to know the correct time.

Ihe El-MAYOR: I only hope after what has been said that the members of the Council will keep better time and be more punctual themselves. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) I join most heartily with the previous speakers in thanking the Mayor for his gift. I have no doubt it will be of great service to all the inhabitants. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Surrox: As I was one of the first to call attention to the shortcomings of the old clock—and, I may say, did not then expect that the Mayor would be so gener- ous as to give a new one—l think I ought to be one to ex- press thanks on behalf of the public of Warrington for the generous gift of the clock. Alderman HARRISON: I think everyone in Warrington will appreciate the Mayor's generosity. There was one idea that occurred to me. The Mayor has been put to censider- able expense in placing the clock in the position it now occupies, but have we any control over it? It has been placed iu a church steeple—are we not on suffraccs every tints we wind it up? (Laughter.) If we were to take it into our heads, with the permission of the Mayor, to remove it to a more eligible site, if one existed, should we be quite free to'do so without the permission of the authorities of Trinity Church? Alderman BURGESS: We have done so twice. Alderman KEAN: The clock is given to the town and Corporation of Warrington. Alderman HARRISON: I know that very well, and I sp- preciate the gift; but have we absolute control. The MAYOR: I should think you have absolute control, because the clock rests on timber. It is no part of the fabric of the church.

Councillor BOLTON: Alderman Harrison ought to be able to settle that question himself. Being a bailiff, could he, if put into Trinity Church to take possession, seize the clock ? (Laughter.) If so, it would belong to the church; f not, it would belong to the Corporation. Alderman THEWLIS : We cm remove it whenever we -hink proper. Councillor MONKS: I notice that the report of Mr. J. Wolfe Barry has been published in one of the local nelss- )apers on Baturday last, but not in the others. Now I think hat in all these matters the report should be sent to all the iewspapere, and that one newspaper should not have a com- plete monopoly or be able to forestall all other sources of information. I should like to ask how it comes about that

SAD ACCIDENT'AT WETTENHALL.—As Mrs. Mary Hough, of Wettenhal!, went to the rain water tub for water last Wednesday, and stayed longer than her husbanl expected she would, he went to look for her, and found she had fallen into the tub and was drowned. This came before Mr. Chur- ton, the coroner for West Cheshire, when a verdict was given accordingly. POLICE COURT, OVER—On Monday, before Jos. Slater, Esq. (Mayor), Mary White was brought up by P.C. Pear- son for being drunk and using indecent language in Win- nington-street.—The police officer proved the charge, and added defendant "was a most disreputable character."— The Mayor fined her £1 and costs, but said the next time she came before the court she would have ta go to prison.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICES: CHRIST CHURCH.— The annual harvest thanksgiving services at this church, were held on Sunday morning and afternoon, the preachers being the Rector (the Rev. T. P. Kirkman, M.A.,F.R.5.) and the Rev. R. Smith, Rector of Lowton. The texts of the respective preachers were taken from the 14th verse of the 29th chapter of the Ist book of Chronicles, and the 6th verse of the lath Psalm. The decorations consisted of a large variety of very tasteful and eleborate designs' worked out in corn, ferns, grass, heather, ivy, oak leaves,and moss; and dressed with the most attractive fruits and flowers. Very conspicuous was the delicate ornamentation of the pulpit and reading desk; but on turning to the chancel, one /bet a still more extensive display of talent. At the bottom of the large window, which was prettily latticed to at least half the height, was the text, "I am the true vine" in wheat surrounded by a choice selection of flowers. AS is usual, the flower/ And fruit on the communion table were of ttt'i Lest quality. Just outside the gorgeously-clothed railing was a minature clover stack and several choice plants, which must have been greatly admired by the v,nusual throng of visitors. The decorations of the oth1 f, end of the church were also very tastefully comp!.;'ted. Under the gallery—on whieb might be seen tat "Thou crownesr the year with Thy Puun.....:;„ and amidst a rich. ;apply of vegetables kindly contrikuted by some of the farmers of the parish—was the font, adorned in a meat pleasing style. On the top of it there appeared to be a crown) from the centre of which WAS suepended a remark.:;bly fine bunch of grapes, The window ledges were also beautifully covered with corn, ferns, grass, moss, owers, and fruit, which added greatly to the completeness of the decorations. The ladies, who exhibited such artistic taste in their labour of love were Mrs. and Miss Kirkman, Miss Saxon, Miss Ball, the Misses Birchall, the Misses Bate, the Misses Southern, the Misses Whittles, Miss Robinson, and Miss Owen, who deserve special praise and thanks for the time and trouble they must have expended in order to so admirably deck the church; also Messrs Whittles, J. Clough, T. Marsh, and H. Green. As regards the services, which were full choral, no better could have been desired. The anthems, "0 taste and see" (Sir John Goss) and "Thou crownest the year with Thy goodness" were the general favourites. The choir deserve high commendation for the good style in which they rendered them both, especially the latter. In some of the hymns, chiefly owing to their appro. piateness and being well known, the choir were enthusias- tically joined by the congregation. The musical portion of the services were most efficiently conducted by Mr. Ball, the organest and choirmaster of the church, who pres!ded at the organ in his usual excellent style. There were good congregations at each service, especially in the afternoon; and the collections, which were in support of divine service and church repair, amounted to £9. SPEKE.

Hinv FISTIVAL AT SPRIER. —• Special SWAM, to celebrate the ingathering of the harvest, were held at All Saint's Church, Speke, on Sunday. The sacred edifice pre- sented a very beautiful appearance, being profusely decor- ated with fruit, flowers, and corn, by members of the con- gregation-, some of whom are evidently disciples of Oscar Wilde, the aesthetic sunflower beicg very prominent among the decorations. The musical portion of the service, with one or two exceptions, was fairly rendered. Practical ser- mons were preached by the 'clear, the Rev. F. B. Watkins, M.A., and a collection taken at the end of each service in aid of church expenses. WINSFORD.

TIM PRIMITIVE MIITMODISTS.-011 Sanday last two sermons were preached by the Rev. J. Shephard, of Ludlow, in the High-street Chapel, to very excellent congregations, as far as 'numbers and giving are concerned. The choir took two anthems, in the afternoon "Awake the song of jubilee," and in the evening "Daughters of Zion both were well rendered. The collections amounte, d to the handsome sum of Zll 13s. 5d., wtich goes toward the expenses of restoring the chapel. WINSFORD V'ontn.rrzEns.—The prize shooting of the E. corps of the 3rd Cheshire It. V., Winsford, took place at 'the range in Weaver, on Sattrday. Wind and showers were unfavourable to good sheoting. Many of the corps are Crewe men, and some limitations to which they did net agree being imposed great 'dissatisfaction prevailed, as Winsford members could compete for all, and they only for the Captain's prize and drill prizes. Sergent-S. Hulse flood Ist in all, though 70 prizes were won. ITEMS OP CHESHIRE EWS. At Sale petty sessions, on Tuesday, George Dale, land- lord of the Stamfori. Arms, Bcllington, .was fined '.CS and costa for selling adulterated whisky. At Sandbach Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Wm. Steele, butcher, was fined £lO and costs for exposing for -sale in the local market 28a33. of diseased meat. He hat been pre- viously fined for a like offence. It is announced that the Rev. Canon Feilden, rector Of Bebington, Chester, has been offered and -has accepted the rectory of Rolleston, Burton-on-Trent, vacant by the death of the Rev. Canon Ram. Sir Oswald Mosley, Bart., is the patron of the living. WEST CZESIIIRE CHEESE Fara.--There was the largest pitch of cheese at Nantwicb, on Thursday morning ever known. The bulk of the cheese was ripe and in excellent condition. Trade was dull for inferior and medium lots, and prices were down 5s per cwt. Fine Cheshire, however, fully maintained its price. The best dairies realised from 70s to 759 per cwt:; medium, 50s to 60s; and inferior, 40s to 50s. ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN A POLICE 'CELL.—At Crewe, on Thursday, Wm. Johnson, a youth, was charged with at- tempting to commit suicide in the police cell. Hearing a noise in the cell on Wednesday night. two constables went in and found the prisoner lying on the floor, apparently strangled. A scarf was drawn tightly around his neck, and he was unconscious. He was a longtime before he recovered. He afterwards made another -attempt. The prisoner

was -sent to gaol for seven days. THE EXTRAORDINARY FREAK D 7 CHESTER BUTCHERS. —At Chester City Police Court, on Tuesday, the charge against the four Chester butchers arising out of the extra- ordinary outrage at the Lache Lodge, near Chester, was again brought forward. Mr. Cartwright. on behalf of Col. Murray, appeared to prosecute, and Mr. W. H. Churton re- presented the prisoners. At the cutset, however, it was stated that Mrs. Walsh was still in a delicate condition and unable to attend, and an adjournment was therefore granted for four weeks. PEASANT SHOOTING IN CHEBRIRE.—The weather opened magnificently in Cheshire on Monday morning, a cold wind with brilliant sunshine prevailing. As a result of the suc- cessful breeding season, birds are .'everywhere found to be more plentiful than they have been or the last six or seven years. The keepers on the Duke of Westminster's estate at Eaton have been especially fluccessful in rearing the young birds. Parties were out at Eaton and on the estates of Lord Combermere, Lord Egerton, the Margais of Cholmondeley, and Lord Crewe. Large bags were made, and birds were offered for sale at Chester at 103. per brace. A WOMAN SHOT AT CREWE.—A young man named John Berry, a slater, of Sydney, went to a shooting gallery in Crewe Market-place on Saturday night, apparently the worse for drink, and had a wordy altercation with the per- son in charge, a woman named Annie Moore, because she refused to give him the rifle. He took it from her saying he would shoot her. The gun went off, the bullet entering the woman's thigh. The man was immediately arrested. The wound is not a dangerous one, the bullet having passed through the flesh and lodged inside the shooting stall.—On Monday, Berry was charged with shooting at Annie Moore, and doieg her grievous bodily barna.—?risoner denied that he threatened to shoot the woman.—The Bench said that as the prosecutrix regarded the affair as an accident, and did not wish to press the case, they would flee •prisoner 40s, in- cluding cods, or 21 days' hard labour.

EARLESTGIEN GOOD TErmaßtsm.—The weekly meeting of the members of the Hope of Earlestown lodgc of Good Tetnplars was held in the lodge-room, Bridge-ctreet, on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. Bro. Henry Warburton, W.C.T.. presided. One new member was initiated and several candidates proposed. THE SECOND COMING OF CHRIST: LECTURE AT ELRLE:r• TOWN.—" The Second Coming of the Lord, as foretcld in all the Scriptures, and new at hand" was the subject of a lecture delivered in the Co-operate Hall, Earle-street, Earleatown, on W-edaesday evening last, by "an Evangelist, serving under the Lord's Restored Apostles." There was a moderately large cc.agregation.

- CLOSING 15INNiR 01 iTIR-NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS CRICKET AND BOWLING Cum.--Saturday last was the day appointed Cor closing the above dab for the season. A bowling handi- cap was arranged for about 40 prizes, but owing to the heavy night and morning's rain the competition was post- pcced for a week. About.3o members mustered, and some• enjcvable practice games were played. The usual dinner Wok place at the Pied Bull jnn, at half-past seven in the evening, Mr. R. Brierley in thaghair. Several old familiar faces were unavoidably absent. On the removal of the cloth a number of toasts, sons, Ac, perz given, and responded to in a meet enjoyable manner. AN BIWINE OFF THE LIKE AT I:ARLESTOWN.—On San- day nig ht,eonsiderable delay was experienced by a number of passengew through the engine of a train running off the metals at Eselestown Station. On the arrival of the Lon- don train, dueat Earlestown at 1.1-34, the engine was taken on another line in order to allow a train !or Wigan to run on to the station,. As the London engine •WaS being backed, the engine from wme cause or other left the line at the points. No one was, fortunately, injured, but tg:,.e passengers for Warrington and the south were delayed until after mid- night. CirrioN To BICYCLISTS.—ThOmaS Merry pleadeo gtuity, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, to riding a bicycle without having a lighted lamp affixed after sunset, on the 16th ult., in Earle-street, Earlestown.—He was fined ss. and costs. Sunmores AT THE VULCAN WESLEYAN SCHOOL.—The anniversary services in connection with the Vulcan Wes- leyan Sunday School were held on Sunday last, when excellent sermons were preached by the Rev. G. Smith, of St. Helens. The services were well attended. MAGIC LANTERN ENTERTAINMENT AT EARLESTOWN:—. In connection with the Wesleyan Methodist Band of Hope, an entertainment was given in the Wesleyan School, Cross- lane, Earlestown, on Thursday evening. There was a very good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. J. Prescott. DAMAGIEG A PIGEON COTE AT THE Vl=Ate.—James Horatio Tomlinson, a lad was summoned for damaging a pigeon cote to the amount of 65., the property of Henry Bent.--The complainant keeps pigeons in a shed at the Vulcan. On the 17th September he saw a piece of glass on the floor, and on examining the place found one of the windows had been broken. A man looked through and shouted to complainant, "A boy's inside now." The com- plainant thereupon unlocked the door, and saw the defen- dant inside. The pigeons had flown out ef the shed through the broken window. Defendant told him that he was only after the pigeons to throw them up.—The lad now stated that he did net break the window.—The complainant: I asked him If he had broken the widow, and he said he had. —The defendant was fined 45. and costs, in addition to being ordered to pay the damage, amounting to els. ALLEGED TRENT OF FOWLS AT SANSEY.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Robert Forbes, Thomas Forbes, and Joseph Bellion, of Warrington, were charged with stealing three fowls, the property of Mr. Grange, farmer, Sankey, on thenight of the Bth ult.—The evidence was. to the effect that a noise was heard among the fowls, and three men we seen leaving the place, but they could not be identified. Three hens were subsequently missed, and as the prisoners were stated to have been seen coming from the direction of Grange's house they were taken into custody.—Mr. Moore appeared for the prisoners, and spoke in streng terms of the, evidence of a witness named Ward. He alluded 'to him as a perjured villian, and said tie statement was nothing bat a lot of bare-faced lies. He also threateted have him brought up en a charge of perjury.—The 'magis- trates discharged the prisoner. Monday last was the dr, upon which the meeting should have taken place, but the only members who turned -up were Messre. B. B. Glover, T. Forster, and T. Hunt, in aidition to Mr. kr. E. Wortley (law clerk), Mr. R. Brierley ('surveyor), and three representatives of the Press. As there‘was not a quccum of members present, it was de- cided that the meeting be held on Mestday next. ThE .ASSISTAIST OVERSEER Ac,l) COLLECTORSHIP OF RATES. THE GUARDIANS AND MR. PILLING'S RESIGNATION. At the fortnightly meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians, held on Wednesday, at the Workhouse, under the presidency of Mr. John Greening (chairman.) The DEPUTY CLERK (dr. S. Sutton) read the following letter :—" Local Government Board, White Hall, 21st September, 1883.—Sin lam directed by the Local Govern- ment Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 6th inst., from which it appears that Mr. J. Pilling, the collection of poor rates, and .assistant overseer, for the town- ship of Warrington, in the Warrington Union, is completely ine,apacited from performing his duties. • I am therefore directed to point out that the regulations of the Board require that the duties of the above - mentioned office shall be personally performed by the officer appointed, and to state that as Mr. Pilling is unable to comply with the requirements in this respect arrange- ments 21:could be made for his relinquishing the office at an early date.—l am, air, your obedient servant, WALT'S/J. SENDA.LL, assistant secretary."—The DEPUTY CLERK : I received the following this mornlng from Mr. Pilling.—The CHAIRMAN : Did you communicate the letter from the Local Government Board to Mr. Pilling ?—The DEPUTY CLERK I don't know. He then read as follows :—" Folly-lane, Warrington, 24th September, 1883.—T0 the Guardians of the Warringtou Union.—Gentlemen,—My health having completely failed me I must beg you to accept my resigna- tion of the office of collector of poor rates for the township of Warrington : I have to thank you for the great kind- ness and consideration which you have invariably extended to me —I have the honour to be, gentlemen, your obedient servant. JOHN FILLING, X his mark; witness George peeme, John Pierpc,int." Mr. BLACKHURST : Now I suppose it is necessary for the • Board to pass a resolution about the resignation ?—The CHAIR- MAN: Yes.—Mr. BLACKHURST : And then it will be for some member of the Board to give notice that on a certain day a successor be appointed ?—`f he DEPUTY CLERK: Either to give notice or to direct the clerk to advertise that on a certain day the appointment will be made.—Mr. BLACK- HunsT : Then I beg leave to propose that the resignation of Mr. John Pilling be accepted, and that the Clerk be instruc- ted to advertise for a successor.—The CHAIRmAN: We will just take the resignation of Mr. Pilling first.—Mr. HURST : Would it not be well to take the two at once? (Cries of "No.") Very well, then, I propose that the re- signation be accepted.—Mr. JOLLEY : I beg to second that with great regret. It is one of these things we have no control over, but we should acknowledge Mr. Filling's long and very faithful services. The CHAIRMAN said in accepting the resignation he felt that the Board were losing a man who had served the town most efficiently for a great number of years. A more honourable man, and a man who could attend to the diaties better, he did not think could be found. In Mr. Pilling the Unien bad had an officer whom it was his wish they should obtain a successor as good. (Hear, hear.) Such men were mot found every day. Mr. Filling's health during several years had not been such that he could exercise any super- vision over the work, but it had been deputed to other people. Nevertheless Mr. Pilling had been responsible for all that bad been done, and he very much rtgretted himself that Mr. Filling's health was in such a state that he had to resign his appointment. (Hear, hear.) The resolution was carried.—Mr. BLACKITuRST: Now then, I beg leave to give notice that we proceed to the appointment.—Mr. JEANS: One thing before we pass on, I think, in accepting Mr. Filling's resignation, we should pass a resolution of thanks to him for kis long services. After a man bad served the town so well for a long period of years it would be gratifying to him to know that his services had been appreciated, and I think the least we can do is to pass a resolution that the Clerk be instructed, in communicating this resolution to Mr. Pilling, to express at the same time the Board's apprecia- tion of his services during so long a period.—The CHAIR- XAS ; I set out with the intention of moving such a resolu- tion in the remarks I made, but unfortunately I forgot what I intended to say. lam very much obliged to Mr. Jeans for bringing the matter forward. It is a very proper course to take.—Mr. DAREISHIRE remarked upon the honesty and straightforwardness with which Mr. Pilling had performed his duties, and said he hoped such a sentiment as had been expressed would be conveyed to Mr. Pilling.—The resolu- tion was unanimously agreed to.—Mr. BLACKEURST then moved that the Clerk be instructed to take the usual means ler the appointment of a successor to Mr. Pilling, and sug- gested that the Clerk should adopt what was the usual course and advertise for a successor.—Mr. COOPER: it is not usual for you to advertise if you have made up your minds to elect anybody.—Mr. BLACKHURST: Row can they make up their minds? I would take the usual course and throw it open to the world.—The DEPUTY CLERK said it was optional for the Guardians to adopt either course. But he did not see that there was any advantage in either course, because even if notice was given by the Guardians that they would at the next meeting move the appointment of a successor it was open to any man who thought fit to apply just as though he had seen the advertisement in the paper. If they advertised, the terms, salary, 4:c , would have to be stated in the advertisement. If they did not advertise the Board simply gave notice that they would at the next meeting, without stating any terms, move the appointment of a successor, and he thought there would be no disadvantage in not advertising as the appoint- ment was sure to be well known.—Mr. COoPER : It is well known.—Mr. JOLLEY : Then I propose that we pro- ceed with the election of a successor to Mr. Pilling at tko next Board ii,e.o.e„, rt cll Itnown to moat Guardians that there are already two candidates in the field, and if you remember some time ago pledges by the members as Guardians, not as individual ratepeyers, were given for a certain person.—Mr. BLACKHURST : But that goes for nothing now.—Mr. JOLLEY : I think it would be a wise course under the circumstances to proceed to elect a successor in the usual way at the next Board meeting with- out advertising.—The DEPUTY CLERK said the only course was for someone to give notice that he would move the appointment of a successor on a certain day.—Mr. BLACKHURST did not think that was desieable. He thought the vacancy should be thrown open for public competition, and as to the remarks by Mr. Jolley as to an understanding, he had to say that circumstances altered cases altogether. Circumstances were now different to what they were, and he thought the proper course was to act openly and above beard, and advertise for a successor. —The CHAIRMAN : We are not going to do anything else I hope.—Mr. JEANS: I think the proper course is to apply to the Local Government Board for an order to appoint.—The DEPUTY CLERK: No, sir; we have that order already. We had it at the time of the appointment of Mr. Pilling, and we can always fill up a vacancy without a fresh order.—Mr. JEANS: If you have already the order, what I had to say is of no effect.—The CHAIR- MAN observed as to what Mr. Jolley said about the appointment that day fortnight, that it was quite competent for anybody to make application to the Board for the post.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE did not see why the Board should depart from the usual course. They had never advertised the vacancy.—The Dneoury CLERK said there was one advantage in advertising that he had overlooked. There was a resolution on the books that in the event of any appointment being advertised, canvassing the Guardians was a diequalification.—The CHAIRMAN said before they went any further, they should decide as to whether the vacancy should be advertised.—Mr. BLACK- Benin moved that it be advertised.—Mr. BROWN seconded. --Mr. DAREYERIRE moved an amendment that it be not ad- vertised.—Mr. COOPER seconded.—After some conversation the matter was put to the vote, when eight members being for and eight against the motion, it was carried by the casting vote of the Chairman who, Mr. Blackhurst said, was put on his mettle. The CHAIRMAN: I am not afraid.— Major CARTWRIGHT : Not you! I never knew you afraid yet. That is the beauty of yeti !—The CHAIRMAN ex- plained that he voted in favour of the motion on the ground that in advertising they prohibited canvassing.—Major CARTwRIGHT: They generally do that through their father- n-law !
MEETING OF RATEPAYERS. LIVELY PROCEEDLNGS : THE RATEPAYERS SURPRISED.

On Thursday morning-a-re- , eetine of the ratepayers of the township of Warrington was , beltd at the Sessions House, Irlam-street, for the followit 'g special purposes :—" Tu receive the resignation of John Pilling, the assistant over- seer of the poor of the said town& tiii), to nominate and elect a discreet Person to be assistant oe erseer of the poor of the said township of Warringtou, and t, I determine and specify the dutiea to be by him executed ant l performed, and to fix such yearly salary for the execution of the said office as shall be thought fit." The room was crowded with rate- payers, who at times proved very noisy, and occasionally it was with difilculty that the chairman co aid obtain a bear- ing for the a k Pea era, and even for himself.. . Alderman Kean, the senior overseer, was elected to presit to, and amongst -those present were the other overseers, M essr. G. Black- .hurt, A. Mackie, and John Harrison • Ald, linen Burgess, Alderman Davies, Alderman Harrison. Cot inciliore Platt, Litton, Francemb, J. re -.°TDoint, Whittle Woolfall, and Hutchinson ; Messrs. W. D. je„B E. Nichoisoi 1, U. pilling, Sampson' J. Bonne% Thomas Hall, John Tat, C. Seward, John E. Davies, J. Smethurst, J. Shaw Green, , I. Roberts, T. Woods, Josiah Whittle, J. L. Tunetaii, J. Hal npson, H. Thornton, John Evans, and H. B. White (vestry a irk). The \Traria CLERIC having formally read the no 'ice con- vening the meeting and Mr. Filling's resignation, The Ctratheeser said they had beard Mr. Pilling% resig. 'nation read, and he had no doubt they regretted the ei, cam. stances which had brought it about. The next hueineet 's to fix the duties and salary of the assistant overseer, as 'be oer explained that the salary at the present time was £2OOl 4. annum, out of which sum bad to be paid the clerks assn ' ing the assistant overseer, the cost of bill posting, and otht r duties to be performed by the assistant overseer. Mr. H. TEORNTOX asked what were the other sources of k

income and the amounts. The CHAIRMAN replied that there was a certain sum paid in connection with the registration of voters, and something was paid for the collection of the rural sanitary rate. Mr. THORNTON : Do they amount to something like £2OO per year?

The CHADDIAM : £5O. Alderman HARRISON then moved the following resolution: —"That the duties to be executed acd performed by the amistant overseer of the township of Warrington shall be all the dnt6s of the office of the overseer of the poor of the
• --.- satd township, save and except the duties to be performed
h---y the overseers under theAcie for the registration' of vetere;

and that the yearly sum of £2OO as and for the yearly salary be paid to the said assistant cverseer for tne execution of the said office." Mr. T. WOODS seconded the resolution. Mr. THORNTON moved as an amendment that the Balmy be £lOO a year, as the rates were heavy and the ratepayers pockets ought to be considered. Mr. JOSEPH Twiss seconded the amendment, which was lost, the resolution being carried by a large majority. The CHAIRMAN asked for the nomination of a gentleman as assistant overseer. Mr. R. BOLTON, 103, General-street, proposed, and Mr. JOHN ROBERTS, Winwick-road, seconded, the nomination of Mr. John Laverock Tunstall. Councillor FRANCOMB, in supporting the nomination, said it seemed to him it would be wrong to throw overboard a man like Mr. Tunstall. He had been discharging the duties for four years, and he believed Mr. Tunstall had dis- charged them well. He had got good testimonials, and had been highly spoken of in the newspapers and% by everyone he had come in contact with. Although he had not the slightest feeling against Mr. Greeeehe thought it would be a great pity to throw a man like Mr. Tunstall over, unless they had some cause for it. (Hear.) Mr. Tunstall gave everybody satisfaction, and he hoped that gentleman ould be elected by a very large majority. ' Alderman BURGESS was about to make another nomina- tion, when The CHAIRMAN 3aid he saw they had get a little out of order, as the proposer and seconder of Mr. Tunstall had not paid their rates. (Laughter.) There would, therefore, have to be a fresh nomination. Mr. C. HIGGINBOTTOM said the rates of the seconder of the proposition were paid on the previous day. Mr. HY. ROBERTS thought the question .was not as to whether the rates were paid, but as to whether the indi- vidual's name was en the rate book._ The CHAIRMAN said he was legally advised that unless the rates had been paid ratepayers could not vote.l Mr. H. ROBERTS deferred to the chairman's ruling, but protested against the interpretation of the clause. _While not a lawyer he prefessed to know a little of the. law on the subject, and he contended that a person on the rate book was entitled to vote. The CLERie : Ha most have paid any rate which became due three calendar months immediately preceding the vestry meeting The-CH.Airolkil Gentlemen, you see the advantage of punctual payment. Alderman BURGESS understood from the chairman-that the nomination he had before him was informal. The CHAIRMAN: He had better now have a freih nomi- nation altogether.• Councillor FRANCOMB proposed the election of Mr. Tun- stall, and Mr. Jolter ROBERTS seconded. Alderman BURGESS then said it was his intention to propose a gentleman for the office of assistant overseer, but he was told that a miserable technicality was being taken advantage of for the purpose of preventing the ratepayers exercising their privilege of taking a part in the proceedings. He protested most distinctly against that miserable subter- fuge. (Hear, hear.) He thought it was not worthy of the office whence it had emanated—he did not mean the lawyers. i Perhaps some gentleman would now propose n his stead the election of Mr. J. Shaw Green as assistant overseer. He should have been very glad, indeed, if he could have done so, for he took a very active part in assisting in the appointment of Mr. Pilling 44 years ago, and he had a stroll.' desire to take part in the proceedings that morning, but cella not do so. Mr. TUNSTALL said he had no ill-feeling against Mr. Green, and, after the remarks that had been made, he had much pleasure in proposing Mr. Green for the office. (Hear, hear.) A VOICE: Have you paid your rates, Mr. Tunstall? Mr. TUNSTALL : I have paid them this morning specially. (Laughter.) Mr. JOSEPH GARNER seconded the nomination of Mr. Green. The CRAlReaterr : I think the next thing will be to take a show of hands, and first of all I will ask you for a show of hands in favour of Mr. Tunstall. Alderman Davies said he lied had the opportunity of learning what an assistant overseer ought to know as regarded rates. It required a technical education, and in saying that Mr. Green had not had the opportunity of acquiring the technical knowledge required to discharge the duties of the office, he had to state that Mr. Green was a very intelligent, praiseworthy, and rising young man; and he trusted and believed he would get on in life. He referred to the tecl- nical education required to assess railways, gas, and water- works, and said Mr. Tunstall had obtained that education. He concluded by remarking that they would to some ex- tent injure the future prospects of Mr. Green by carrying the election to a poll, which he hoped they woUld not do. Mr. H. ROBERTS said a ratepayer who had not paid the (present rate could not vote at the meeting, and he asked if a ratepayer who had not paid his rates could speak at the meeting, because he understood Mr Davies'e rates were not paid. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: There is no regulation as to that. (Laughter.) Alderman DAVIES: I should like to tell Mr. Roberts I do not think the collector of rates ever canoe to my office twice for my rates. Mr. H. ROBERTS said he simply raised the question as a legal point. Alderman DAVIES : It was raised at the wrong moment. I had spoken. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: I have to tell you now the seconder of Mr. Green's nomination has not paid his rates. (Laughter.) Mr. GARNER: They are not due. The Clienteles: Yes; due on demand. Mr. T. WOODS: Can we pay them now and vote? The Cevatx Yes. Mr. Woods then paid his rate, amid cries of well done. Mr. Join; EVANS then seconded Mr. Green's nomination. Alderman BURGESS said to the Cheirmen, as assistant- overseer, and to those connected with the overseer's office, that that technicality was known, cherished and brought there with an intention, but it would have been much better if people had been told that they were disqualified if their rates were not paid. He had not been -asked for his rates, and, as he heard Alderman Davies say, he did not know that he had ever been asked twice in his life for them. (A Voice : "You take plenty of credit.") He wished to say that the step he took 44 years ago in assisting in the ap- pointment of Mr. Pilling, he never-had had cause to regret but rather to rejoice in. He thought they had done their duty in appointing Mr. Pilling, but while they gave Mr. Pilling the appointment they did not give him the rever- sion of it. (Hear, hear.) It was not for Mr. Filling when he found aga creeping upon him end that he was becoming incapacitated to discharge the duties of the office to take into the overseer's office a locum tenens, and as it was said train him that he might hand over to him an office which was in the gift of the ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) He pro- tested against any such family arrangement. Mr. TUNSTALL : I am not one of the family. Councillor PlERooierr : _Perhaps Alderman Burgess will explain what relation Mr. Pilling is to Mr. John Tuneall. Alderman BURGESS: Mr. Pierpoint con perhaps tell us what relation Mr. Pilling is to Mr. Pierpoint, and we can trace the rest. Mr. Tusarean: He is a clever man if be can. Alderman BURGESS said the appointment was in the gift of the ratepayers, and it was not to be disposed of as a family compact. They had done their duty by Mr. Pilling as he bad done his duty by the ratepayers. Mr. Pilling had given them his services; tbey had given him their pay ; and with the termination of the appointment their connection with Mr. Pilling ceased. It was for the ratepayers to consider whether the office would be best promoted in the hands of Mr. Green, or in the hands of Mr. Tunstall. He ventured to tell the noisy portion of the meeting that the poll which , would be taken on the question would show a very different result to what they anticipated. They would see that the ratepayers would exercise their own free and • independent judgment, and would not have an important office like that of assistant overseeer handed down from generation to generation just as it might suit two or three persons. He hoped the election would be conducted with good feeling and good temper. and believed he would have reason to congratulate Mr. Green on the result. Councillor J. Putitroierr denied that there was any rela- tionship between Mr. Pilling and Mr. Tunstall. Mr. W. D. JEANS remarked that Alderman Burgess in his tirade against Mr. Tunstall said it was not proper this appointment should be made a family compact. With that he agreed, but be did not agree with some of the proceedings of the party with which Alderman Burgess was connected. He had in his hand a circular signed by Ziba Armitage and Jno. Platt, in which they said the election which was about to occupy their attention was a most important one as effect- ing the interests of the Liberal party in Warringtoa. He would like, in a thoroughly independent spirit, to ask whether it was for the interest of the Liberal party in Warrington that the vacancy should be filled by a Liberal. Why, he would ask, a Liberal? If the man appointed carried out his duties honestly. whether he was Conservative or Liberal, he would not be biassed by political feeling. With regard to Mr. Green's candidature, he was very sorry to have to op- pose him. He was an old clerk and friend of his for up- wards of 20 years, and he had not the slightest idea a week ago that he would have to oppose a gentleman he had the greatest respect for. As to Mr. Tunstall, all he knew was that for the last four or five years he had occupied the posi- tion of deputy assistant overseer, and had practically per- formed the duties, and performed them to the setisfacion of every person with whom he had come in contact. Councillor MecatE, alluding to the remarks by Alderman Bargees, pointed out that the overseers bed had nothing to do with the arrangements for the evening. Alderman HARRISON supported the nomination of Mr. Tunstall, who, he slid, had been something more than a locum tenens, as Alderman Burgess had been pleased to call him. He had bad sole and exclusive management of the office, Mr. Tunstall was a thoroughly educated men in everything that belonged to the office, and he believed if ever there was a man capable of grasping with technical subjects it was Mr. Tunstall. (Hear, hear.) He was held up in the Liberal paper of Warrington sea man exceedingly )tr aa ln, d but gave competent to fulfil the duties of the office, and they heard o.
