they mean to say that if the gentleman who had been acting 1 at locum tenens for Mr. Pilling had been a Liberal they would have voted for him? (Cries of "That is not the question," "Certainly not," and "No.") Mr. JEANS; I, as one Conservative, say, had Mr. Tunstall been a Liberal I should have supported him. Mr. NICHOLSON expressed himself in a similar manner. I The CHAIRMAN: Had Mr. Green been,in Mr. Tunstall's I position and given the same satisfaction I*should have sup- ported him. Councillor Jothkr PIERPOINT rose to speak, but was greeted with cries of " You'r'e a relation," "Sit down.' Mr. H. ROBERTS (proceeding) said he did not quite see why Mr. Tenstall's claims were put forward in the pressing manner they were. Some months ago Mr. Tunstall stated he was not Mr. Filling's servant nor Mr. Filling's deputy, but was doing the work for Mr Pilling as a professional ac- c.mntant. Where then did Mr. Tunstall's claims come in over and above those of Mr. Green? Mr. Tunstall's special claims ought to have no weight with the public of Warring- ton in reference to this appointment, because it had been simply a matter of business with him from beginning to end. He. took the responsibility for the circular that had been alluded to, and mentioned the fact that only the previous night the Conservaiive Associatien were called together to decide upon the steps to be taken.

(Interruption.) Mr. E. J. NICHOLSON confirmed the advice given by the very cler4;,- and stated that it Was perfectly obvious that thd responsibility of making this a party contest rested entirely upon Mr. Roberts's side. Mr. Tunstall was objec- tionable to a certain party because he happened to be a Conservative; and were they going to throw over a man who had shown himselt worthy of the office—(" No, no")— because of.that ? lie thought many Liberals would 'follow the example of Mr. John Itylands. Councillor PLArr observed that a, great deal had been said about throwing over Mr. Tunstall, but was Mr. Tun- stall being thrown over? He maintained that he waA not, as he did not at present hold the position of assistant overseer. Therefore, let the matter be fairly fought out before the ratepayers. Mr. Pilling had held the appoint- ment for 40 years. For thatlength of time a Conservative had filled the office, aud he asked them now to give the Liberals a chance. Mr. Pilling,- during the long time he had held office, had received £20,000 or £30,000 of the rate-:1 payers' money, and.fot him, after that, quietly to try to put in another man, in order that he might still get benefit out of the ratepayers, was more than they could stand. On that ground he preferred his candidate (Mr. Green) to I another. A show of hands was then taken, and the Chairman de- clared it to be in favour of Mr. Tunstall. Alderman DAVIES appealed to the Liberals not to go to a' poll, but— Mr. THOMAS HALL (Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.) de- manded a poll on behalf of iNfr. Green. Vhe CHAIRMAN announced that the 'poll would be forth- with taken at the Public Hall until seven o'clock that even- ing, and would open at 8 o'clock on Friday morning 'and close at seven in the evening.. A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman for pre- siding, and the proceedings terminated.
THE POLL.

Immediately the meeting of the ratepayers terminated, the overseers and the vestry clerk proceeded to the Public Hall, where the poll was ...at once opened in the ante-room— Alderman Kean (as senior overseer) presiding. The arrange- ments for taking the poll were made by the vestry clerk, , and everything seemed to have been carefully prepared in anticipation of a poll being demandede A large staff of clerks were in attendanp, and they recorded the names of] the voters in specially prepared books, while almost as soon ' as the poll opened placards announcing the event were posted in the town. The decision of Mr. White regarding , the payment of rates appeared to bave taken by surprise ; everyone except Mr. Tunstall's supporters, who seemed to have been posted on the sabject, and consequently the voting was mostly in favour of Mr. Tunstall, whose agents were most assiduous in their efforts to bring the friends of that gentleman early to the poll. Early in the morning Mr. Tunstall circulated the following letter throughout the township:-- "A el y Bryn, Llandudno, October Ist, 1883 —Dear sir,— As a rule I avoid pledging myself to vote for any candidate in an election such as the present, but under all the circumstances, and knowing the way in which you have per- formed the duties of the office of assistant overseer, I had no hesitation in promising to vote for you. Unfortunately, I fear I have made a mistake. I thought the meeting would be on Thursday week, but I see by the paper it is to be this week, in which case I shall not be in Warrington. Mr. Green, no doubt, is a very suitable man for the office, but your claim is so strong, that I regret very much that he has been brought out.—Yours truly, JOHN RYLANDS." In the afternoon came a handbill addressed to the Liberals of War- rington, which stated :—" The arrangements which have been made for taking the poll are so disgracefully inadequate as practically to deprive the great bulk of the Liberal party from exercising their privileges. The poll is being taken at the Public Hall, Rvlands-street, and will be open up to seven o'clock this Thursday evening, and also from eight o'clock in the morning until seven o'clock to- morrow, Friday evening, at which hour it will close. Liberals vote at once for Mr. Green and thus defeat this most contemptible trick." At seven o'clock the poll was closed, and although there was no officiel =enlacement n! the result of the day's proceedings, certain figures were published giving Mr. Tunstall a majority of about 300. The cabs on Thursday were all engaged in the interests of Mr. Tunstall, but on Friday the friends of Mr. Green had recovered from their surprise, and worked with an evident intention to defeat the tactics by which they had been so unexpectedly taken abeet. Esperienaod ctaraQ.a.ara wora placed on their accustomed rounds, and conveyances were ' employed to bring the ratepayers favourable to Mr. Green's candidature to the polling booth. Voting was brisk from the time. the poll opened—eight o'clock—until afternoon. Cabs, wagonettes, 'buses, dzc., brought up loads of Mr. Green's supporters, and the vehicles employed by Mr. Tunstall were quite as active, the vicinity of the Public Hall, and the streets of the town generally, presenting a far more lively aspect than they have done during recent muni- cipal contests. The supporters of Mr. Green had been aroused by the following placard which appeared on the walls at an early hour: "Ratepayers of Warrington. Do not be robbed of your votes. An infamous 'dodge' has been resorted to in the hope that you will tamely Subrnit. Vote to-day (Fri- day) at the Public Hall for Mr. Green, and show the authors of this miserable .scheme that you are not to be treated with contamp'," As a set-off to this was the fol- lowing placard, which emanated from Mr. Tunetall's side : —" Electors of Warrington. Do not be 'gulled. The Liberal agent has obtained counsel's opinion; it is as fol- lows':—The whole prcceedings are perfectly in order and legal. Vote for Tunstall." On the cabs engaged by Mr. Tunstall was an invitation to the ratepayers to "Vote for Tunstall '-" and later on in the day the conveyances used by Mr. Green, which had hitherto borne no distinguishing mark, exhibited placards asking the ratepayers to " Vote for Green, the winning candidate." This asser- tion was confirmed by a great number of .ratepayers brought up by Mr. Green's conveyances, which were filled with voters throughout the day, and caused the friends of Mr. Tunstall to be less jubilant than they were on the pre- vious evening. The lull in the voting in tha afternoon was of 'heti deira- tion, and as the evening wore on the excitement of the rate- payers increased. Crowds of people congregated opposite the Public Hall, and made it difficult for the drivers of the vehicles to get near the entrance to the polling booth. In- side the booth after tea the scene was ode of the greatest excitement. The room was filled with Yot'ers, who had to fight their way to the tables to get their votes recorded so great was the crush of ratepayers, and strong policemen barred the doors to prevent any except those immediately concerned in the proceedings gaining access to the room, and also to regulate the number of voters in the place. At one time the throng was so great that the Town Clerk (Mr. W. H. Brook) with the assistance of a police-constable closed the doors, but Alderman Burgess promptly protested against this exclusion of voters. As the hour fixed for closing the poll approached, the scene became one of intense excitement and even con- fusion. THE CLOSING SCENE: AN EX tENSION OF THE

div.head: POLL REFUSED.
div.p: POLL REFUSED.

At twenty minutes to seven o'clock, there being present hundreds of people waiting to be polled, and having been informed by his committee that at least one-third of the constituency had not voted, Mr. Green applied to the Chairman to extend the polling another day.—The re- quest was at once declined.— Mr. Green: I should like to know the grounds of your refusal. The Chair- man: Legal grounds.— Mr. Green: Then I want to know what are the legal grounds. The Chairman: • I must refer you to my adviser. Mr. Alderman Burgess , (who was present): I ask you to say in my presence that this poll is refused.—The Chairman: It is.—Mr. Alderman Burgess: I ask you to repeat it, because it will be heard of at another day.—Mr. Green (to the Chairman) : I now appeal to you sir, whether you will prolong the poll later this evening ?—lhe Chairman: I cannot.—Mr. Green: ' Then I ask you, sir, if there are 100 people in this room at seven o'clock, shall yea close the poll ?—The Chairman : I shall if there are I,ooo.—Mr. Green: Then this action of yours is practically disfranchising at leest one-third of the ratepayers of this borough. I wish It te go forth to the public that 30 years ago, when a ieoll on the church rate was taken, three days was not considered ; too much to poll 25,000 inhabitants, bat where the popula- i tton of the borough is over 4,000 inhabitants a day-and-a- -! half is by you considered sufficient to poll then. I there- , fore protest against it in the name of the inhabitants of this borough.—Here the matter ended. Tee voters continued to be driven up to the poll in large dii numbers, and at seven o'clock it was evident that a great many had not been able to exercise their privileges. It was impossible with the accommodation crowde . into a corner of the room for the great number of ratepayers 1 who presented themselves to get near the poll clerks, and I it was marvellous how the stream of persons who had given in their names and were anxious to leave the room was maintained. At length the final moment arrived. The pre- siding overseer surveyed the assembly with a lively interest, pirtisans stood in groups in the room discussing the situa- tion, and the poll clerks were still beseiged with ! r ttepeyers desirous of recording their votes, when Alderman Kean said the time was up, and declared the poll closed. He announced that the counting of the votes will commence this morning at nine o'clock by gentlemen appointed for the purpose.
• „ Mr. Green then came forward, and in tha name of rate Payers of Vac township.who bad not voted protected o!-Iinst the clo3a of the poll. He believed that a day and a

div.head: TP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 183.
div.p: TP, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 6, 183.
DISTRICT NEWS. ASHTON.

NEW MAGISTRATE.—On Wednesday the name of Mr. Josiah Craskell, of Aslaton-in-Mackerfield, near Wigan, was inserted in the conniussion of the peace for the county of Lancaster. We would draw the attention of our readers to the lecture on "Protestantism," to be given by the Rev. Canon Taylor, D D., of Liverpool, in the Cave-Browne Protestant Institute, Heath-lane, Ashton, on Monday evening next. The lecture is sure to prove a very interestinc, and instruciive one. We hope there will be a large attendance. EARLESTOWN GOOD TEMPLARS AT ASHTON.—A pleasant gathering was held in the British School, Ashton, on Wed- nesday evening, when about 20 members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templars attended to give an entertainment, under the auspices of the Ashton Excelsior Lodge. Bro. Henry Warburton, W.C.T., of Earlestown presided. During the evening recitations were given by Bros. G. E. Warburton and Wm. Williams, readings by Bro. E. Newman and Bro. Barnett, and songs by Bros. W. Walker and J. Bassitt. Sisters Morris, Willis, and Pilling, of the Ashton lodge, also gave songs, which were vary much ap- preciated. The entertainment was a most enjoyable one, and at the close a vote of thanks was accorded to the Easlestown friends.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

GOLEORNE INDFZENDENT METHODIST CHAPEL. - The Independent Methodists of Golborne held their anniyersary services on Sunday last. The preacher, both afternoon and evening, was Mr. Matthew Kennedy, of Oldham, president rof the Connexion, The stun of £2O 2s. 7d. was realised • by the collections. FORMATION OF A BRANCH OF THE CHURCH TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—On Monday evening last a meeting was held in the Golborne Church School, tor the purpose of forming a local branch of the Church of England Temperance Society. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. C. T. Quirk, M.A., vicar of the parish. The Rev. J. N. Quirk, M.A., vicar of Rotheram (son of the respected and esteemed vicar of Golborne), was also present, and during the evening gave a most earnest and impressive address on the temperance cause. It was subsequently moved by Mr. R. Yates, and seconded by Dr. Mapei, that a local branch of the Church of England Temperance Seeiety should be forsied in Golborne. The motion was carried unanimously. The meeting concluded with a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman. BILLIARDS AT GOLEORNE.-At the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday, before Colonel McCorquodale, H. Houghton, and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqs., John Bent, of the GolbGrne Inn, Golborne, applied for a billiard license for his house.—ln reply to the clerk, he stated that his house was rated at £23, and he bad been in it since November last.

—Superintendent Weir: Why de you apply' for a billiard license, I suppose you think it will draw more people and give more facilities for gambling—The Applicant : I think there will be less.—The Superintendent: Is it not usual to play for something when they play at billiards ?—The Ap- plicant: Yes, so much a game.--The Superintendent : Is not that gambling 2—Colonel McCorquodale: I don't think he needs to answer the question about gambling. Is there nothing else against the man 2—Superintendent Welt: There is nothing else against him at all.—Colonel McCorquodale: It is a very innocent amusement, and affords good exercise for people.—Superintendent Weir: I grant that.—Colonel McCorquodale: The application is granted. ALLEGED POLLUTED WATER AT GOLBORNE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Satu-day, before R. Houghton and A. C. McCorquodale, Esqe., Mr. Moore (solicitor, War- rington), said he had an application to make, but unless another magistrate appeared he could not proceed with it. He appeared on behalf of the Golborne Parochial Com- mittee, who asked for an order to obtain a sample of water from a well on premises occupied by Mrs. Hareison. He believed Mr. Houghton was a member of the local authority, and declined to act as magistrate under the circumstances. —The Clerk said there was not the slightest chance of there being another magistrate there that day.—The Chairman (Mr. Houghton) said it was an unfortunate thing that Mr. Moore and his clients were present, as he had pre- viously stated it was improbable there would be Itwo magistrates in attendance, in addition to himself.—Mr ' Moore said he would not make the application that day.— Mr. Worsley (of Warrington) representing Mrs. Harrison, said it was to her a case of considerable hardship that she should be brought there time after time. It was the sixth time she had been brought to that court in connection with the case. Mr. Worsley added that the water had been analysed and declared to be good.—Mr. A. C. McCorquodale, J.P. : If the water is all right, why not hand a sample of it to Mr. Moore ?—Mr. Moore : That is all we want.—The Chairman: It is an unfortunate thing from beginning to end in my opinion.—Mr. Moore: I quite agree with you that it is. My friend won't even give me a drone( water. (Laugh- ter.)—The Chairman: Perhaps you would be glad of a drop of whisky with it. (Renewed laughter.)—Mr. Moore: I don't know; it just depends upon the taste.—The matter then dropped. A GOLZORNE MARRIED COUPLE IN TROUBLE; AN AMUsiNG CAM—Before R. Houghton and A. C. McCor- quodale, Esqs., at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Thomas Mains and Mary Mains, man and wife, were sum- moned for being drunk and disorderly at Golborne, on the 115th September.—The husband said: I am guilty of liaving two glasseS Of telier.—The Clerk: You are not charged with having a glass of beer, you are charged with beino, drunk and disorderly.—The husband: Well, I was not (frank.— The wife (pushing her husband) : Tha' was drunk. (Laughter.)—P.C. Whiting deposed that he saw the de- fendants drunk aud creating a disturbance, with a crowd of about 100 people running after them.—The husband: I'w3s going to my mother's when you turned me back. (Laugh- ter.)—The Clerk: He says you were drunk and disorderly. —The husband: My wife went to buy me a pair of breeches. (Loud laughter.) Did you see them stoning my wife down James-street P—The witness: No.—The husband: They did do. P.C. Ratcliffe corroborated the last witness's .. statement. The wife : I think be might have turned them all back agaiu.—The husband: Then I was going on the railroad.—The wife Th h nahin2 to do with it. (Laughter.)—The husband: They stoned me off the railroad, and I was not drunk then. Is that right, or is it not? There was none there to defend me, and they fol- lowed me to the door.—The Chairman: You should keep sober,—The defendant: I was not drunk then, please your honour. I don't get full of drink; I don't care much about drink, but I bad two glasses of beer. I will own to the truth. (Laughter.)—The wife said the crowd stoed her, and she thought the policemen ought to have turned the crowd back. She bad only had one gill of beer, and that made her drunk.—The Chairman: You should not have taken one gill of beer.—The Wife: It is the first time, and I hope it will be the last.—The husband: You wanted me to speak the truth, and I have done so.—The Chairman: You will be fined 5s and costs each. HAYDOCK.

BREACHES OF THE PEACE AT HAYDOCIE —For committing a breach of the peace, at Haydock, on the 13th September, John Walsh and James Topping were each bound over to keep the peace.—Ellen Ince, for whom Mr. Moore appeared, was summoned for using bad language to Harriet Littler, at Haydock, on the 22nd ult., and was bound over to keep the peace.—Mr. Moore also appeared for a Mrs. Burchall, who was summoned by Mrs. Littler (complainant hi the last case) for a similar offence. The defendant in this case was also bound over for her good behaviour. BRUTAL WIFE ASSAULT AT HAYDOCK.—Christopher Car- ney, a collier, residing at Haydock, was charged at the Newton Patty Sessions, on Saturday, with assaulting his wife Catherine the previous Tharsday.—Mr. Knowles ap- peared for the complainant, and Mr. Hain, of St. Helens, represented the defendant.—Mr. Knowles characterised the assault as a most brutal one, and said that during a period if 20 years the defendant had been in the habit of assaulting hie wife and then deserting her for a week or two, until the matter had blown over. It appeared that on the day in question she was seated on a chair in the house when her husband entered. Without any provocation he seized her by the hair of her head, dragged her to the floor, and kicked her several times on the back and sides. She got to the door, but he still continued his brutal and violent conduct, in consequence of which she went into a neighbour's house. He followed her there, and as she declined to leave at his request, he again seized her and severely struck her on the face, giving bar two black eyes, and rendering her insen- sible. In consequence of his repeated violent conduct, a separation order was asked for.—Mr. Hains opposed the ai:- plication, maintaining that the summons had been taken out under the wrong section.—The magistrates over-ruled the objection, however, and fined the defendant 40. and costs, in additien to granting a separation order, with an allow- ance of 12s. a week for the defendant's wife and her children.

div.head: HUTTON.
div.p: HUTTON.

lII.TYTON LITERARY AND SCIENTIFIC SOCIETY. The annual meeting was held in the reading-room of the Work- ing Men's Club, The Rev. W. T. Southward, M.A., pre- sided. It was resolved that the society be dissolyed, the attendance at the meeting not warranting its continuance. Only seven persons were present. RAINFORD.

THEFT AT A SLR—Ann Mills, a married woman, who lives at Rainiord, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions with having stolen two feather pillows, the property of Thomas Horrocks, an assistant to Messrs. Birchall and Son, auctioneers, St. Helens. On the 23rd ult. it seems there was a sale at Barton now, Rainford, at which both the prisoner and the prosecutor were present. The prosecutor bought the two pillows, which he left lying in a room, and the prisoner bought a box. Some time after the prisoner was carrying her purchase home, but was met by P.C. Dutton before she got there, who broke the box opt,n and found the pillows. The prisoner denied that she had known anything about the pillows being in her box, but it transpired that she had shown them toe person who,n ' aloe bed met on her way home. A fine of 103 was imposed. DANGEROUS ASSAULT WITH A HAMAIER.—Jas. McLaugh- lin, a young man, who lives at Itainford, was on Monday charged at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, with hay- , ing unlawfully wounded John Welsh.—Welsh said that he was a labourer, and lived at Hollyfold Farm, Bickerstafre. On Sunday afternoon he and a number of friends were sit- ting at the woodside, near itainford Junotiou, when be savr the prisoner and his brother coming running across a field. Prisoner had the hammer produced (a dangerous heavy looking instrument) in his hand, and he (prosecutor) asked him what he was going to do with the hammer. Prisoner replied that ho WAS going to strike them with it, and would let prosecutor have the that blow, and thereupon struck him a blow on the cheek, which Imrst a whole threugh.—On the application of Superintendent Johnston, a remand was granted till Monday.

DESTRUCTION OF AN HOTEL—The Grind Hotel at Giess- bach, near Brienz, has been totally destroyed by fire. There was no loss of life. THE ASIITON STRIKE : RESUMPTION OF WORK. The weavers who turned out again at Ashton-under-Lyne, on Thursday, held a m ,eting yesterday, and after explanations from their leaders, returned to work.

THE FRAUDS BY A BARRISTER'S CLERE.—At Biming- ham, yesterday, Benjamin Robert Danks, clerk to Mr. Jesse Herbert, barrister, was brought up on charges of forgery and embezzlement. Prisoner was committed to the assizes on the charges above mentioned. ANOTHER IRISH MEETING PROCLAIMED.—The Irish Government, in consequence of recent outrages in the dis- trict at Ennis, and the probability of disturbances, has pro- hibited the holding of the 'National League meeting announced to be held at Ennis to-morrow (Sunday). At Rochdale, yesterday afternoon, a man named Samuel Barker, living in Jermyn-street, cut his wife's throat with a razor. The woman lies in a dangerous condition, and Barker is in custbdy. When arrested he was apparently suffering from delirium tremens. FATAL ACCIDENT TO A CREWE DOCTOR.—Mr. Hughes, surgeon, of Crewe, wno was thrown out of his trap by the horse takingiright on Tuesday.morning last, died at noon yesterday from the terrible injuries he received. He never regained consciousness after the accident. Deceased was medical officer for the Crewe district under the Nantwich Beard of Guardians, and was very popular. The Central News learns that Mr. Bright has written a letter on the marriage laws to a well known clergyman, in which he says convocation only talks and cannot act. The bishops can advise the clergy or bishops, and the clergy bannot roll back the tide of opinion on the question now under discussion, and we must wait a little longer and the matter will be settled. EARLS DALHOUSIN AND CADIPERDOWN AT DUNDEE.— Yesterday Earls Dalhousie and Catnperdown were presented with the freedom of Dundee. The ceremony took place in the Albert Hall, in the presence of a large assemblage. The freedom of the borough would also have been conferred on Lord Roseberry had that nobleman been at home, but the ceremony had been postponed till he returns from abroad. DAVITT'S VOTE —ln the City of Dublin ReViBlOEl Court, yesterday, before Mr. MaeDermott, Q.C.. the Con- sevatives asked to have the name of Mr. Michael Davitt, who has been admitted to the franchise in respect of the National League premises in Sackville-street, erased from the list on the ground that he had been convicted of trea- son-felony. Mr. Macpermott refused to grant the applica- tion. The decision was greeted with applause. At the Poor Law Conference, in Manchester yesterday, Mr. Hibbert, M P., called attention to the decrease in 1 pauperism, and said he believed it was owing to the spread

Of habits of temperance amongst the people. The revenue had been affected thereby to a serious extent, but if it also decreased the cost of the poor law system it would add materially to the prosperity of the c,untry. THE MINER.'S CONFERENCE concluded at Manchester yesterday. Resolutions were passed authorising district lodges to present notices for an advance of wages by the 25th inst., and urging delegates to present reports to the next conference, and be prepared to say then whether if em- ployerg refused the advaPcep N9tieel to dp,aso wQrls" *119414 be given, and on what date a strike should commetice. Al! districts were invited to join in the movement, and it was decided that next conference should be held in Manchester on the 13th Inst.

THE SLAVE TRADE IN Aratca. The Foreign Office haring applied to the Admiralty for the services of Capt. C. E. Foot, R.N., the Central News understands that officer has been granted leave for two years, and is to be appointed consul in the Nyasica and other lake districts for the pur- pose of suppressing the slave trade and assisting in the de- velopment of civilisation and commerce in Central Africa. The Central News also understands Commander C. S. Gis- sing, R.N., will be appointed vice-consul, to act as Captain Foot's assistant.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS

he fortnightly meeting of this Board was held in the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday morning, Mr. W. Tvrer presiding. There were also present Messrs. J. Fidler, T. S idler, W. Gerrard, J. T. Hall, E. Syder, W. Birchall, J. Jackson, J. S. Buckley, J. Lowe, H. Hulme, R. Leigh, J. Griffith, T. F. Hill, T. Dobell, J. Leatherbarrow, W. Swift, W. Newsome, J..Kenwright, S. Marsh, W. A. Meadows, P. Longton, James Fisher, T. Gilbody, the Revs. J. Barnacle, F. Finegan, and T. Chambers; and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).
BUSTER'S REPORT.

The Workhouse Master reported that there were 414 in- mates in the Workhouse this week, as against 416 last week, and 467 in the corresponding week of last year. There ware 167 children in the Kirkland schools. The number of vagrants relieved during the past week was 52, as com- pared with 148 in the corresponding week of last year.

div.head: ACCOMMODATION FOR INFECTIOUS CASES.
div.p: ACCOMMODATION FOR INFECTIOUS CASES.

A. letter was read from the Local Government Board, in answer to Mr. Hartley's communications respecting the pro- posed additional accommodation in the workhouse for cases of an infectious nature. The Local Government Board stated that they would instruct one of their medical lfficers and their architect to attend a conference with the Guar- dians. They would, however, again communicate with the Board on the subject.

div.head: EXPENSES OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: THE EXPENSES OF GUARDIANS.

Another communication was received from the Local Government Board with respect to the appointment of Guar- dians to attend Poor Law Conf6rence, &c and as to their expenses. The Board limited the number Of guardians to be appointed to attend mference to three, and in case of central conferences in London only one would be allowed The expenses allowed would be 7s. 6d. per day when not absent at night, and 15s. when absent at night, exclusive of travelling expenses. Till COST OF DRUGS, &C. Mr. HARTLEY said that the Local Government Board intimated that they had paid 324 4s. 9d. to the credit of the Guardians in respect of their moiety of the salaries of the medical officers and the cost of drugs, &c., during the half-year ending March 29th, 1883.

div.head: .IkIALL PDX LT WIT)VV.S.
div.p: .IkIALL PDX LT WIT)VV.S.

A letter was read from the clerk to the Widnes Local Board with reference to two cases 61 email-pox at that place which the relieving officer had informed the Local Board could not be taken to the workhouse hos- pital, but which the Health Committee of the Bard thought ought to have been taken there. The relieving officer, it was understood, held that unless the patient was a pauper, in actual receipt of relief at the time of taking the disease the case could not be sent to the hospital. He (the clerk) would be obliged if the Guardians would inform him what was the rule,—Nr, TIALL proposed that the Widnes Board of Health should be informed that they must provide accommodation for their own patients, and this motion, after a short discussion, was carried.

div.head: ALLEGED SCANDAL AT THE WORKHOUSE,
div.p: THE ALLEGED SCANDAL AT THE WORKHOUSE,

The Vigiting Committee reported that they had inquired into the matter of the alleged scandal in the hospital, re- ported to last meeting, and were satisfied that no baeach of discipline or immorality had taken place, and that no blame whatever attached to any of the officers.

div.head: INCREASE OF SALARY.
div.p: INCREASE OF SALARY.
The Finance Committee recommended that relleving,, offic.r Bullock's salary should be increased from £lOO to £l2O per annum —Adopted.

div.head: LOB. DERBY AND HIS EMPLOYES.
div.p: LOB. DERBY AND HIS EMPLOYES.

Mr. FISHER said that a statement was made there at last meeting with reference to Lord Derby and one of his ser- ' 'rants, a woman who was said to be a lodge-keeper, and in receipt of relief. That might be so, but it had come to his knowledge that neither this widow or her late husband ever was a servant of Lord Derby or his father. The gentleman who made that statement he knew very well, and was sere I would be the first to c3rrect it if be had been misinformed. 1 It certainly ought to be corrected so as not to lead the pub- tic to believe the statement.—Mr. NEWSOME, who had trade the statement, asked that the relieving officer should he called in. The statement he made he took from the printed record of their own Union. Before any dieeussion took I place they should know upoa what ground they I proceeded. They were not going to have a discussion propped up unawares —Mr. FIDLER: He cannot say it is unawares, because this is the first opportunity I have bad of bringing it before the Board again.—The CHAIRMAN then ' read the entry in the relief book relating to the Case The woman's name was Ann Challoner, and she was described as living at Paddock Ledge, resident in the district 70 years, and of the occupation of a lodge-keeper to Earl Derby. She was living rent free, and in receipt of relief for poverty.— Mr. NEWSOME: On the ground of that statement in your books I founded my statement. She is down in your books as a lodge-keeper at Knowsley, and I ask for inquiries to be made.—Mr. SYDER said the woman's husband got the lodge to live in, but was now dead. On his death she was desired I to go into the almshouses provided by Lord Derby for such I old people, but as removing from the house would have caused her great grief, Lord Derby in his kindness said he I would let her stop. She was scarcely able to go out, and her remaining in the house was a disadvantage to Lord Derby and everybody else that went through the ga'e Lord Derby of course had nothing to do with the ' case. In her time he (Lord Derby) had opened an in- : swance for her and her husband and all his employ4ii, and sail if they put down one shilling he would put another against it to provide for their old age. It appeared, how- ever, that her husband or her had not taken advantage of this opportunity of providing for themselves, and she had ! consequently become a charge on the union. He (Mr. 1 Leeler) could not see what charge there was in the world 1 against Lord Derby, who was one of the kindest of land- lords, and kind to his servants and everybody about hlm.— Mr. CuaeinEus said he was surprised to read the remarks of Mr. Newseme at last meeting. Lord Derby had a perfect right to allow this woman to receive relief from the rates, to which he was so large a contributor. Did it fdlow that bemuse he allowed a poor Woman an asylum for life, he mast also supply her with 4s. or ss. per week to keep herself?—Mr. HALL explained that the woman had never applied for relief herself, but that her case was brought under the notice of the relieving officer by Mr. Bolton, the curate at Knowsley. Besides, the woman's hus- band had only been employed by a Mr. Forshaw, who was one of Lord Derby's employes.—The CHAIRMAN said he did not know whether Mr. Newsome had exceeded his duty in bringing the matter before the Guardians, but be thought he had exceeded his discretion in doing so. Lord Derby was not either legally or morally bound to maintain the woman, an ! the matter could only be brought forward to c3sl' a reflection on Lord Derby.—Mr. NEWSOME said it was wonderful how strongly a nomber of gentlemen took up the cudgels on behalf of Lord Derby. If it bad been a menu- f icturer in the district, or a farmer, they would not have been so ready.—Mr. PARKINSON, relieving officer, was called ii', and said the woman told him she Was lodge-keeper to Lord Derby.—The CHAIRMAN asked how many persons went through the gates.—Mr. PauxeNsoN thought there would net be more than two or three in a week.—Mr. JACK- :4)N suggeeted that the case be taken out of the books altogether. The Knowsley Guardians ought not to have put it on.—The CHAIRMAN thought, however, that it would be better not to do anything at present, and the matter then dropped.—This concluded the business.

div.head: WARRING-ToN RURAL SANITARY ALTITORITY.
div.p: WARRING-ToN RURAL SANITARY ALTITORITY.

Yesterday, the monthly meeting of this Autlioilie :22 held at the Workhouse. Present—Messrs. W. Darb:vshire (chairman), N. Houghton, W. Gibson, J. Houghton, R. Kilshall, J. Swinton, R. Owen, S. Sutton (deputy clerk). R. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and G. Rawlings (inspector).—rital Statistics The MEDICiL OFFICER reported that during the month ending September 30th, there had been 28 births and 5 deaths in Ihe district. The excess of births over deaths was 23. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 41 per thousand, against 16.3 in the corresponding month of last year. The health of the district was exceptionally good, and he had no deaths to report from zymotic diseases.—The Removal of Refuse : A letter was read from the Lec it Government Board with reference to the removal of excrement and refuse, and stated that it seemed to the Board that the present system con- stituted a serious danger to the health of the inhabitants, and the Board were of opinion that the Authority should no longer hesitate to adopt the advice conveyed to them in the Board's letter of the 22nd June, 1881, viz., to undertake the removal of excrement, &c., in their district by their own officers at frequent and regular intervals.— The MEDICAL OFFICER in his report recommended that an extra amount of vigilance on the part of the inspector be placed on the contractor, and in case he failed to comply readily and strictly to the words of his contract then, he thought, the Authority ought to take immediate steps to remove him and have some one else, or as suggested by the Local Government Board, have the work done by their own official.—The Authority approved the medical officer's suggestion, and directed the clerk to inform the Local Government Board that the work was now done satisfac- torily.—Mr. NEWTON, the contractor, attended the meeting, land stated that in consequence of the increase in the num- kr of houses in the district he was losing money on his contract, and wished the Authority to reconsider the matter. —The consideration of the application was adjourned.— Longford Depot: Dr. SEPIITON, reporting as to the works of the Corporation of Warrington for the deapatch of excreta, &c, said he had visited the works, and found a great enisance, which proceeded in a great measure from the burn- ing of animal and vegetable refuse, as well as from some escaped gases whidh passed through the furnace. He must say that the Corporation were doing all in their power, and with the beet means at their disposal, to mitigate the nuisance from this disagreeable work. Another and most intolerable nuisance connected with these works were the vans which were almost constantly passing through this portion of the Authority's district. He did think the Cor- poration ought to resttict the time and leave some portion of the day free from this great nuisance. He was afraid that in case of infectious diseases this was one certain means of sowing the disease broadcast.—Penketh Drainage: The SURVEYOR reported at length on this subject. The means that could he adopted to render the drainage effectual and to leave the brook unpolluted would be a system of sewers laid to receive all sewage matter from the houses and convey it to the river direct. He paw two difficulties in this, which could only be overcome at considerable expense —the first, that the sewer would have to be caeried under the London and North-Western Railway and canal; and the second, that it was not at all unlikely the Local Govern- ment Board would require the Authority to deal with the sewage by filtration or precipitation before emptying it into the river, which would necessitate the purchase of land varying in extent, according to tine process to be applied. Prebably the cost would reach £1,300, without adding for carrying under railway and canal, or for any works for de 'ling with the sewage before it was turned into the river. —'rho consideration Of the subject was deferred until next m ting.—Latchford Drainage: The SURVEYOR reported th the plans for this drainage will be laid before the Pay- in and Sewerage Committee of the Corporation of Warring- te,i on Monday next by the Borough Surveyor, who wrote hi e that he saw no objection to them from a,n engineering 'IA of view,—This was all the busiceas.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers, 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Oct. 4th):— Tnough at the commencement of the week under notice the markets bid fair to have a brisk record the anticipation has not been realised; prominent securities being adversely affected by the untoward events at the reception of the Spanish King in Paris, and the inclement weather helped also by poor returns of railway earnings. Foreign funds, though Spanish and Argon- tineipublic work e thibit some advance, are on the whole weaker, foremost being Mexican 3 per cent., which though above lowest are 15 8 down on the week. Egyptian unified are 4 and Daira Sanich 1, Italian 1, Turkish stamped 1 to 1. and Russian lower. The transactions in the several series of miscellaneous shares show a pretty good aggregate and after banks. Coal, Iron, &s., and mining have come in for the greatest proportion- ate share of the business passing, the latter showing stronger than for some little time past. Mexican rails show a remewed fall compared with last week's prices, but to-day's figures at close are distinctly in advance of the lowest of the week. Stand- ing last week at 8314 they have be forced down to 75 on re- duced traffic return, they have however rolled to over 77, at which price they stand this evening. COAL, IRON, ,ke., AND MlNlNG.—Compared with a long time past the week's business is very good, and some shares that have recently been weakening have had a rally. Bolchows and Ebbw Vales most particularly. Higher: Bolchows fully paid,, ditto £l2 paid 1, Ebbw Vale Steelte 7-16 to 9-16, Great Laxey Lead Mine', and Indian Glenr ,ck Gold 1-16. half was not sufficient time to take the votes of the rate- payers. He had asked Alderman Kean if he would extend the time. The presiding overseer said he was told by the legal adviser of the ovei seers that he could not extend the time. Mr. Green said having heard that he protested against the close of the poll. He said a day and a half was altogether inadequate in which to record the number of votes that eould have been given had the rate- payers known a poll was being taken.—On the proposition of Mr. Tunstall, seconded by Mr. Green, a vote of thanks was accorded to Alderman Kean for presitliog, and the Alderman in acknowledging the compliment remarked that , he had been chairman of the Overseers for about 13 years, and he never yet had been charged with being impartial. It had given him great pleasure to learn that his conduct had given satisfaction, and he hoped that he would be as impartial in the future as he had been in the past. The proceedings then terminated. . MEETING OF MR. GREEN'S SUPPORTERS. Soon after the poll closed, the supporters of Mr. Green I flocked to the Co-operative Hall, where a meeting was held to express indignation at the way in which the election had been carried on. Amongst those present were :—Alderman Burgess, Councillor Monks, Mr. Green (the candidate), Mr. H. Roberts, Mr. W. Roberts, Mr. Barlow,. and many o'hers. The following resolution was ppt and carried unani- mously :—" This meeting is of opinion that a large number of the ratepayers of the township of Warrington have had no knowledge of the fact of a poll being taken yesterday and to-day for the election of an assistant overseer, owing to the same having ben insufficiently published; and does further express its indignation at the utter inadequacy of the arrangements for taking the sad poll; and is of opinion that the whole thing bas been part of a deeply-laid scheme, I originated and carried out for the purpose of depriving the 1 majority of the ratepayers of the township from exercising i their undoubted privilege." -

letter tet the Clam Sir,—Will you allow me through the columns of your valuable paper to ask a question ' and offer ; a few sugges- tions? The question is, "Can any one inform me what dictionary Doctor Pompous uses to get his definition of the word 'neutral ' from, when in the present affair he puffs one candidate up and never mentions the other ? " The suggestions are: That I would advise Alderman Harrison before he makes another splendid and most vindictive oration to make use of one or other of many assurance companies in town for fear of an apoplectic seizure. The next is: That the Tory party should build a technical college and appoint Mr. Tunstall president of same, for surely his born talents will be wasted in such a paltry office as assistant overseer. The next one is : That all true Liberals should note the threat levelled at Mr- Green, and. couched in such beautiful language by J. Davies. Esq., that if he contested the appointment it would spoil his future, which means no work from Tories for Mr. Green, I buppose. Let the Liberals see to it that it is not so, and so spoil the prediction of the would-be prophet.—l am, sir, yours-, drc., A WEST COUNTRY BOY.
